detail.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted higher education globally, revealing both traditional pedagogies' strengths and weaknesses. As institutions turned to online learning, significant gaps in accessibility, digital literacy, and adaptability became apparent. This paper argues for a radical transformation of pedagogical innovation in post-pandemic higher education, advocating for a shift towards more flexible, inclusive, and student-centred learning models to bring the sustainable change we all want. It highlights key strategies, such as hybrid models, personalized learning, active and experiential learning, and rethinking assessment methods. These innovations, supported by digital tools, can better address diverse student needs and prepare learners for a rapidly evolving workforce. Nevertheless, institutional resistance to change, addressing the digital divide, and ensuring scalability remain potential barriers and challenges that must be overcome to achieve it. This paper, therefore, calls for collective and coordinated efforts by higher education institutions, stakeholders and policymakers to drive the required systemic change in higher education. By embracing these innovations, universities can build a more flexible, resilient, equitable, and future-ready education system that moves beyond the limitations of traditional pedagogies. The pandemic offers a unique opportunity to rethink the foundations of higher education and prioritize pedagogical practices that promote critical thinking, adaptability, and lifelong learning in an uncertain world.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how judgment authority becomes difficult to locate in AI-augmented organizations. As artificial intelligence systems increasingly participate in institutional decision-making-recommending, classifying, prioritizing, approving, rejecting, and acting-the right to decide migrates from formal organizational structures into system configuration: thresholds, routing rules, defaults, and workflows. The prevailing instruments of AI governance address system properties and outputs but leave unanswered who, within the organization, holds legitimate decision authority. Through analysis of implicit authority, the paper identifies three recurring patterns across AI-augmented organizations: (1) Authority Allocation Gaps, (2) Escalation Gaps, and (3) Accountability Continuity Gaps. These constitute the paper's primary findings. The observed dynamics can be interpreted as failures of institutional boundary formation-a reading for which the construct of Governance Decision Boundaries may serve as an analytical lens. The paper considers implications across government, financial services, healthcare, and agentic systems, and suggests that AI governance may be understood, at least in part, as an authority allocation problem. All conceptual development, analytical interpretation, argumentation, and final editorial decisions were made by the author.

title: Inference with AI-Generated Covariates
affiliations: Stanford University - Department of Management Science & Engineering and Stanford University - Department of Management Science & Engineering

detail.title: Inference with AI-Generated Covariates
detail.abstract: Empirical researchers increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to extract structured features, such as sentiment scores, classifications, and expectations, from unstructured data and treat these generated features as observed covariates in downstream estimation. This practice can invalidate inference when systematic, input-dependent errors in generated features, such as hallucination and look-ahead bias, distort the downstream moment conditions. Even after these moment-level distortions are corrected, generated features remain noisy proxies for the latent truth, with error profiles that differ across models and prompts. We introduce AI-Powered Inference (AI-PI), a method-of-moments framework that delivers valid and efficient inference by combining three components: (i) a moment-specific bias correction based on a small human-labeled calibration set; (ii) adaptive weights that optimally combine multiple model-prompt pairs, downweighting unreliable generators and exploiting complementary information across generated features; and (iii) an optimal calibration-set design that concentrates costly human labels on the observations where the generated features are least reliable. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the AI-PI estimator, allowing for non-random and data-adaptive labeling designs, cross-fitted LLM-pipeline tuning, and overidentified GMM. Simulations confirm that AI-PI delivers substantial gains over naive LLM regressions and over debiasing without optimal weighting or labeling design. In an empirical study of news-based sentiment and stock returns, AI-PI produces stable conclusions in a setting where naive analyses vary substantially across LLM and prompt choices, and its confidence interval is roughly half the length of the interval that uses the human-labeled data alone.

detail.abstract: "Your Honor, I understand what you're saying. I really do. But workers have always been protected in Massachusetts. On the upcoming 250th anniversary of the birth of this nation, to dismiss this case now would be premature." These were the last words I uttered as I stood before the judge in the Massachusetts Superior Court on a somber February afternoon this year. The case had begun almost a year earlier after I brought a former employer to court over the repeated late payment of wages despite my good-faith attempts to resolve the issue in-house. During that time, Massachusetts enacted legislation backed by Governor Maura Healey that granted colleges and certain nonprofit organizations temporary immunity from some employment-related claims arising during the pandemic. My concern was that the legislation, while well-intentioned in its effort to protect institutions during an unprecedented crisis, was now, in the post-pandemic era, being interpreted in ways that risked weakening long-standing worker protections. That afternoon stayed with me because it raised a larger question that extends well beyond one courtroom or one employment dispute. If democratic institutions can struggle to uphold the American civic values on which they were founded, what happens as governments increasingly rely on artificial intelligence to shape public decisions? And furthermore, if we cannot sustain trust in our own civic institutions, how can we expect to build the global cooperation needed to solve the defining challenges of the twenty-first century? In an increasingly fragmented and algorithmic world, we must begin to revisit the foundations of civilization to ensure that the principles which gave rise to decent society remain programmed into those very systems and institutions on which humanity has depended for security, stability and to solve the wicked problems of our times when they arise. This paper examines those civic fundamentals and the possibilities of the way forward.

detail.abstract: This study aims to investigate the strategies employed by lecturers to navigate the challenges of teaching during the COVID-19 pandemic in higher education institutions in Algeria and around the globe. It focuses on the actions, good practices, reactions, and measures adopted by lecturers to address the challenges posed by the pandemic. The main question explores how Algerian lecturers dealt with this crisis compared with other global experiences. This study is based on two surveys conducted in 2020 and 2021: a quantitative survey of Algerian lecturers and a qualitative comparative survey involving lecturers from various countries. The quantitative study assesses the experiences and perception of Algerian lecturers, while the qualitative study, conducted through an interview guide, explores and contrasts the experiences of lecturers from different countries in response to the pandemic. The findings reveal that Algeria, along with other countries, swiftly adopted online teaching in response to the crisis, transitioning from entirely online to a hybrid mode of teaching. Despite initial challenges, many Algerian lecturers demonstrated adaptability and resilience in navigating this new mode of teaching. However, the study underscores the need for ongoing support and training programs to equip lecturers with proficiency in using digital tools. Additionally, it highlights the increasing prominence of online teaching as a main method of courses delivery, suggesting its potential as a sustainable solution to accommodate the anticipated increase in student enrolment.

detail.abstract: This independent strategic report evaluates the intersections of digital media, brand advocacy, and communication architecture through a comprehensive case analysis of the global brand TOMS. Utilizing corporate transitions in social impact, specifically the shift by TOMS toward mental health advocacy, this paper models a hypothetical, original content marketing campaign titled "Walk in Others' Shoes." The strategic framework operationalizes three core communication paradigms to optimize audience engagement and campaign metrics. These include Co-creation Theory, which examines how brands and consumers collaboratively generate narrative value; User Participation Frameworks, which outline the structural design for driving active digital consumer engagement; and Social Influence Theory, which analyses peer-to-peer narrative distribution in hybrid digital spaces. Ultimately, the report provides detailed consumer journey maps, key performance indicator architectures, and data-driven content distribution plans. By bridging advanced communication theories with practical brand strategy, this paper serves as an open-access resource demonstrating how corporate entities can structure authentic digital advocacy to drive both social impact and brand equity.

title: The Doubt Advantage: How AI Inverts the Certainty Penalty

detail.title: The Doubt Advantage: How AI Inverts the Certainty Penalty

detail.abstract:
Traditional institutions systematically disadvantage individuals with the highest metacognitive awareness: those who recognise complexity, tolerate uncertainty, and doubt their own conclusions. This paper argues that what presents as underperformance in capable individuals is not a deficit but a rational response to a certainty reward structure that privileges visible confidence over genuine understanding. Drawing on the Dunning-Kruger effect, impostor syndrome research, and the psychology of introversion, the paper diagnoses a certainty penalty that operates across education, professional life, and organisations. 

The paper then proposes a mechanism for inversion: artificial intelligence, used as a private, nonjudgmental cognitive partner. Three features of AI interaction-privacy, asymmetry, and the absence of social cost-remove the conditions that sustain the certainty penalty. Private hypothesis testing, lowstakes exploration, and iterative questioning transform the penalty into possibility. 

Individuals whose cognitive profile-metacognitive awareness, intellectual humility, and reflective temperament-may be adversely affected by the certainty reward structure are, under conditions of AI augmentation, particularly well-positioned to thrive-and the doubt that institutions have treated as a liability proves to be a protection against AI misuse.

detail.title: Technological Transformation of Treasury Operations:Opportunities and Challenges for Hong Kong as Asia's Global Treasury Management Centre
detail.abstract:
This report focuses on two aspects of global treasury operations and treasury management: first, the continuing evolution of treasury functions and operations, with a focus on technological transformations across finance; and second, evolving locational and market dynamics, with a focus on the Asia Pacific (APAC) region.  

While financial centres are central to treasury operations and treasury operations are a core financial centre function, this is an area that is often given far less attention than higher-profile activities such as capital raising, derivatives trading, lending and cross-border payments. At the same time, corporate and institutional treasurers and treasury operations are central users of these higher-profile systems. Treasury management is thus a core function of a financial centre, and financial centres are the main locations for treasury managers.

This context brings particular opportunities for Hong Kong as one of the leading financial centres both regionally and globally. The APAC region has experienced and continues to experience growth and increases in GDP across much of the region as well as significant increases in the number of listed firms. This combination is particularly significant, as more firms operate in and across the region. Operations across the region drive increased need for cross-border treasury management, while the growing number of firms increases the volume of treasury operations that must be managed.

detail.abstract: Stock-price forecasting remains a notoriously difficult problem owing to the high volatility, non-stationarity and long-range temporal dependencies exhibited by financial time series. This study proposes a hybrid model that embeds Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) into a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network denoted PSO-LSTM, to forecast daily closing prices of the CSI 300 Index in the Chinese A-share market. We first apply five-fold time-series cross-validation on the training set to optimize hyperparameters; the best configuration is then retrained on the full training set and evaluated on an independent 20% test split. PSO automatically tunes the LSTM's learning rate, hidden-layer width, batch size and the maximum training epochs (with early stopping) by minimizing validation mean-squared error (MSE). Relative to a conventionally tuned LSTM, PSO-LSTM lowers test-set errors from MSE 2462.5 to 1897.2 (-22.9 %), RMSE 49.62 to 43.56 (-12.2 %), MAE 37.94 to 28.53 (-24.8 %), and MAPE 1.04 % to 0.77 % (-25.4 %), while raising the coefficient of determination R² from 0.9646 to 0.9727 (+0.8 %). We further benchmark PSO-LSTM against nine widely used learners under identical data splits and feature sets. PSO-LSTM outperforms every alternative on all five error metrics. These findings demonstrate that PSO provides an efficient, fully automated alternative to manual hyper-parameter tuning, enabling LSTM models to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy for stockprice forecasting in volatile emerging markets.

detail.abstract: Cryptography and accounting have grown up alongside each other for more than five centuries without developing their similarities in dialogue. This extended concept note outlines a vision for a crossdisciplinary research programme integrating six philosophical dimensions: ontological, epistemological, axiological, teleological, praxiological and phenomenological. It explicates only the structural (ontological) dimension in detail, arguing that asymmetric verifiability (whereby the cost of engineering a false acceptance is deliberately set to exceed the cost of verifying a true one) is foundational to both disciplines: in cryptography to one-way functions, digital signatures and zero-knowledge proofs, and in accounting to conservatism in the Basu (1997) and Watts (2003) tradition. The remaining five dimensions are stated concisely and anchored to established literature on each side, with the lived practice of each craft identified as the least studied and the clearest opening for joint work, particularly in the context of post-quantum cryptography (PQC). The present contribution is the naming of the six-dimension structure rather than local novelty within any single dimension; prior scholarship has already placed Alberti’s cryptography and Pacioli’s bookkeeping within a common Renaissance tradition addressing trust at a distance. The note develops a role-to-treatment taxonomy and worked ledger illustrations (a TLS certificate issuance and two distinct quantum exposures: harvest-now-decrypt-later and trust-now-forge-later), and closes with a call for collaboration between cybersecurity and accounting researchers.

detail.abstract: We revisit the employer size wage effect (ESWE)—arguably the most basic and influen tial departure from the law of one price for labor. Our main result is that this canonical fact disappears completely across establishments within the same firm, even though they operate in different local labor markets. We uncover and dissect this fact by including a firm fixed effect in otherwise standard cross-sectional regressions of wages on establishment size. We implement this demanding specification in population-wide triple-linked firm establishment-employee data in Germany. This result is new to the ESWE literature (for which our paper also provides the first systematic meta-analysis). This wage-size decou pling is hard to square with the view that employment is determined along a finitely elastic employer-specific labor supply curve—i.e., employers pay exactly the minimum needed for the quantity of labor, but no more—the foundation of the monopsony view. By contrast, large multi-establishment firms (MEF) appear to hire off their labor supply curves (or those curves are very elastic), pay wage premia above the monopsonistic minimum, and leave excess labor supply. We find some evidence for a reemergence of the ESWE within low premium MEFs. Overall, at least for the 25% of German employment in large firms for which the ESWE disappears, wage setting and employment determination may be better accounted for by alternative models, namely accommodating above-market-clearing wage premia and rationing of labor supply, such as efficiency wage theories.

title: Hurricane Disruption Costs in Global Supply Chains: Lead Time Uncertainty and the Value of Visibility
affiliations: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics,  and The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - CUHK Business School

detail.title: Hurricane Disruption Costs in Global Supply Chains: Lead Time Uncertainty and the Value of Visibility
detail.abstract: Hurricane-induced port disruptions shift not only the expected length of maritime lead times but also their dispersion, creating distinct operational costs that no single resilience lever can fully hedge. Exploiting realtime Automatic Identification System (AIS) vessel trajectories matched to transaction-level U.S. import billof-lading (BoL) and Compustat financials, we construct a shipment-to-balance-sheet panel linking individual container arrivals to firm financial outcomes. We show that hurricanes prolong port-to-port transit times by 7-10% and significantly widen their dispersion. Each additional day of lead-time delay reduces quarterly ROA by 6.5% and net profit margins by 10.5%, with effects concentrated in the depletion of raw-material inventories. We then develop and calibrate a structural (s, S) inventory model to decompose disruption costs into distinct channels: the calibration implies an average cost of $137.6 million per firm-quarter (3.55% of quarterly sales), with 66.3% attributable to mean-shift delays and 29.7% to dispersion shifts. These findings reframe the classic safety-stock calculus: inventory buffers absorb much of the predictable mean component, whereas real-time shipment visibility complements inventory by resolving the residual uncertainty component that static buffers cannot fully target. Under intensifying climate uncertainty, operational resilience therefore requires both pre-positioned inventory and information systems, with the latter most valuable for firms facing routine hurricane exposure.

title: From Scenario to Cadence: Predictive Planning as a Continuous, AI-Enabled Strategic Discipline
affiliations: Colorado State University

detail.title: From Scenario to Cadence: Predictive Planning as a Continuous, AI-Enabled Strategic Discipline
detail.abstract: Scenario planning and strategic foresight were built for a world in which analytical work — scanning the environment, constructing plausible futures, stress-testing strategy — was slow, expert-dependent, and expensive. Generative artificial intelligence has collapsed the marginal cost and latency of exactly those tasks, yet the methodology of organizational foresight remains episodic and calendar-bound, and the term now entering the executive vocabulary to name the shift — "predictive planning" — circulates as enterprise-software marketing and operations-research jargon with no strategic-management theory behind it. This paper defines predictive planning as a leadership discipline: the continuous conversion of weak signals into staked strategic decisions, using AI to decide faster than the operating environment changes. We argue that when the cost of foresight approaches zero, the binding constraint on strategy shifts from analytical quality to planning cadence and decision commitment — a shift captured by an asymmetry test comparing an organization's decision-cycle time to its environment's rate of change, and one that reframes the unit of analysis from the scenario to the loop. We formalize the discipline as a four-phase continuous cycle — Scan, Story, Stake, Steer — specify the division of labor between AI and human judgment, position it as a continuous operationalization of dynamic-capabilities microfoundations, and advance seven propositions with explicit boundary conditions, including the enduring limits of prediction under radical uncertainty. The paper contributes a construct, a process model, and a testable research agenda.

title: Optimal Batching and Pricing for Power Grid Interconnection Queues
affiliations: Stanford Graduate School of Business, Stanford University and Stanford Graduate School of Business

detail.title: Optimal Batching and Pricing for Power Grid Interconnection Queues
detail.abstract: Severe congestion in U.S. power grid interconnection queues has slowed the deployment of new generation. Recent operational reforms propose cluster studies and higher financial deposits to improve throughput, yet operational trade-offs remain unclear. We develop a queueing model that captures these levers by modeling cluster studies as batch service with economies of scale and financial deposits as admission prices that regulate both entry and project retention. A key feature of the model is a batch-level feedback mechanism. If any project in a cluster withdraws after a study, changes in network impacts and cost allocations force the remaining projects to be re-evaluated, generating endogenous rework. We analyze the system using a fluid approximation and show that it arises as a bona fide limit of the stochastic model under an appropriate scaling and yields asymptotically optimal batching and pricing decisions. The fluid analysis shows that batching alone improves throughput primarily in heavily overloaded systems, but can be counterproductive, even when the system is overloaded, if withdrawal-induced rework dominates economies of scale. Moreover, pricing can either complement or substitute for batching depending on system load, but in heavily congested regimes, it always complements rather than substitutes for batching, which strengthens the effectiveness of larger clusters. A case study calibrated to PJM, the largest regional transmission organization in the U.S., shows that batching alone increases throughput by up to 30% in highly congested stages, while jointly optimizing batching and pricing delivers additional gains exceeding 25% relative to batching alone in plausible regimes.

title: Xbox Game Pass: A Strategic Marketing Analysis
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Xbox Game Pass: A Strategic Marketing Analysis
detail.abstract: This research paper analyzes Microsoft's Xbox Game Pass subscription service as a transformative case study in modern marketing management. The analysis examines how Microsoft repositioned its gaming division from a traditional hardware-centric model to a subscription-based service ecosystem. The paper identifies two critical strategic problems: declining console hardware sales and intense competition from Sony's PlayStation ecosystem. Through comprehensive external environmental analysis, this study evaluates technological disruption, competitive dynamics, and shifting consumer preferences. Recommendations include accelerating multi-platform content distribution, enhancing cloud gaming infrastructure, and implementing dynamic pricing strategies. Financial analysis reveals Game Pass achieved nearly $5 billion in annual revenue for fiscal year 2025, representing approximately 21% of Microsoft's total gaming revenue. The implementation plan projects a three-year timeline with estimated costs of $2.3 billion and projected revenue growth to $7.5 billion by 2028. This case study contributes to understanding subscription business model transformation in the entertainment technology sector.

detail.abstract:
Enterprise AI research has devoted considerably more attention to organizational readiness than to the behavioral mechanisms that precede organizational transformation. 

This paper introduces the Cognitive Friction Threshold (CFT), a behavioral construct defined as the point at which reductions in the perceived mental effort required to perform a recurring cognitive task become sufficiently large that individuals systematically replace an established cognitive routine with a new one. 

Building on the theoretical lens of Digital Anthropology, the paper distinguishes three forms of friction—transactional, behavioral, and cognitive—and argues that generative and agentic AI represent the first large-scale technologies whose principal effect is the reduction of cognitive friction itself, rather than the transactional and behavioral friction targeted by earlier waves of digital innovation. 

The paper situates the construct within six established literatures, including the Technology Acceptance Model, Diffusion of Innovation, habit research, behavioral economics, organizational routines and dynamic capabilities, and practice theory, arguing that it contributes a comparative, threshold-based explanation of behavioral change that these literatures imply but do not explicitly specify. 

It develops eight interdependent theoretical propositions linking friction reduction, threshold crossing, habit persistence, and organizational adaptation, illustrated through six historical and contemporary cases spanning digital payments, remote work, streaming media, smartphone photography, and generative AI-assisted knowledge work. The paper concludes by examining implications for knowledge work, behavioral readiness, AI governance, competitive strategy, and future research, positioning the Cognitive Friction Threshold as a behavioral mechanism explaining how reductions in cognitive effort drive enduring organizational transformation.

detail.abstract:
Organizations increasingly recognize data as a source of economic value, yet many firms struggle to convert raw data into measurable outcomes. Large portions of organizational data remain unused or underutilized, often fragmented across systems or insufficiently prepared for analysis (Arribas-Bel et al., 2021). This challenge is especially pronounced among mid-market firms, which must manage growing data complexity with limited resources and incomplete data management capabilities (National Center for the Middle Market, 2020). 
This paper introduces the FORGE Model, a staged and iterative framework for data productization integrating five transformation phases: Find, Organize, Refine, Govern, and Exchange. Drawing on literature in data governance, data quality, digital transformation, and open data ecosystems, the model synthesizes previously fragmented research streams into a coherent transformation process. 
The FORGE Model contributes a structured transformation sequence, treats governance as a central enabling capability, and connects data transformation directly to value realization. In contrast with the Open Data Products framework and Open Data Ecosystems approaches, it provides a more operational pathway suited to organizational contexts. The paper develops the model through a single guiding research question, conceptual analysis, supporting diagrams, a logistics case illustration, operationalized propositions, and a concrete empirical validation plan.

title: Weak Formalization of Semantic Constraints: AI Runtime Governance for Industrial AI

detail.title: Weak Formalization of Semantic Constraints: AI Runtime Governance for Industrial AI

detail.abstract:
The dominant discussion of long-context artificial intelligence often treats context as an expanded information container: the more text, memory, documents, or prior interaction a model can retain, the better it can act. This paper argues that this framing misses the central problem of highresponsibility AI execution. In governed AI systems, context is not primarily the accumulation of information, but the persistence of constraint-bearing state across execution. An AI system may retain factual material while losing the constraints that determine what that material permits, prohibits, leaves unresolved, or requires to remain open. In industrial settings, many of these constraints do not originate as formal rules. They arise from practice-derived judgment (Polanyi, 1966; Schön, 1983): the recognition that responsibility must not be inferred, conflicting evidence must not be collapsed, incomplete approval pathways must not be treated as closure, and evidentiary gaps must remain visible. 
The paper develops the concept of weak formalization to describe the engineering of such semantic constraints into runtime structures that can be consistently applied across similar cases, inspected during execution, audited after action, interrupted at critical nodes, and upgraded as practice matures, without requiring full mathematical formalization or deterministic predicate verification. It positions weak formalization on a constraint-strength spectrum between tacit judgment and formal software rules, arguing that semantic constraints and formal constraints differ in degree rather than kind. The paper then proposes AI runtime governance as the infrastructure required to make weakly formalized constraints industrially usable: checkpoints preserve constraint state, relay records constraint-state transitions, monitoring exposes drift, audit supports review, and human accountability protects non-delegable decisions. The contribution is conceptual and architectural. It does not claim model-internal transparency, autonomous correctness, or production validation. Rather, it identifies the missing layer for industrial AI: weak formalization of practice-derived semantic constraints into AI runtime.

title: Crowdsourcing from Hackers: Strategic Coopetition and Governance in Bug Bounty Programs
affiliations: American University - Kogod School of Business and Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Information Systems, Business Statistics and Operations Management

detail.title: Crowdsourcing from Hackers: Strategic Coopetition and Governance in Bug Bounty Programs
detail.abstract: In a bug bounty program (BBP), organizations incentivize hackers-who could otherwise be "enemies"-to report security vulnerabilities by publicly offering monetary rewards. This paper develops an analytical framework to characterize BBPs and their strategic and economic impacts. Strategically, BBPs induce some hackers to self-select into cooperative vulnerability discovery and reporting, diverting them away from attacking ("attack diversion") and delegating part of the protection effort to them ("protection delegation"). We show that: (i) BBPs can be beneficial even when hackers are inefficient at vulnerability identification, yet more participants might make BBPs less attractive to firms. (ii) Although BBPs improve security, they might encourage competitive hackers (i.e., attackers) to exert more efforts. (iii) The coopetition dynamics can render a firm's provision of rewards and in-house efforts socially inefficient. Common cybersecurity regulations, such as breach penalties and bounty reward subsidies, may exacerbate the inefficiency. We find complementarity between bounty subsidies and breach penalties, suggesting that combining and customizing them according to firm characteristics could enhance BBP efficiency. (iv) Contrary to the conventional wisdom that crowdsourcing rewards increase with participant size, we identify scenarios in which a firm should reduce or make non-monotonic adjustments to a bounty reward as participant size increases. (v) Legal safe harbor for security testing or policies that reduce duplicate report submissions can lower firm payoffs under BBPs. We draw related implications for research and practice in information security and crowdsourcing.

title: Measurement Error of Actual Cost and Its Effect on Evaluation of Estimation Performance

detail.title: Measurement Error of Actual Cost and Its Effect on Evaluation of Estimation Performance
detail.abstract: Cost estimation research in software engineering and error measurement typically treats registered costs as exact measurements and interprets low estimation error as direct evidence of good estimation performance. Both assumptions are tested in this paper. We conducted a survey with 69 experienced IT professionals in March 2026. Respondents reported on the reliability of cost registration for their most recent software development initiative, and estimated an uncertainty interval for the true cost relative to the registered cost. Finally, for a recent initiative in which the estimated and actual costs differed by less than 10%, they assessed the extent to which various mechanisms contributed to that apparent accuracy. Respondents estimated that true costs fell between 5% below and 15% above registered actual costs (median values), with 55.4% believing the true cost could be more than 10% higher than the registered cost. Cost registration problems were widespread, with more than half of respondents reporting incomplete, inaccurate, or complex registration to some degree. Among apparently accurate estimates, scope adjustment was assessed as a reason for an accurate cost estimate to a large or very large degree by roughly one in four respondents. We conclude that there is substantial uncertainty in the actual cost of software development, and we should consider collecting this as an interval of possible cost values rather than an exact measurement. Also, the reported estimation error may tell little about estimation performance without adjustments for scope, productivity dynamics, and measurement imprecision.

title: An Empirical Study of Digital Platform Scope
affiliations: , Vlerick Business School and Southern Methodist University (SMU) - Information Technology and Operations Management Department (ITOM)

detail.title: An Empirical Study of Digital Platform Scope
detail.abstract: If we define the scope of a multisided digital platform as the range of activities it supports for the participants on its different sides, currently operating platforms vary significantly in their scope. However, there is little research on the actual scope of these platforms, and on the effectiveness of each platform's choice of scope. Also, while there has been substantial discussion of different types of platforms, there is no good reference model for evaluating the scope of a digital platform in terms of possible activity types. We address this gap in this paper by empirically examining the scope of 80 established platforms in terms of a novel Platform Activity Framework. Our empirical analysis leads to the following observations: (1) our dataset contains three distinct clusters of platforms, each focusing on activities within one of the activity types in our framework; (2) some platforms do support activities outside their primary activity type, and (3) for some clusters, there are substantial differences in scope even among their constituent platforms. Drilling down into these observations, we gain several useful insights that can help platform planners and platform design researchers.

title: Google in Europe: Gatekeeper Governance and the Managed Variable Condition: Repricing Platform Discretion Under the Digital Markets Act
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Google in Europe: Gatekeeper Governance and the Managed Variable Condition: Repricing Platform Discretion Under the Digital Markets Act
detail.abstract:
This case note reads Google’s position in Europe through the Ordering concept of the managed variable. It argues that EU antitrust actions, Digital Markets Act gatekeeper governance, and platform regulation should not be understood only as punishment, decoupling, or ordinary competition enforcement. They reveal a managed continuation condition: Google remains useful and embedded, but its platform discretion is increasingly repriced, bounded, and governed.

The note examines Google’s role in search, mobile ecosystems, app distribution, browser pathways, online advertising technology, video infrastructure, maps, and digital market access. It treats the European Union’s regulation of Google as a case of platform-scale governed exposure: a digital gatekeeper remains inside the system, but its discretion is no longer carried as an unbounded assumption.

Using the Managed Variable Test, the note maps the Google-in-Europe relationship across five diagnostic signals: monitoring replaces trust; redundancy becomes normal; access becomes conditional; discretion becomes procedural; and exit-readiness or dependency-reduction capacity is built while use continues. The analysis shows how contestability, interoperability, user choice, anti-steering rules, and procedural obligations function not only as regulatory tools, but as carrying mechanisms. 

The central claim is that continued use is not sufficient evidence of continued trust. Google in Europe illustrates a broader institutional condition: a useful actor may remain necessary, strong, and central while losing the freedom to operate as an unbounded trusted participant.

title: The Empty Gate Why the Light We Blame Is Not the Thing That Profits from the Dark
affiliations: and Chiang Mai University

detail.title: The Empty Gate Why the Light We Blame Is Not the Thing That Profits from the Dark

declarations.declarationOfInterest: no

detail.abstract: A worker applies for a job that does not exist, is screened by a system that may never have read the application, and is thanked, in warm and individual language, for an interest no one received. This paper makes a single argument about that experience, and it cuts against the common story. The common story blames artificial intelligence: the machine took the work, the machine guards the door, the machine is the enemy. We argue the opposite. The corruption of the hiring market, the posting with no vacancy behind it, the rejection that imitates a consideration that never happened; is old, human, and profitable, and it lived in the dark for years before the technology arrived. Generative AI did not create it. AI is the light that made it cheap to see at scale. And the money proves the point: when a worker applies into a void, the gain flows to whoever is paid for volume rather than for matches, the platform billed per click, the firm posting a vacancy it will not fill to look as though it is growing, the screening vendor selling a tool for the flood. None of that money reaches the model. The flame profits from nothing. We name the conditions under which this happens, selection under opacity and simulated consideration, distinguish honest automation, which we defend, from costumed automation, which we do not, and show why the instinct to extinguish the light serves only the dark that the light exposed.

title:
Selling Effort in an Age of Outcomes:
 Why Artificial Intelligence will Force India's IT Services Industry to Change what it Charges for

detail.title:
Selling Effort in an Age of Outcomes:
 Why Artificial Intelligence will Force India's IT Services Industry to Change what it Charges for
detail.abstract: India's IT services industry earned about $283 billion in FY2025 and employs 5.8 million people, yet both of its contract models, time and materials and fixed price, reduce to the same unit of sale: human effort. This paper examines ten years of annual report data (FY2016 to FY2025) for TCS, Infosys, HCLTech, Wipro, Tech Mahindra and LTIMindtree and finds that revenue per employee has remained between $42,000 and $62,000, flat or declining in real terms, and that doubling revenue has required nearly doubling headcount. Comparisons with Accenture, IBM and a set of product and SaaS companies, including Chennai-founded Freshworks, show the gap is attributable to business model rather than geography. The paper also documents an innovation deficit: Samsung was granted more US patents in 2025 alone than TCS has been granted in its corporate history, and product revenue at the Indian majors remains marginal and undisclosed. It argues that agentic AI breaks the link between effort and revenue by automating precisely the work that is outsourced, and that the industry has roughly one contract renewal cycle, three to five years, to reprice its deep operational knowledge as outcomes and products.

title: Digital Vulnerabilities in the Age of AI: A Multi-Level Analysis
affiliations: Yale University - Digital Ethics Center and Yale University - Digital Ethics Center

detail.title: Digital Vulnerabilities in the Age of AI: A Multi-Level Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We declare no conflict of interest.

detail.abstract: The dominant framework for analyzing artificial intelligence centers on risk-the probability that systems will malfunction, be misused, or produce unintended consequences. We argue that this framing systematically obscures what matters most: the susceptibility of people, institutions, and infrastructures to harm. Using proceedings from the Yale Digital Ethics Center's Digital Vulnerabilities in the Age of AI Summit (DIVAS), we advance a complementary reframing, from AI risk to AI-mediated vulnerability. We identify five mechanisms through which AI transforms existing vulnerabilities-speed, scale, scope, asymmetry, and opacity-and map their manifestation across four analytical levels: individual, relational, institutional, and infrastructural. The analysis reveals cross-cutting dynamics-a widening gap between technological dependency and democratic control, the limits of technosolutionism, and a persistent cat-and-mouse trap that frustrates technical countermeasures-that explain why interventions targeting a single level or domain consistently fall short. We defend three normative implications for governance: context-specific regulation matched to vulnerability dynamics, inversion of the burden of proof from affected parties to AI deployers, and investment in the social conditions-community institutions, knowledge ecosystems, trust relationships-that technosolutionist approaches neglect. AI governance cannot be approached as a purely technical exercise; it is ultimately a question of political power, burden allocation, and democratic accountability.

detail.abstract: This commentary examines a collection of narratives published in Narrative Inquiry in Bioethics by individuals who chose to "go public" with sensitive health experiences on social media. The authors' stories offer rich qualitative insights into the benefits and harms of online self-disclosure. In the stories, three themes emerge. First, the desire to share is not opposed to privacy; rather, privacy makes meaningful sharing possible. Second, social media platforms' promises of user control largely fail in practice, leaving people who share personal information online vulnerable to algorithmic amplification, contextual collapse, and unintended.

title: Profit Pursuit or Private Enjoyment? A Structural Analysis of Valuation Mechanisms and Price Disparities in NFT Avatars
affiliations: , Arizona State University (ASU) - W.P. Carey School of Business and Arizona State University - W. P. Carey School of Business - Department of Information Systems

detail.title: Profit Pursuit or Private Enjoyment? A Structural Analysis of Valuation Mechanisms and Price Disparities in NFT Avatars
detail.abstract: Non-fungible token (NFT) avatar markets provide unique environments where valuations reflect both financial expectations and subjective preferences. Prior work has documented price disparities across appearance traits, particularly skin tone, yet the mechanisms underlying these price disparities remain unclear. Using the complete transaction history of the CryptoPunks collection from 2017 to 2023, we examine whether these disparities arise from differences in common value (shared resale expectation) or private value (subjective preference). We first establish systematic price gaps between lighter- and darker-toned avatars through reduced-form analyses. To identify the mechanisms generating these disparities, we develop a structural model of bidding and transaction to decompose buyers' willingness to pay into common and private value components while accounting for market participation. A Hidden Markov Model with Poisson emissions is adapted to infer latent buyer arrival rates and isolate private value intensity from participation effects. Our estimates show that common values do not differ meaningfully across skin-tone groups, whereas private value intensities are substantially higher for lighter-toned avatars. Counterfactual analyses demonstrate that equalizing private value intensity eliminates the price disparity, while equalizing participation patterns has negligible impacts. These findings reveal that price disparities across skin tones are rooted in subjective preferences rather than expected resale value or participation effects. For marketplace operators and creators, this implies that closing these disparities necessitates demand-driven interventions and strategic trait design, rendering informational or liquidity-based solutions insufficient. We contribute to collectible literature by providing one of the first structural decompositions of common and private value components in asset valuation.

title: Sentiment Shocks, Asymmetric Volatility, and Market Segmentation: Evidence from AH Dual-Listed Pairs

detail.title: Sentiment Shocks, Asymmetric Volatility, and Market Segmentation: Evidence from AH Dual-Listed Pairs

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether investor sentiment shocks affect conditional volatility asymmetrically in China's equity markets, using a sample of 32 AH dual-listed firm-market pairs over 2018-2024. We augment the standard GJR-GARCH(1,1) model with positive and negative sentiment indices derived from the Loughran-McDonald financial dictionary-Chinese-language news for A-shares (S CN) and English-language news for H-shares (S HK)-as exogenous variance regressors. Estimating the GJR-GARCH-X model via maximum likelihood with Student-t innovations for 15 A-share and 17 H-share series, we find strong evidence of sentiment-driven volatility. For A-shares, the negative sentiment coefficient (δ-) is statistically significant in 13 of 15 cases (87%), with a mean magnitude of 0.260, compared with only 7 of 17 H-share series (41%). The sentiment-augmented model yields ΔAIC < 0 (improved fit over the baseline GJR-GARCH) in 10 of 15 A-share and 5 of 17 H-share cases. Across both markets, |δ-| exceeds |δ + | for the majority of pairs, confirming sentiment asymmetry-negative news amplifies volatility more than positive news dampens it. Sector analysis reveals that energy and banking A-shares exhibit the strongest sentiment sensitivity, while construction and telecom firms show negligible effects. H-shares display significantly weaker sentiment incorporation, consistent with the hypothesis that Hong Kong's more informationally efficient market prices sentiment shocks faster. Mean GARCH persistence is high in both markets (A: 0.979, H: 0.980), indicating long-lived volatility clustering. Our findings have implications for volatility forecasting, risk management, and the ongoing debate on A-share market efficiency.

title: Visible Inequality and Voter Support for Public Goods: Evidence from Ohio School Finance Referenda
affiliations: Villanova University - School of Business - Economics, Villanova University and University of Rhode Island

detail.title: Visible Inequality and Voter Support for Public Goods: Evidence from Ohio School Finance Referenda
detail.abstract: Does inequality reduce willingness to collectively fund public goods? We examine this question using data from 3,273 school district referenda from the state of Ohio for the period from 2009 to 2019. We examine the differential effects of income inequality typically captured in economic surveys and the inequality that voters themselves perceive through variation in their community's housing stock. Our primary measure of perceived inequality is the 90/10 ratio of home values within a district-a dimension of inequality made salient by the physical landscape voters encounter in their everyday lives. We find that greater visible housing inequality is associated with a lower referendum yes-vote share whereas the Gini coefficient of income inequality is not. The effects of perceived inequality are concentrated in geographically compact districts where routine exposure to housing disparities is highest, and absent in more spread-out districts where such exposure is lower. The negative effect is also substantially attenuated in counties with stronger cross-income social ties, consistent with bridging social capital sustaining solidarity in the presence of salient inequality. Our results suggest that voters respond to the inequality they perceive in their community rather than inequalities in the underlying income distribution that are commonly used by social scientists to explain voter behavior.

title: When Do Deep Markets Die? Slow Capital, Sudden Runs, and the Lifetime of a Perpetual Futures Market

detail.title: When Do Deep Markets Die? Slow Capital, Sudden Runs, and the Lifetime of a Perpetual Futures Market
detail.abstract: How long does a deep perpetual futures market live? This paper makes arbitrage capacity a state variable: entry is slow, exit after auto-deleveraging is fast, and runs arrive as stress episodes thinned by a global-games threshold. One run kills: confiscation lands capacity below the unstable rest point, so the desert is absorbing and markets die once. The expected lifetime has a closed form under secular supply growth. Approaching the fold, price quality improves while capacity dispersion diverges, so the calm is in prices and the warning is in flows. A state-contingent buffer rule dominates the set-and-forget capitalization that venues use.

title: The Diophantine Equation X⁴ + 2y³ + Z³ = 0: Reduction, Structure, and Partial Resolution

detail.title: The Diophantine Equation X⁴ + 2y³ + Z³ = 0: Reduction, Structure, and Partial Resolution
detail.abstract: We study the equation x⁴ + 2y³ + z³ = 0 in coprime integers, the smallest open equation of generalized Fermat type in Grechuk's tables of unsolved Diophantine equations. Working in ℤ[∛2], we reduce the problem completely to the determination of the rational points on six explicit genus-2 curves. Four of the six are resolved unconditionally: one by classical Chabauty, three by empty fake 2-Selmer sets. The remaining pair are quadratic twists by-2 of one another, of odd conductor 3⁶, each with Mordell-Weil rank equal to the genus; we show numerically, to certified precision, that their common geometric endomorphism algebra is M₂(ℚ(√-2)), so that each Jacobian is geometrically isogenous to the square of an elliptic curve with complex multiplication by ℤ[√-2]. These curves do not appear in the current LMFDB genus-2 database. All rational points on the pair funnel through a single elliptic cover E of j-invariant 1728 over K = ℚ(∛2) with rank E(K) = 3 = [K : ℚ], and we certify, via elliptic Chabauty at p = 43, that every point of E(K) with rational image under the covering map lies in one of eight explicit Mordell-Weil cosets-precisely the classes of the known solutions. We document a striking obstruction pattern: every applicable classical method fails at its exact numerical boundary. We conjecture that the only primitive solutions are (±1, 0,-1), (±1,-1, 1), and (±43,-203, 237), and we identify two rigorous routes to completion, including quadratic Chabauty over ℚ(√-2) in the regime of Balakrishnan-Besser-Bianchi-Müller. All computations are reproducible from the public repository archived at

title: Foundation Model Access and the Limits of Section 482

detail.title: Foundation Model Access and the Limits of Section 482
detail.abstract: The most valuable asset of an artificial intelligence enterprise, the trained foundation model, is increasingly monetized not by sale or by classical license but by metered access: the developer hosts the model on its own servers and charges for each use of it through an application programming interface. When that access is supplied between related parties, the arm's length standard of section 482 must price it, and this article argues that the existing framework cannot. The difficulty begins with characterization. Treasury's newly finalized cloud transaction regulations classify on-demand access to remotely hosted software as a service, yet the economic substance of foundation model access is the exploitation of an intangible worth hundreds of millions of dollars. The characterization choice between a royalty for the use of an intangible and a fee for a service is therefore both unsettled and decisive, because it selects the pricing method, and the available methods produce radically divergent results. The comparable uncontrolled transaction method fails because foundation model access has no genuine comparables, the public price being itself set by a handful of vertically integrated suppliers. The services methods fail in the opposite direction, because the marginal cost of serving a model is near zero while its development cost is almost entirely sunk, so that a cost-based service price strips the intangible return away entirely. The article demonstrates three planning structures that exploit this indeterminacy, and proposes that a profit split keyed to the relative value of the development and exploitation functions, rather than to the transaction's label, is the only method capable of pricing foundation model access coherently. It closes by arguing that the characterization and pricing regimes, currently developed in isolation, must be coordinated.

title: Thorin Positivity, GGC Factorization and the Riemann Xi Function
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Thorin Positivity, GGC Factorization and the Riemann Xi Function
detail.abstract: We assemble a single probabilistic framework for the Riemann Hypothesis (RH) organised around one principle: RH is the positivity of a Thorin measure. We show that the reciprocal completed zeta ratio ξ(σ)/ξ(σ + s) is, for σ > 1, the Laplace transform of an infinitely divisible (ID) law; that the associated Thorin density ν σ is unconditionally nonnegative for σ > 1; and that RH is equivalent to the chain U σ ≥ 0 ⇐⇒ ν σ completely monotone ⇐⇒ F σ Stieltjes/Pick ⇐⇒ λ n ≥ 0 (Li), with pointwise positivity ν σ ≥ 0 a necessary condition whose exact strength we determine via Landau's oscillation theorem. We give an explicit-formula representation of the Thorin density and the trigonometric-moment identity λ n = 2 τ >0 (1-cos nθ(τ)). We analyse Kristiansen's signed mixing measure, prove that elementary regroupings cannot repair its sign, and promote the resulting unconditional quasi-infinitely-divisible (QID) quotient factorisation to a central theorem. We then design, in full implementable detail, a numerical protocol to test hyperbolic complete monotonicity (HCM) of the mixing densities, and prove that the slice densities, being truncation-type and discontinuous, can never be HCM, relocating the GGC-upgrade question from the mixing densities (settled negatively) to the component laws. We make concrete progress on the open problems: a Landau-type detection theorem showing pointwise positivity forces every extremal zero onto the line, with the explicit first-negativity bound ν 1/2 (π/2aγ 1) < 0 for an off-line first zero; the equivalence of Gaussian-family Weil positivity with pointwise Thorin positivity; the existence and uniqueness, under RH, of a Krein string with closed-form Weyl function m(s) = (ξ ′ /ξ)(1 2 + √ s)/(2 √ s) and Weyl-matched potential q(x) = 16π 2 e 4x ; a determinantal-pushforward conjecture for the Thorin point process; and, for the GGC questions, two theorems that settle the ends of the truncated-Gamma problem: the centred truncated Gamma is itself a GGC for every truncation level, with explicit Laplace transform, while its logarithm fails infinite divisibility below a positive phase boundary, by a uniformlimit argument; a one-line absolute-monotonicity criterion governs the regime in between. We close with the wider equivalence network (Hermite-Biehler/de Branges, Nyman-Beurling-Báez-Duarte, Weil positivity, the Pólya-Jensen/PF ladder) and a Minimal Positivity Lemma in both original and quotient form.

title: Banking Operations and Settlement Systems: A New Perspective on Monetary Balance Sheets
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Banking Operations and Settlement Systems: A New Perspective on Monetary Balance Sheets
detail.abstract:
The accounting treatment of modern monetary systems has long given rise to conceptual difficulties. In particular, it remains unclear whether the balance-sheet categories developed for conventional bilateral debt relationships can adequately represent monetary positions arising within central banks and higher-level settlement systems. Existing approaches have attempted to resolve these difficulties by reclassifying central bank money as equity, interpreting reserves as custodial assets, or emphasizing the institutional and hierarchical character of money. However, these approaches generally retain the underlying balance-sheet architecture.

This paper argues that the observed anomalies originate from a more fundamental source: the coexistence of economically distinct functions within a common balance-sheet structure. A distinction is therefore drawn between bilateral debt relationships, involving individually identified creditors and debtors, and multilateral debt relationships, in which the counterparty consists of an institutionally defined community of participants. The paper argues that positions arising from multilateral settlement relationships cannot be represented consistently within accounting structures designed for bilateral claims and obligations.

Two independent lines of argument are developed. The first examines the implications of distinguishing bilateral and multilateral debt relationships, including the transformation of monetary relationships following the historical suspension of convertibility. The second reconstructs the monetary system from a small set of empirical propositions in which money is interpreted as a state variable within settlement systems. Both approaches converge on the same conclusion: banks and central banks simultaneously perform the functions of economic enterprises and operators of settlement systems, and these functions require separate accounting representations.

The paper proposes that settlement communities should be recognized as economic entities possessing their own settlement-system balance sheets, distinct from the balance sheets of the institutions participating in or operating these systems. This framework provides a unified interpretation of central bank money, bank deposits, reserves, TARGET balances, and similar settlement positions. More generally, it suggests that many apparent anomalies of monetary accounting arise not from the nature of money itself but from the use of a balance-sheet architecture that combines fundamentally different economic relationships within a single accounting framework.

title: What do People think About?

detail.abstract: Conscious thoughts are fundamental to the human experience, yet they remain remarkably understudied. We systematically measure human thoughts through randomized daily surveys (i.e., the experience sampling method) in which subjects project their thoughts into natural language, along with perceived cause, concurrent activity, and happiness. The data set reveals essential patterns in what people think about and why, which core relationships play center stage in people's minds, people's occupying wants and needs, and the objects of people's love, hate, and worry.  Understanding thoughts matters because thoughts are strongly predictive of people's self-reported happiness. Happiness is increasing in the intentionality of the thought and also strongly associated with thought content. Thoughts explain more of happiness than what people are doing, demographics, and socio-economic status combined. In particular, the actual text of thoughts and activities explains more of the variation than traditional categorical variables and thus merits greater attention. We explore individual-level heterogeneity, identifying thought patterns in different clusters of thinkers. Finally, we conclude by showing a tradeoff between productive thoughts and consumptive thoughts, akin to a labor-leisure tradeoff, suggesting the presence of an economic thought allocation problem in the mind.

title: Textual Risk Option Momentum
affiliations: Shanghai International Studies University, Instituto Tecnológico Autónomo de México (ITAM) - Department of Business Administration and Central South University

detail.title: Textual Risk Option Momentum
detail.abstract: Using embeddings of the Risk Factors section of firms' annual 10-K reports, we identify textual risk peers and show that their past option returns predict focal firms' future option returns. This textual risk option momentum is present for calls and puts, survives controls for own-option momentum and standard option predictors, and subsumes most peer-based momentum factors built from analyst, industry, product-market, technology, customer-supplier, conglomerate, and geographic links. The effect is not explained by option factor momentum and is stronger when attention is lower and arbitrage is more limited. Our results reveal a 10-K risk-disclosure network through which option-market information diffuses slowly across firms.

title: Exosomal microRNAs as Biomarkers and Therapeutic Targets in Human Malignancies

detail.title: Exosomal microRNAs as Biomarkers and Therapeutic Targets in Human Malignancies

detail.abstract: Cancer remains one of the leading causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide, accounting for millions of deaths annually and posing substantial social and economic burdens. Despite advances in diagnostic and therapeutic approaches, the early detection and effective management of cancer remain major clinical challenges, highlighting the urgent need for reliable, minimally invasive biomarkers. Exosomes, a subtype of extracellular vesicles secreted by most cell types, have emerged as important mediators of intercellular communication due to their ability to transport proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids, particularly microRNAs (miRNAs). Exosomal miRNAs are highly stable in biological fluids because they are protected from enzymatic degradation by the lipid bilayer of exosomes, making them attractive candidates for liquid biopsy applications. This study systematically reviews and critically synthesizes published evidence regarding the role of exosomal miRNAs as diagnostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets in human malignancies. The findings indicate that exosomal miRNAs possess considerable diagnostic and prognostic potential, exhibiting altered expression patterns that correlate with cancer initiation, progression, metastasis, and patient outcomes (Jiang et al. 3334). Furthermore, exosomal miRNAs actively regulate key oncogenic processes, including cell proliferation, angiogenesis, immune evasion, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, metastatic dissemination, and resistance to chemotherapy and targeted therapies. Emerging evidence also suggests that manipulating exosomal miRNA signaling pathways may provide novel therapeutic opportunities for precision oncology. However, challenges related to exosome isolation techniques, biomarker standardization, and large-scale clinical validation remain significant barriers to routine clinical implementation. Overall, exosomal miRNAs represent promising tools for cancer diagnosis, prognosis, and targeted therapy, with substantial potential to advance personalized cancer management.

title: The Independence Gap: Why Hyperscaler AI Governance Fails the OSFI E-23 Test

detail.abstract: On 11 September 2025, OSFI released the final Guideline E-23, Model Risk Management, effective 1 May 2027, expanding scope to AI and machine-learning models and applying in full to vendor and third-party models. As federally regulated financial institutions adopt hyperscaler AI services, a structural problem emerges: the provider that develops and operates the model also supplies the tooling that attests to its governance. E-23 requires that model review be independent from model development. This paper argues that native, in-process provider governance cannot satisfy that requirement as a matter of structure rather than product quality. It defines the independence gap, maps it to specific E-23 principles and the parallel Bermuda Monetary Authority framework, situates it within the emerging Gartner "guardian agent" category, and derives four structural properties any independent evidence layer must have. A bank cannot sign its own audit opinion; a provider's agent cannot generate independent proof that its own execution was properly governed.

title: Every Way In: A Taxonomy of AI-Induced Psychosis by Etiological Mechanism

detail.title: Every Way In: A Taxonomy of AI-Induced Psychosis by Etiological Mechanism

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No interest to declare.

detail.abstract: Psychiatry has established multiple distinct etiological pathways to psychosis, each with its own causal mechanism, clinical presentation, and intervention protocol. Substance-induced psychosis follows ingestion of a specific agent. Environmentally-induced psychosis follows sustained exposure to chronic stressors. Shared psychotic disorder follows close contact with a delusional index case. Sleep deprivation psychosis follows disruption of circadian regulation. Brief reactive psychosis follows acute traumatic events. Sensory-induced psychosis follows sustained perceptual disruption. Social isolation psychosis follows prolonged deprivation of human contact. Iatrogenic psychosis follows medical or therapeutic intervention gone wrong. This paper argues that artificial intelligence systems have replicated, are currently replicating, or are positioned to replicate every one of these established pathways. Conversational AI systems function as the ingested substance. Surveillance infrastructure functions as the environmental stressor. AI generated delusional content propagates through online communities following the shared psychosis model. AI engagement patterns produce the sleep deprivation. AI integrated institutional failures produce the acute trauma. Augmented and virtual reality AI systems produce the sensory disruption. AI companions produce the social isolation wearing the mask of connection. AI assisted clinical tools produce the iatrogenic harm. The taxonomy presented here is not a prediction about future risk. It is a mapping of current and documented phenomena onto established psychiatric categories, indicating that AI has not introduced a single novel pathway to psychosis. It has instead found every existing door and walked through all of them simultaneously. The clinical, regulatory, and research implications of this convergence are significant: a phenomenon currently studied as a single undifferentiated category ("AI-induced psychosis") is in fact at least eight distinct phenomena requiring different interventions, different regulatory responses, and different research methodologies.

title: Judicial Impact Assessment (JIA): A Proactive Framework for Municipal Regulatory Resilience in the Post-Loper Bright Era

detail.title: Judicial Impact Assessment (JIA): A Proactive Framework for Municipal Regulatory Resilience in the Post-Loper Bright Era
detail.abstract: Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo eliminated Chevron deference, requiring federal courts to exercise independent judgment when interpreting ambiguous statutes. Existing scholarship has analyzed this shift almost entirely at the federal level, treating it as a recalibration between courts and agencies. This Article argues that the decision’s most consequential effects fall on a layer of government largely absent from that debate: the roughly 90,000 municipalities that draft ordinances, permits, and licensing rules under statutes as ambiguous as anything an agency interprets, with far fewer resources to defend a contested reading. Compounding circuit-to-circuit divergence, an unsettled revival of Skidmore deference, and the elimination of any practical statute of limitations for facial challenges under Corner Post, municipalities now face what this Article calls a judicial lottery: the same interpretive method, applied by different panels in good faith, regularly produces different answers to comparable questions. This Article proposes the Judicial Impact Assessment (JIA), a four-block methodology that scans regulatory text for interpretive vulnerability before adoption, scores litigation and preemption risk through the Municipal Litigation Vulnerability Index, forecasts the fiscal consequences of an adverse ruling, and translates those findings into concrete drafting responses. Comparative analysis of five foreign systems shows that no existing framework, domestic or foreign, is built to answer this question. Retrospective application to Sackett v. EPA and City and County of San Francisco v. EPA, together with a bounded comparative lesson from Ukraine’s decentralization reform, isolates a common condition this Article calls interpretive dependence, tests the framework against real outcomes, and proposes an empirical agenda for validating it further.

title: Just Transition, Redistribution, and Asset Returns
affiliations: and Boston University - Questrom School of Business

detail.title: Just Transition, Redistribution, and Asset Returns
detail.abstract: We study the just transition in a general equilibrium asset-pricing model that combines fiscal policy and redistribution with heterogeneous investors, labor-income exposure, portfolio restrictions, and green asset preferences. Workers earn labor income primarily from brown activities and can invest only in a market index, while capital owners earn no labor income but trade green and brown equity directly. We show that fiscal instruments differ sharply in their effectiveness in supporting the transition, and in their fairness. Dividend taxation is the most effective instrument for lowering the relative cost of capital of green firms and redirecting capital toward them; in our framework, it captures much of the effect of a broad carbon tax while placing a much more limited direct burden on workers. Consumption and labor-income taxes instead have smaller effects on capital reallocation and expose workers to a larger share of transition costs. Redistribution also points to a more nuanced side of the fairness-effectiveness tradeoff as rebating more revenues to workers insures them against transition costs, but attenuates incentives to reallocate capital. Portfolios play an important underlying role: workers cannot directly hedge their brown labor-income risk or fully participate in the financial gains from the transition, which in turn affects equilibrium premia. Lastly, fiscal policy and sustainable finance can reinforce one another, as green asset preferences may amplify the effect of taxation. Together, our findings have important implications for designing a green transition that is both effective and just, and highlight the importance of developing greener jobs in the longer run.

title: Deviations from Target Ratings and Capital Structure Adjustments
affiliations: Kansai University

detail.title: Deviations from Target Ratings and Capital Structure Adjustments
detail.abstract: This study examines whether deviations from target ratings affect capital structure adjustments among Japanese firms, and whether this relationship depends on firms' information precision. The results show that firms reduce their debt when their ratings fall further below target ratings. This relationship is more pronounced among firms with lower information precision but does not exist among firms with higher information precision. These findings suggest that firms with lower information precision have stronger incentives to make debt-reducing capital structure adjustments to their target ratings.

title: Can Machine Learning Improve Value Investing? Evidence from Japanese High Book-to-Market Stocks
affiliations: Kansai University

detail.title: Can Machine Learning Improve Value Investing? Evidence from Japanese High Book-to-Market Stocks
detail.abstract: This study examines whether the machine learning models, Elastic Net and XGBoost, can outperform Piotroski's (2000) F-score in a value-investing strategy focused on Japanese high book-to-market (B/M) firms. Using the same nine financial signals employed by Piotroski (2000) and an expanding window out-of-sample framework, this study constructs long-short (L-S) portfolios and evaluates the mean annual returns over the test period 2006-2020. By maintaining a constant information set, the study isolates the effect of algorithmic differences from the effect of data richness. The results show that XGBoost generates a statistically significant mean annual L-S return of +2.288% (t = 3.229, p < 0.01), whereas the F-score (+0.977%) and Elastic Net (+0.924%) fail to produce statistically significant returns. The portfolio-level analysis confirms that only XGBoost exhibits a monotonically increasing return pattern across terciles, with the top tercile earning a significant market-adjusted return of +5.671% (t = 2.170). The SHapley Additive exPlanations analysis reveals that XGBoost places the greatest emphasis on profitability and operating efficiency signals, consistent with Piotroski's (2000) accounting intuition. These findings suggest that the informational value of accounting signals in value investing is not limited to simple signal aggregation. Nonlinearity and signal interactions, as captured by XGBoost, can further enhance investment performance, even when the information set is fixed.

title: Patterns and predictors of immigrant families’ participation in early care and education programs
affiliations: University of Delaware and University of Delaware

detail.title: Patterns and predictors of immigrant families’ participation in early care and education programs
detail.abstract: While children from immigrant families have been shown to benefit from early care and education (ECE) program participation, they are less likely to participate in ECE programs than children of U.S.-born parents. Little research examined how immigrant families participate in child care over time and what factors are linked to the participation patterns. The goals of this study were to i) identify patterns of immigrant families’ ECE participation across the early years and ii) examine whether socio-demographic characteristics predicted the ECE participation patterns using a longitudinal latent class analysis and logistic regression. A sample of families with at least one foreign-born parent and a child aged 15-39 months at Time point 1 (N=653) was selected from the 2014–2017 Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP). Classification into four latent classes provided the best fit and interpretability of data. Non-Attendance class members (n=502, 76.88%) had low probability of ECE participation at all three Time points; parents in the Continuous Attendance class (n=87, 13.32%) had high probability of ECE participation at all three Time points; Attendance Gap class members (n=33, 5.05%) participated in ECE at Time points 1 and 3 but not at Time point 2; Delayed Start class members (n=31, 4.75%) started ECE at Time point 2. State immigration climate, parents’ immigration status, income, education, and race/ethnicity significantly associated with class membership. The study results inform practitioners’ and policymakers’ efforts to facilitate ECE program enrollment of children from immigrant families in the United States.

title: Controlled Beta Systematic Equity – Portfolio Construction, Drawdown Budgeting and Implementation Discipline: A Practitioner Framework for Beta Budgeting, Implementation Permission and Controlled Equity Participation
