detail.abstract:
Systematic equity research is often framed as a signal discovery problem. For a portfolio manager, the more important problem is translation. A ranking signal does not become a credible portfolio process until it has a beta budget, drawdown budget, sizing logic, exposure controls, turnover discipline, cost assumptions, liquidity limits, attribution and monitoring.

The approach proposed here treats controlled beta as an implementation design problem, not as an incidental result of incomplete hedging. The relevant category is systematic equity long/short with intentional equity participation. It is distinct from beta neutral equity market neutral because the portfolio retains a budgeted market component while controlling drawdown behaviour, implementation cost and governance risk.

The practical contribution is to separate signal strength from portfolio permission. Beta is treated as a scarce portfolio budget rather than a residual exposure. Drawdown is treated as a construction constraint rather than a statistic reported after the fact. Specification selection is then assessed through an implementation spectrum, a beta budget frontier, parameter stability, turnover, transaction cost awareness, liquidity control and monitoring rules.

The evidence is historical simulation, not live performance and not a forecast. A bounded empirical case keeps the discussion concrete, but the paper is not a strategy presentation and does not disclose proprietary signal logic. The objective is to show how a controlled beta systematic equity process can be designed, tested, sized, constrained and reviewed as a portfolio process.

title: The Systemic Risk of AI

detail.title: The Systemic Risk of AI

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: No case studies or participants were used.
declarations.funderStatement: Self funded.

detail.abstract: Using an analysis of 9 frontier AI labs and over 2,000 firms that depend on their technology, we parameterized the systemic dependence of the AI market. Our empirical simulation found that a 5-day systemic outage or breach of service provision obligations by a single frontier provider could cost $30 to $120 billion, while a simultaneous multi-lab outage or breach could cost up to $270 billion, conservatively estimated. The 2024 CrowdStrike outage, which produced roughly $5.4 billion in realized downstream losses from a single vendor, sits inside this range as an empirical floor and sanity benchmark, if aggressively contained. Gains in technology provision add economic value, but are asymmetric: amounting to as much as $5 billion to the firms that can adopt the new capability, with continued losses to those whose obligations relied on features that are discontinued. In our model, we use a classical general-equilibrium production economy of complete information with no financial frictions, no liquidity constraints, no productivity shocks, sunspots or behavioral assumptions. Systemic risk is caused by latent, non-identifiability in productive inputs — permissible within the classical Arrow-Debreu framework — which experiences a regime shift, of which all participants are aware and must respond to competitively. A frontier outage or innovation gain alters the production technology of every dependent firm at once, propagating as a quantity failure or gain that is economically meaningful, rather than simply a price adjustment. Although parameterized on the AI economy, the model is general and applicable to financial systemic risk as well as counterparty trade risk. Policy implications are discussed.

title: Asset Purchase Programmes and the Exchange Rate

detail.title: Asset Purchase Programmes and the Exchange Rate

publicationDetails.detailsText: European Stability Mechanism Working Paper No. 77

detail.abstract: In this paper, I evaluate the impact of COVID-era asset purchase programmes (APPs) on the dollar exchange rate in both emerging markets (EMs) and ex-US advanced economies (AEs). In an event study analysis that includes APP announcements for 23 EMs and seven AEs, I find that APPs appreciated the exchange rate in EMs after controlling for the policy actions of the Federal Reserve (Fed), including Fed swap lines, the policy actions of other AEs, and the simultaneous policy actions of the implementing country itself. I interpret the results through the lens of long-run uncovered interest rate parity deviations driven by sovereign credit risk, showing that asset purchase surprises lower the promised yield but do not necessarily decrease the underlying risk-free rate in EMs. These results suggest that APPs might help Ems stabilise exchange rates during episodes of distress without necessarily intervening in the foreign exchange market.

detail.title: More Tariff Pass‑Through Is in the Pipeline

publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The past year brought dramatic changes to U.S. trade policy, including sweeping new tariffs, as well as a Supreme Court decision that further reshaped the tariff landscape. Many businesses saw their costs increase significantly and faced complex decisions about whether to absorb the tariffs through lower profit margins, raise their prices to recover the higher costs, or some combination of the two. Last year, we found that most businesses had passed on at least some of these higher costs to their customers through higher prices. Now, over a year later, have businesses finished adjusting prices, or do further tariff-induced price increases lie ahead? Our latest regional business surveys reveal that nearly half of firms that have paid tariffs still plan additional price increases to offset these costs, with some expecting to raise prices six months or more in the future.

title: Machine Learning Approaches to Socioeconomic Features Dimension of Food Security in Nepal

detail.title: Machine Learning Approaches to Socioeconomic Features Dimension of Food Security in Nepal
detail.abstract: Previous studies seemed to suffer from some gaps—especially, in their predictive accuracy— because they employed traditional statistical methods to predict food security and insecurity in Nepal. To plug this gap, therefore, the present study applied machine learning (ML) algorithms to examine the socioeconomic dimension of food security in Nepal. Using large-scale survey data of Nepal Living Standards Survey IV 2022/23 (NLSS-IV) by the Government of Nepal, this study selected households' socioeconomic attributes, representing 9600 households of Nepal. This study employed supervised ML algorithms to predict food security and insecurity levels, including random forest (RF), decision tree (DT), and logistic regression (LR) learning algorithms that aimed to optimize the predictive capacity of food security in Nepal. The model performance matrix showed that LR and RF performed with a higher accuracy for predicting the likelihood of being a food-secure household, as they exactly fell into this class. The ML algorithms revealed that the social features, rather than economic features, may be crucial in predicting food security outcomes. Based on their effect size, the following are the crucial features for predicting food security in Nepal: household size, caste/ethnicity, geographical location, poverty status, income, residential status (urban or rural), family members, road facility, gender, agricultural land, remittance, marital cooking energy, and marital status. These results thus offer some policy insights to policymakers and stakeholders that it is crucial to intervene in the social differentiation and economic distribution for securing food availability adequately in proper quality in Nepal

title: Gold's Missing Anchor: The Real-Rate Decoupling and the Reserve-Safety Premium
affiliations: Bogazici University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Gold's Missing Anchor: The Real-Rate Decoupling and the Reserve-Safety Premium
detail.abstract: Gold has historically moved inversely with the real interest rate. That relationship broke after 2021: real yields rose to decade highs while gold doubled. On the pre-2022 anchor, by the end of 2025, gold trades at more than four times its real-rate-implied value. The break is in the level, not the mechanics: gold's high-frequency sensitivity to real rates barely moved, so a new, slow-moving demand sits on top. I interpret it as a repricing of reserve safety, with de-dollarization its leading component, and bring four kinds of evidence: a reserve-portfolio model with seizure risk that reproduces the pattern; gold-specificity against the metals complex and the sovereign safe havens; robustness to fiscal, monetary and retail explanations, with gold ETFs net sellers; and a price-based measure that recovers a demand shift the opaque official quantity data miss. A model pricing gold off real rates alone now misses an important component.

detail.title: Recurrent Neural Networks for Real Estate Evaluation in the Italian Market

publicationDetails.detailsText: Ca' Foscari University of Venice, Department of Economics Research Paper Series No. 22/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: Department of Economics, Ca' Foscari University of Venice Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Accurate evaluation of real estate prices represents a complex task, that holds significant relevance for the majority of the actors involved in a society, as homebuyers/sellers, investors, and policymakers. Over the last decades, in parallel with technological advancements, scholars and practitioners proposed several models and methodologies, spanning from simple hedonic regression models to sophisticated machine learning algorithms, in the attempt to improve the accuracy of price forecasts. Nonetheless, the interest towards the development of more precise and performing methodologies remains high, not only for static valuation but also, more recently, for dynamic approaches. Focusing on dynamic valuation, we turn the attention towards the Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) models: while widely tested for stock prices forecast, RNNs have seen limited to no application in the domain of real estate valuation. In this study, using official data on prices of Italian residential properties, we propose and implement two different architectures for RNN models to perform both price prediction and relevance analysis with respect to the explanatory variables. Differently from other studies, we utilize data for the whole Italian territory, focusing, rather than on individual properties' valuation, on a range of prices for groups of properties identified by house type, geographical position and state of conservation. Specifically, the output variables of our analysis are represented by the minimum and maximum prices that determine this range. The results of our analysis indicate that a Standard Recurrent Neural Network forecasts well the prices in small municipalities (with less than 15 000 inhabitants), while a Double-Input Layer RNN, with an input layer dedicated to static features and a separate input layer for dynamic features, performs better in medium-sized (with a number of inhabitants between 15 000 and 50 000 inhabitants) and large municipalities (with more than 50 000 municipalities).

title: Relationship between Past use and Medicating Intention within the Theory of Planned behavior: A Case of Non-prescription Anthelmintic Medications in Vietnam

detail.title: Relationship between Past use and Medicating Intention within the Theory of Planned behavior: A Case of Non-prescription Anthelmintic Medications in Vietnam
detail.abstract: Past behavior has been suggested as a potential predictor of future behavior in social cognition models but has not been tested in the context of consumer medicating behavior. The purpose of the present study was to examine the relationship between past behavior, operationalized as the frequency of past use, and intention, as defined by the theory of planned behavior. First, based on the theory of planned behavior (TPB), this study tested the predictive utility of an intention of Vietnamese mothers to administer non-prescription anthelmintic medications to their school-age children. Second, it examined the predictive validity of past use on intention. Third, it identified moderating effect of demographic variables on the relationship between past use and intention. A convenient sample of 395 mothers in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, was included in the present study. The original model of TPB explained 32.3% of the variance in the intention to use non-prescription anthelmintics. The addition of past use frequency added 11.7% of the variance in the intention after controlling for the TPB original constructs. Monthly household income of mothers significantly moderated the relationship between past use and intention. Age and educational levels of mothers did not moderate the relationship. Theoretical and managerial implications as well as research limitations are discussed.

detail.abstract: This study presents a comprehensive marketing mix model (MMM) analyzing 104 weeks of consumer packaged goods (CPG) market performance to quantify the contribution of price, television, radio, in-store activations, promotional discounting, and digital campaigns to new volume sales. Using ordinary least squares (OLS) regression with standardized predictors, the model explains 80.3% of weekly sales variance (R² = 0.803). Base price elasticity emerges as the dominant negative driver (standardized β =-1,033 units per standard deviation), confirming that price management is the single most powerful short-run sales lever available to brand managers. In-store activity (β = +352) and television investment (β = +216) are the two strongest positive media contributors, while promotional discounting delivers a statistically significant +6.7% average volume uplift during activation weeks (p < 0.01). Digital campaign channels-Facebook, Twitter, and branded website campaigns-display neutral to negative weekly associations, likely attributable to reverse causality and lag misalignment rather than genuine negative effects. The Stout brand equity index exerts a meaningful negative coefficient (β =-585), suggesting that premium brand positioning may suppress short-run volume in pricesensitive periods. These findings offer directly actionable guidance for marketing budget reallocation, promotional scheduling, and media channel sequencing in the CPG sector.

title: Issuing Away The Treasury Specialness: Debt Supply, Market Power, and Monetary Policy

detail.title: Issuing Away The Treasury Specialness: Debt Supply, Market Power, and Monetary Policy
detail.abstract: This paper aggregates security-level issuance data from 1999Q1 to 2024Q4 to estimate maturity-specific demand curves for Treasury convenience yields. They are downward sloping, heterogeneous across maturities, and affected by monetary policy through both level and slope effects. These estimates are then embedded in a quantitative debt-management model in which the issuer internalizes maturity-specific demand when choosing the composition of debt issuance. The main finding is that the observed maturity structure generates substantially lower seigniorage revenues than the revenue-maximizing allocation, especially after the GFC. This revenue loss is driven primarily by the post-GFC expansion in debt supply, which compresses convenience yields and reduces Treasury market power. Monetary policy amplifies these fiscal effects by changing the sensitivity of convenience yields to issuance.

detail.title: A New China Strategy for South Korea’s Advanced Industries

publicationDetails.detailsText: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade Research Paper No. 24/iKIET/205
publicationDetails.journalName: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics & Trade Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Advanced manufacturing industries targeted by the Made in China 2025 strategy, such as robots, semiconductors, electric vehicles (EVs, including autonomous driving), and batteries, have grown exponentially since 2015. With the exception of semiconductors, several categories within robots, batteries, and EVs have exceeded the localization targets outlined in the strategy. China now holds an overall value chain advantage over South Korea in these sectors. Across R&D, procurement (supply chain), production, services, and demand markets (both domestic and overseas), China maintains an edge in robots, EVs, batteries, and autonomous vehicles. Korea retains superiority in equipment procurement, sales and maintenance services, and overseas demand for the semiconductor industry, driven by its memory chip competitiveness. Korea also maintains a slight lead in robotics R&D capabilities for product development and design.

While the expanding rivalry poses threats to Korean industries, opportunities exist to differentiate in advanced and niche markets. China’s price competitiveness, its expanding dominance in new AI-based markets, and its internalizing supply chains are common threats. However, leveraging its overall technological prowess and process expertise in materials, components, and equipment, Korea maintains a qualitative advantage in certain categories. Korea must seek to enter global premium markets, such as the US and the EU, emphasizing stability and reliability.

Up to now, Korean industry has pursued an “ultra-gap” strategy, in which firms sought to maintain wide competitive moats against their Chinese competitors. This strategy is no longer viable. Korea urgently needs to shift its policy toward competitive cooperation and strategic utilization and secure a position in the future ecosystems that China aims to dominate, actively utilizing China’s high-tech and technological ecosystems. We must discover new cooperative models that combine China’s technology, production base, and data with Korea’s innovative ideas.

title: An Intelligent Scheduling System for Heterogeneous UAV Multi-trip Delivery: A Two-phase Hybrid Metaheuristic for Makespan Minimization
affiliations: UCSI University, UCSI University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: An Intelligent Scheduling System for Heterogeneous UAV Multi-trip Delivery: A Two-phase Hybrid Metaheuristic for Makespan Minimization
detail.abstract: The rapid adoption of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in last-mile logistics creates a pressing need for intelligent scheduling systems that allocate diverse delivery tasks across mixed fleets under tight operational constraints. This paper addresses the Heterogeneous UAV Multi-Trip Delivery Problem (HUAV-MTDP), in which UAVs of differing payload, speed, and endurance perform multiple trips to minimize the fleet makespan, a direct proxy for system throughput and service level. We formulate the problem as a mixed-integer linear programming model that jointly captures task-to-UAV assignment, vehicle-task matching, and multi-trip routing, and we design a two-phase hybrid metaheuristic, ACO-GA-WA, as the decision engine. The first phase applies Ant Colony Optimization for global exploration; the second couples a Genetic Algorithm with a continuous-domain recombination operator and an adaptive information-transfer bridge that tunes evolutionary parameters from the colony's search statistics. Across instances of 20 to 120 tasks, ACO-GA-WA reduces the median makespan by 8.8%, 2.6%, and 4.8% relative to ACO, GA, and a simplified ACO-GA, respectively, while achieving the lowest variance and the fewest spatio-temporal conflicts; its advantage widens as problem scale grows. The framework returns an executable schedule, comprising per-UAV manifests, trip itineraries, and the optimized makespan, providing a practical decision-support tool for heterogeneous UAV delivery operations.

detail.abstract: The COVID-19 disruption forced the most comprehensive shift to online delivery in U.S. graduate education history. This study examines whether that change represents a permanent restructuring or a transient adjustment, and how it relates to differential doctoral completion outcomes across fields with different research methodologies. We apply a multilevel quasi-experimental design to two federal census-level datasets: the Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS; 18,826 institution-year observations, 2014-2022) and the Survey of Earned Doctorates (SED; 34 subfields, 2012-2022). Each institution serves as its own control in a fixed-effects panel model (institution-level ICC = .702), supplemented by interrupted timeseries and sector-disaggregated analysis. The online enrollment surge was not transient: by 2022, online-engaged enrollment remained about 6% points above pre-pandemic projections, with hybrid delivery accounting for the larger share. Within institutions, the pandemic produced a sharp increase of nearly 13% points, roughly half of which persisted into 2022. Doctoral completion trajectories diverged: co-presence-dependent fields (e.g. history, foreign languages, anthropology) experienced sustained declines, while computationally oriented fields (e.g. computer science, engineering) grew. A trend-adjusted model attributes a 20.6% post-pandemic completion advantage to computationally oriented fields beyond preexisting divergence. The post-pandemic environment is a sustained, stratified system rather than a return to baseline. The design documents fieldlevel trajectories but cannot assign them to individual-level modality exposure. Findings inform online doctoral program design, hybrid modality investment, and accreditation monitoring.

affiliations: and The University of Sydney Business School

detail.title: Credit Allocation and Lending Decisions Across Monetary Policy Regimes: Evidence from Fintech Lending
detail.abstract: This paper examines two distinct stages of fintech platform screening: funding allocation and post-listing rejection. Using loan-level data from Prosper Marketplace, we investigate how borrower credit quality and contractual exposure influence these decisions across different monetary policy regimes. During monetary easing following COVID-19, loans with lower credit scores and greater contractual exposure were more likely to be allocated to retail funding channels. During the subsequent tightening period, funding shifted toward institutional investors. However, retail investors did not fully withdraw from lending to lower-creditscore borrowers and continued to fund a subset of these loans with stronger observable financial characteristics. We further show that borrower credit quality and contractual exposure play important roles in post-listing rejection decisions, although their effects vary substantially across monetary policy regimes. Overall, the evidence suggests that fintech platforms actively adapt screening and credit allocation decisions in response to changing macro-financial conditions.

title: Cumulative Territorial Fractures: A Feedback-Loop Theory of Social Marginalization and Environmental Risk in Peripheral Urban Neighborhoods

detail.title: Cumulative Territorial Fractures: A Feedback-Loop Theory of Social Marginalization and Environmental Risk in Peripheral Urban Neighborhoods
detail.abstract: Most urban-vulnerability research treats the co-occurrence of social marginalization and environmental hazard exposure as a static spatial correlation: certain neighborhoods happen to be both poor and exposed. This article argues that, for a specific and empirically important class of peripheral urban neighborhoods, the relationship is not co-occurrence but a self-widening, path-dependent process, in which social marginalization and environmental exposure feed each other forward through time rather than merely sitting side by side at one moment in time. The article proposes Cumulative Territorial Fractures (CTF) as a dedicated theory of this dynamic, adapting Gunnar Myrdal's principle of circular and cumulative causation-developed to explain widening core-periphery divergence between regions-to the intra-urban, neighborhood scale, and integrating it with the "pressure and release" progression-ofvulnerability model from disaster studies and the environmental-justice literature's account of disproportionate hazard siting. Unlike existing socioenvironmental fragmentation frameworks, which document where social and environmental deficits co-locate at a given moment, CTF theory specifies why the gap between fractured and non-fractured neighborhoods tends to widen rather than close over time, and under what conditions that widening becomes difficult to reverse through single-cycle intervention. Five testable propositions are derived, and a longitudinal Fracture Widening Index-comparing successive census waves rather than a single cross-section-is proposed for testing the theory against Témara using Morocco's 2014 and 2024 general population censuses (RGPH).

title: The Boundary Principle: A Universal Four-Stage Architectural Cycle of Transformation and Invariant Revelation in Coherent Systems
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Boundary Principle: A Universal Four-Stage Architectural Cycle of Transformation and Invariant Revelation in Coherent Systems
detail.abstract: Transformation is typically treated as domain-specific: psychologists analyze identity crises, AI researchers study catastrophic forgetting or mode collapse, and physicists investigate breakdowns of classical models. This paper argues these reflect a single architectural mechanism, the Boundary Principle. Coherent systems, when pushed to the limits of their predictive frameworks, undergo a four-stage sequence: Expansion, Suspension, Confrontation, and Integration. Illustrated intuitively in psychology, narrative, and machine learning (with empirical patterns from multi-AI collaboration and trading systems), the cycle is demonstrated rigorously through mathematical and physical invariants: the Golden Ratio φ, the exponential base e, π, Planck's constant h, and the Feigenbaum constants δ and α. The Principle generates falsifiable predictions across AI, neuroscience, immunology, and psychology. It offers an information-theoretic analog via coordination invariants (S = C/V), positioning the framework as a candidate general law for how systems reveal deeper structure at the edge of coherence.

title: The Invisible Investors Patient Advocacy Organizations as Uncredited Capital Allocators in the Orphan Drug Pipeline, A Case Study of The MED13L Foundation

detail.title: The Invisible Investors Patient Advocacy Organizations as Uncredited Capital Allocators in the Orphan Drug Pipeline, A Case Study of The MED13L Foundation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is a volunteer, fundraiser, and research affiliate of the MED13L Foundation, the organization that is the subject of this study, and is the sibling of a person with MED13L syndrome. All four interviewees are officers or board members of the MED13L Foundation, and two of them, Katie Boychuck and Nicholas Seaver, are also parents of children with MED13L syndrome. The author received no financial compensation for this work. The MED13L Foundation did not fund the study or control its findings.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper is a case study of an organization and does not involve human-subjects research, patient data, or clinical cases. It draws on interviews with four named professionals who participated and consented to be quoted.

detail.abstract: Of the roughly 10,000 known rare diseases, only about five percent have an approved treatment. The reason is mostly economic. A therapy for a few hundred patients rarely promises the kind of return that would justify a drug company's investment without serious up-front de-risking. Driven by the hope of a treatment that no one else will pursue, patient advocacy organizations take the work on themselves. They fund natural history studies, build patient registries, secure diagnostic infrastructure, convene scientific advisory boards, and pay for the translational research that reclassifies a disease from invisible to investable. In financial terms, this is capital allocation in its earliest, pre-commercial stage. These organizations fund the science and de-risk the pipeline that later-stage investors require, yet under the standard model, they see little of the downstream financial value their work creates. This paper studies that gap through the MED13L Foundation. Since expanding its research mission in 2022, the Foundation has invested just under 1.6 million dollars across basic science, translational therapeutics, and natural history for a syndrome with over 700 families who have a confirmed diagnosis today and an estimated prevalence of 5.75 per 100,000 births. Drawing on four interviews with the Foundation's leadership, its legal counsel, and a capital markets professional on its board, the analysis finds that the exclusion is not the result of a single cause, but of three overlapping problems. Universities own the sponsored research by default. Any commercial partner has to make enough money on the deal to justify it. And most foundations lack the information or expertise to negotiate a position in the first place. The paper tests a common claim that reforming the Bayh-Dole Act would fix the problem, and finds otherwise. The people who actually do these deals say the statute is rarely enforced, so it is not the real barrier. Two further constraints emerge from the deal side. Timing matters because the window to capture value really only opens during strong biotech cycles. Platform technologies possess a decisive edge because a therapy that treats only one ultra-rare disease is very hard to fund, while one that works across many is not. The argument is tested against five precedents in which value was actually captured, and the paper closes with practical levers a foundation can put to use.

title: The Anatomy of Censorship and Propaganda: Evidence from Russian Wikipedias
affiliations: Paris School of Economics (PSE), University of St. Gallen - Swiss Institute for International Economics and Applied Economic Research, National University Singapore and Université Paris-Dauphine, PSL Research University

detail.title: The Anatomy of Censorship and Propaganda: Evidence from Russian Wikipedias

declarations.funderStatement: Ruben Durante gratefully acknowledges financial support from the European Research Council (ERC) under the European Union’s Horizon Europe research and innovation program (Grant Agreement No. 101125953).

detail.abstract: Authoritarian regimes shape citizens' knowledge and beliefs through censorship and propaganda. We study which narratives they suppress and promote using a rare natural experiment: Ruwiki, created in 2023 by cloning Russian-language Wikipedia and selectively rewriting its 1.9 million articles under regime-aligned editorial control. We compare the two platforms twenty months after the fork, using within-Wikipedia changes as a placebo benchmark. We find that Ruwiki's editing patterns resemble professional rather than volunteer-driven content production. An LLM-based comparison and machine-learning analyses of text deletions and insertions reveal a coherent ideology organized around three pillars: Russia's image vis-àvis the rest of the world, domestic politics, and culture. The resulting narratives legitimize Russia's past and present acts of aggression, suppress accounts of domestic opposition and human-rights violations, and promote traditional values. Culture's centrality reveals how authoritarian information control penetrates domains far beyond formal politics, including morality, gender, family life, law, and psychology. Article deletions are rare and confined to topics that are difficult to reframe, while editing is broad, consistent with a preference for reframing existing content rather than leaving unanswered queries: 27% of articles undergo at least some change, 2.8% are heavily edited, and only 0.14% are deleted. Rewriting sensitive topics reduces readability, suggesting that ideological control is costly. An external benchmark using official high-school history textbooks confirms that Ruwiki's revisions move articles on modern history toward state-sanctioned narratives. The results show how authoritarian information control constructs a regime-aligned account of the world and Russia's place in it.

title: Measuring Strategic-Economic Return on U.S. Foreign Engagement: A Composite Index Model Using an FY 2024 All-Entities Sample
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Measuring Strategic-Economic Return on U.S. Foreign Engagement: A Composite Index Model Using an FY 2024 All-Entities Sample

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I am a citizen of the United States.

detail.abstract: Foreign assistance and security engagement are often debated by total dollars spent, but aid volume alone does not reveal whether a recipient relationship produces strategic, security, economic, or governance-adjusted return. This paper develops the United States Foreign Engagement Return Index (UFERI), a composite model for estimating strategic-economic return in an author-defined FY 2024 all-entities sample. The model scores each recipient across sixteen benefit variables, applies capped cost and risk drags, and maps the adjusted score to a bounded public-facing index with a sigmoid transformation. The sample is explicitly defined as an author-defined all-entities engagement sample rather than an official ForeignAssistance.gov top-ten ranking. Taiwan is retained as a strategic-security comparator because its relationship with the United States is central to Indo-Pacific deterrence, technology security, and supply-chain risk, even though it is not treated as a conventional ODA style recipient. The model distinguishes military-aid burden across cases and separates geostrategic salience from actual rival-denial capacity. Best-case and worst-case ranges are calculated directly from the stated formula so every point estimate lies inside its scenario band. The baseline results rank Taiwan first, followed by Israel, Jordan, Ukraine, and Kenya. A worked example for Ukraine verifies the calculation pipeline: raw benefit = 5.853, cost drag = 0.100, risk drag = 0.050, adjusted score = 5.004, and UFERI = 50.052. Pearson correlation between funding and UFERI is r = 0.284 (p = 0.427); Spearman rank correlation is rho = 0.661 (p = 0.038). Because n = 10, these statistics are descriptive rather than inferential. The paper's claim is limited: within this small model sample, funding rank and modeled strategic-economic return rank differ materially.

title: Measuring geoeconomic tension: a large-language-model approach for the euro area

detail.title: Measuring geoeconomic tension: a large-language-model approach for the euro area
detail.abstract: We construct an index of geopolitical and geoeconomic tension for the euro area using Large-Language Models (LLMs) that prompt a large dataset of European, local-language newspaper articles. The resulting LLM Geoeconomic and Geopolitical Tension (LGPT) index and its subindices seek to provide an accurate narrative of tensions and their sources over the past quarter century. The multilingual LLM approach allows for a separation between geopolitical and geoeconomic tensions and for granularity in the identification of the source of such tensions including trade, energy and finance. This lends itself to more accurate economic analysis of the impact of geopolitics and geoeconomics on the euro area economy. The LLM approach is efficient and capable among other things of extracting trends regarding the international institutional actors involved in developments. We also illustrate one potential use of the index by estimating the impact of geoeconomic tensions on output and inflation in the euro area in a Bayesian structural VAR framework.

title: Barriers to a European Banking Union
affiliations: , ,  and European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: Barriers to a European Banking Union
detail.abstract: We quantify barriers to cross-border bank lending to firms within the euro area and their consequences for credit allocation and output. Using loan-level data from the European credit registry (AnaCredit) and group structures (RIAD),we estimate barriers to relationship formation, loan pricing, and banks’ branching decisions at the country-pair level. We find that barriers to cross-border relationships between banks and firms and cross-border bank entry are large while wedges on interest rates and loan quantities are comparatively small. The estimated wedges are strongly associated with differences in national banking regulations, measured using a novel dataset on regulatory distances. We embed our estimates into a quantitative spatial general equilibrium model with heterogeneous banks and firms subject to cross-border frictions in relationship formation, loan pricing, and bank entry. Partially relaxing frictions predicts sizable and heterogeneous output gains across euro area countries. These gains are primarily driven by increases in capital and labor rather than improvements in allocative efficiency.

title: Public Transport Availability, Delayed Learning to Drive and Later Life Car Dependence
affiliations: ESRI, Trinity College (Dublin) and Trinity College (Dublin)

detail.title: Public Transport Availability, Delayed Learning to Drive and Later Life Car Dependence
detail.abstract: High levels of car dependency are a major challenge for decarbonisation policy. This paper explores how early-life mobility environments shape long-run driving behaviour through two underexplored questions: whether public transport access predicts delayed learning to drive and whether the age at which individuals learn to drive is associated with later driving intensity. We merge nationally representative survey data from Ireland (N > 2,000) with Public Transport Accessibility Level (PTAL) scores to model (1) age at learning to drive, using survival analysis, and (2) recent driving behaviour, using a hurdle regression model. Higher public transport accessibility is associated with significantly later learning, with individuals in high‑PTAL areas 30% less likely to have learned by age 20 than those with no access. Each year of delayed learning predicts a lower likelihood of weekday driving and a 2% reduction in Vehicle Kilometres Travelled (VKT) on driving days. The findings have implications for understanding the long-term benefits of public transport provision.

title: Modeling the injury severity of riders and pedestrians in crashes involving micro-mobilityvehicles
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL)

detail.title: Modeling the injury severity of riders and pedestrians in crashes involving micro-mobilityvehicles
detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of electrical-powered micro-mobility vehicles in European cities has raised concerns about rider and pedestrian safety. Previous studies have largely analysed the factors that influence the injury severity of cyclists. However, the determinants of injury severity in crashes involving e-bikes and electric personal mobility devices (e-PMDs), which are often faster and heavier than conventional bicycles, remain poorly understood. This study investigates the effects of the characteristics of the road, the environment, and the road users on the severity of crashes involving cyclists, e-cyclists and e-PMD riders. Police crash data were analyzed in Paris and Lyon between 2019 and 2023. The dataset was enriched with the characteristics of the built-environment extracted using GIS. Logistic regression and ordered probit models were then estimated for four crash types: crashes with motorized vehicles, crashes with other micro-mobility vehicles, crashes with pedestrians and single-vehicle crashes. The results show the importance of the rider’s characteristics and pre-crash maneuvers, as well as those of the second-party’s, and also highlight the need for protected cycle facilities, visibility measures for riders, and improved intersection design to mitigate risks for both riders and pedestrians.

title: Sectoral Sovereignty: How European Aviation AI Compliance Operates Under EASA's Vertical Architecture

detail.title: Sectoral Sovereignty: How European Aviation AI Compliance Operates Under EASA's Vertical Architecture
detail.abstract:
Context. The European Union's regulatory architecture for artificial intelligence in safety-critical aviation has shifted twice between November 2024 and June 2026. The original 2 August 2026 high-risk obligations under Article 6(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 were deferred to 2 August 2027 for Annex I product-embedded systems by Article 113(3)(c); the Digital Omnibus on AI, on which Council and Parliament reached provisional agreement on 7 May 2026, would further defer that date to 2 August 2028. Throughout this period, EASA has been executing its own rulemaking response under Task RMT.0742, with NPA 2025-07 published on 10 November 2025 and AI Concept Paper Issue 03 released for comment on 3 June 2026.


Findings. Five findings drive this Dossier. First, the operative compliance regime for safety-critical aviation AI is EASA's sectoral architecture, not the AI Act's horizontal apparatus. Second, vendor compliance tooling does not address the conformity-assessment route that applies to AI safety components in type-certified aircraft. Third, the standards-readiness gap at CEN-CENELEC JTC 21 has become a substantive regulatory-policy mechanism. Fourth, the capital-pace pattern that caught earlier European eVTOL entrants — capital exhaustion against the regulator's actual rather than stated timeline — is the pattern that will catch AI-component projects whose budgets assume nominal deadlines. Fifth, sovereign capability builders with civil-defence dual portfolios are accumulating an unmatchable position during the methodology window.


Implications. Investment decisions, function-ownership decisions, and certification-pathway commitments made between June 2026 and August 2027 will determine which European aerospace and defence operators carry safety-critical AI through to type certification, and which expend capital on the wrong conformity-assessment route. The Dossier provides three proprietary instruments — the EASA-AI Sovereign Calibration Audit (ESCA), the Dual-Compliance Capital Allocation Model (DCCAM), and the Sovereign Position Scorecard (SPS) — that the purchaser uses to make those decisions operationally.


Confidence. CONFIRMED on the legal architecture and primary EASA documents; REPORTED on commercial cases, market structure, and forensic narrative; INFERRED on the deep-pattern synthesis that the methodology window favours sovereign capability builders over compliance buyers.

title: Effects of Building Fabric Requirements on Willingness to Adopt a Heat Pump
affiliations: ESRI, Trinity College (Dublin) and Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI)

detail.title: Effects of Building Fabric Requirements on Willingness to Adopt a Heat Pump

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland

detail.abstract: Decarbonising residential heating requires widespread adoption of heat pumps, yet uptake remains below policy targets. Low uptake may be partly explained by building fabric upgrades that current policy assumes heat pumps require to work efficiently, but the effect of these upgrades on heat pump adoption remains underexplored. This study examines how such requirements influence homeowners' willingness to adopt heat pumps using a pre-registered survey experiment with a nationally representative sample of homeowners in Ireland (n = 574). Participants reported their intentions to adopt a heat pump as they received sequential information on its benefits, installation costs, and personalised upgrade requirements for their own home. Information on benefits significantly increased willingness to adopt, but this effect was fully reversed once participants learned about required building fabric upgrades. Wall insulation in particular had a large deterrent effect, with a marginal reduction in adoption intention of approximately 40% compared to only ventilation upgrades (19.7% vs. 11.6%). An embedded survey experiment testing an enhanced heat pump installation grant substantially increased willingness at the point of cost information, but this effect was largely eroded after upgrade requirements were introduced. Additional interventions, including cost comparisons and information on low-cost financing, had no meaningful impact. The results demonstrate that adoption decisions depend on the full set of costs and requirements associated with heat pump installation. Forecasts that fail to recognise the deterrent effects of these requirements are likely to overestimate heat pump uptake. Policies that subsidise heat pumps alone are unlikely to achieve target uptake where significant preparatory works are required.

title: The Effects Of Uncertain Commuting Costs On American Urban Land Markets: Theory And Empirical Evidence
affiliations: and University of Central Florida

detail.title: The Effects Of Uncertain Commuting Costs On American Urban Land Markets: Theory And Empirical Evidence
detail.abstract: There is extensive empirical evidence showing the negative effects of increasing commuting costs on city size in the Mills-Muth land use model. However, there is only theoretical evidence for the effect of commuting risk, or the uncertainty associated with commuting, on city size in the closed city Mills-Muth model. This study adds to the literature by deriving the open city Mills-Muth prediction for commuting risk and empirically testing both closed and open city predictions. Core results show a negative effect of commuting risk on city size in both models, with a negative effect on incomes and population in the open city specification, as well, with the income effect suggesting reduced labor demand.

title: Forecasting the Future Through a Partisan Lens: Electoral Outcomes and Household Expectations
affiliations: Indiana University Bloomington and Deutsche Bundesbank

detail.title: Forecasting the Future Through a Partisan Lens: Electoral Outcomes and Household Expectations
detail.abstract: Using a unique survey experiment fielded around the 2024 U.S. presidential election, we study how politically salient events shape household expectations. We examine both the first and second moments of expectations, as well as the joint updating of inflation and unemployment expectations. We find sharp partisan updating: Republicans revise both inflation and unemployment expectations downward, while Democrats revise both upward. In contrast, subjective uncertainty declines for both groups. We also examine whether AI-generated personas can reproduce these patterns. Although some models match the qualitative direction of updating in up to 60% of cases, their quantitative performance is weak: Concordance Correlation Coefficients remain low and do not exceed 0.10. These findings suggest that LLM-generated responses capture only limited aspects of partisan distortions in expectations, warranting caution in their use as substitutes for human survey data.

title: How Elections Reshape Beliefs: Cognitive and Social Dissonance in Political Preference Formation

detail.title: How Elections Reshape Beliefs: Cognitive and Social Dissonance in Political Preference Formation

publicationDetails.detailsText: GMU Working Paper in Economics Forthcoming

detail.abstract: This paper examines how voting behavior and election outcomes shape political preferences through two distinct psychological mechanisms: cognitive and social dissonance. Cognitive dissonance leads voters to align post-election evaluations with their own vote choice, while social dissonance captures conformity to majority sentiment after observing the election result. We develop a formal model and test its predictions using seven waves of ANES data (1996-2020), leveraging withinrespondent variation in pre-and post-election candidate evaluations. We show that voters rate their chosen candidate more favorably after elections (cognitive dissonance) and increase ratings of the winning candidate regardless of vote choice (social dissonance). Cognitive dissonance is strongest among nonpartisan voters and amplified by political discussion, while media exposure has no effect. Social dissonance grows with larger victory margins, and both mechanisms vary by gender and age. These findings reveal how psychological forces drive preference formation and contribute to political polarization.

detail.abstract: This article examines the macroeconomic implications of global supply chain disruptions in the context of growing geoeconomic fragmentation and confrontational globalization. The study explores how geopolitical tensions, technological fragmentation, sanctions, energy shocks, and post-pandemic restructuring processes transform the architecture of global production networks and intensify systemic economic vulnerabilities. Particular attention is devoted to the application of the FIGARO (Full International and Global Accounts for Research in Input-Output Analysis) international input-output framework for identifying structural interdependencies, strategic vulnerabilities, and the transmission channels of global shocks across countries and sectors. The research combines approaches from global value chain theory, network economics, and input-output analysis. Using FIGARO data for 49 countries and 21 economic sectors during the period 2010-2023, the paper applies eigenvector centrality analysis to determine the most systemically important suppliers within the global economy. The findings reveal the dominant role of China's manufacturing sector and the increasing importance of U.S. financial, technological, and professional service sectors in global supply networks. The study also demonstrates how the COVID-19 pandemic, energy crises, and geopolitical conflicts accelerated the restructuring of global production systems and increased the significance of resilience-oriented economic policies. The article argues that FIGARO-based network analysis provides an effective methodological framework for evaluating macroeconomic resilience, strategic dependencies, and the vulnerability of small open economies under conditions of global uncertainty. The results contribute to the understanding of structural transformations in the world economy and offer analytical tools for assessing supply chain resilience, reshoring processes, and geoeconomic risks.

title: Does Tightening the Duration of Temporary Contracts Cost Jobs? Evidence from Germany
affiliations: ZEW – Leibniz Centre for European Economic Research

publicationDetails.detailsText: ZEW – Centre for European Economic Research Discussion Paper No. 26-026

detail.abstract: Many countries limit how long a worker may be kept on a temporary contract, yet little is known about how firms and workers respond when this maximum duration is tightened. Does a shorter cap simply displace temporary jobs, or does it push firms towards permanent hiring? I provide causal evidence on this duration margin using a 2001 German reform that restricted temporary contracts longer than two years in previously exempt small firms. Using difference-indifferences combined with propensity-score matching, I find that new jobs became around five percentage points more likely to start with a permanent contract, that contract durations bunched at the cap, and that overall employment was not adversely affected. Once the first capped contracts matured, turnover of short-tenure workers rose by a third to a half, but conversions to permanent contracts dominated this churn margin, and post-reform labour-market entrants saw higher early-career earnings and job stability. The findings speak directly to the current debate over lengthening such caps, including Germany's plan to double its own from two to four years.

title: When Supply Cannot Respond: Commodity Price Cycles and Rare Earths
affiliations: , University of Western Australia - Business School and The University of Western Australia

detail.title: When Supply Cannot Respond: Commodity Price Cycles and Rare Earths

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Digital Finance CRC
declarations.funderStatement: Digital Finance CRC

detail.abstract: Commodity price cycles are typically characterised by booms and slumps arising from the lag between price signals and supply responses. This paper investigates how inelastic supply alters these price cycles using the rare earth element (REE) market as an example. China accounts for approximately 90% of global refined REE production, controlled by two state-owned producer groups operating under supply quotas. We find that REE price series exhibit higher magnitude upside price moves and muted downside price moves relative to benchmark commodities. These findings indicate that the typical commodity price cycle is based on supply elasticity. If supply is inelastic, the market exhibits a spike-and-revert process.

title: How Consumers Pay for Gasoline
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta

detail.title: How Consumers Pay for Gasoline
detail.abstract: Using survey data on consumer payments choice in the United States, the paper analyzes the payment methods that consumers use for purchasing gasoline at gas stations. The use of cash has declined between 2021 and 2025 whereas the use of credit and debit card payments has moderately (and non-monotonically) increased over these years. Cash is more often used in rural areas and cards in urban areas. Cash use declines with household income but not with age. Regression and random forest techniques are then used to analyze the effects of demographic and transaction-specific variables on how consumers pay at gas stations.

title: Corporate Crime Observatory The New Responsibilities of Tax Professionals: From Neutral Intermediary to Conditional Gatekeeper with a Guarantee Function

detail.title: Corporate Crime Observatory The New Responsibilities of Tax Professionals: From Neutral Intermediary to Conditional Gatekeeper with a Guarantee Function
detail.abstract: This article examines the evolving liability of tax professionals in Italian law after the Court of Cassation's March 2026 rulings. It argues that these decisions do not impose a general duty to guarantee the legality of taxpayers' conduct, but selectively extend liability through the rules on complicity in administrative tax offences. The analysis traces the erosion of the traditional neutrality of external professionals and shows how Italian case law has developed a model based on conscious causal contribution, including by omission, and qualified diligence, regardless of personal economic gain. The paper adopts a doctrinal and interpretative approach, complemented by a limited functional comparison. Comparative references to anti-money laundering, DAC6, failureto-prevent models, and SLAPP-related professional misconduct are used not as doctrinal equivalents, but to test a shared boundary problem: when professional assistance becomes participation in abuse.

title: Monetary Policy Uncertainty: Sources and Consequences
affiliations: and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: Monetary Policy Uncertainty: Sources and Consequences
detail.abstract: Why do stocks and bonds sometimes hedge each other and sometimes move together? We show that an unexplored explanation lies in the source of uncertainty about the future path of monetary policy. Using daily revisions in policy rate expectations, we decompose a novel market-based measure of policy path uncertainty into macroeconomic uncertainty and uncertainty about the Federal Reserve's reaction function. These two components generate sharply different macroeconomic dynamics. Macroeconomic uncertainty lowers output and inflation, prompting monetary policy easing, while reaction function uncertainty produces stagflationary pressures and monetary policy tightening. These contrasting dynamics carry through to financial markets. Both uncertainty sources reduce equity valuations, but macroeconomic uncertainty lowers Treasury yields whereas policy response uncertainty raises yields through higher real term premia. Consequently, stock-bond correlations turn negative when macroeconomic uncertainty dominates and positive when reaction function uncertainty prevails. Our decomposition thus provides a structural explanation for why the stock-bond correlation switches sign over time.

reference: Chicago-Kent Law Review
title: Labor Regulation Of AI
affiliations: University of North Carolina School of Law

detail.title: Labor Regulation Of AI
detail.abstract:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology has rapidly advanced in recent years, promising numerous benefits. On the other hand, AI also presents risks, including privacy violations and discrimination. Congress and state legislatures have been slow to react and, as a result, government regulation of AI is virtually nonexistent in the United States. This is particularly true in the workplace, where most employers have complete control over the terms and conditions of work. 

This regulatory gap is not total, however. One of the oldest labor and employment statutes, the National Labor Relations Act, can provide checks on employers' use of AI at work in certain circumstances. Moreover, in the absence of direct government regulation of AI, one group has been able to prompt substantial limits on AI use in the workplace: labor unions. As employers have increasingly used AI, workers have begun feeling the impact of that technology directly. Unions-which have the expertise, opportunity, and incentive to address AI use at work-have been at the forefront in pressuring and partnering with employers to expand the benefits of AI while mitigating its harms. These regulatory efforts are still nascent, but AI's prominence in two major Hollywood strikes and subsequent contracts, as well as the American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organization's (AFL-CIO) partnership with Microsoft, demonstrate labor's important regulatory role in this area.

detail.abstract: Japan's Constitution, enacted in 1946, has never been amended—making it the oldest unamended constitution among current written constitutions. Prior studies have provided important insights into individual sources of institutional rigidity. However, within the scope of the major works reviewed in this paper, these mechanisms have not been sufficiently analyzed as an interdependent cumulative structure, nor systematically connected to the design of an implementation sequence. This paper contributes by reorganizing existing insights into a design-oriented framework for sequential dismantlement. This paper identifies five structural stopping points in Japan's legislative pathway: (A) the high amendment threshold of Article 96, politically entangled with Article 9; (B) the unanimous consent convention in the ruling party's pre-screening system; (C) the House of Councillors' de facto veto power under Article 59; (D) the absence of effective constitutional review; and (E) the chain lock between Articles 9 and 96. These five mechanisms-four active stopping mechanisms and one passive stopping mechanism-reinforce each other, forming a cumulative structure with four brakes and one missing safety device, and zero accelerators. This configuration is not fully captured by Tsebelis's (1995, 2002) actor-centered veto player framework. Drawing on comparative institutional analysis of Germany, France, and the United Kingdom, this paper proposes the Principle of Mutability and introduces the concept of Minimum Viable Change (MVC). It designs a sequential dismantlement strategy that exploits the mutability gradient within the cumulative structure-beginning with the only stopping point that requires neither constitutional nor statutory change. This paper presents an analytical framework and a set of hypotheses derived from structural reasoning rather than empirical testing. Comments and discussion are welcome.

detail.abstract: AgenTrade is a multi-agent algorithmic trading system that produces trade decisions across foreign-exchange, metals, index, energy, cryptocurrency, and micro-futures markets. It is built on a single deliberate principle: a large language model is used only where the task is genuinely open-ended reasoning over ambiguous text, and deterministic code is used everywhere else. This paper is an engineering case study of that principle in practice. It documents the system's architecture, the design decisions that shaped it, and the measured effect of moving work out of language models and into code: a fall in monthly inference cost from roughly $501 to $17 to 27, achieved together with, not at the expense of, determinism, latency, and auditability. The paper also reports a set of production failures and their fixes, several of them silent failures in which the system kept producing confident output from a broken input, and distils the patterns that recur across them, including the distinction between binary flags and weighted scores, the divergence between broker state and client state, and caching on the cadence of the information rather than of the request. The contribution is not a new model or a claimed trading edge; it is a worked, honest example of where the language model should and should not sit in a production multi-agent system.

publicationDetails.detailsText: African Journal of Hospitality, Tourism and Leisure 2025, Vol. 14 No. 4 pp. 904-913

detail.abstract: This research investigates Generation Z's e-commerce behaviour regarding sustainable tourism practices by incorporating the Theory of Planned Behaviour and the Value-Belief-Norm model. A mixed-method approach was employed, integrating quantitative data from 400 surveys analyzed by structural equation modelling and confirmatory factor analysis with qualitative insights from 10 interviews. The findings indicate that internal drivers, including a commitment to sustainability and personal values, are more influential than external factors such as social norms in promoting sustainable behaviour. Financial limitations and systemic restrictions were recognized as impediments, but transparency and confidence in e-commerce platforms strengthen sustainable aspirations. By augmenting the TPB framework with intrinsic values from the VBN model, the study offers pragmatic insights for cultivating trust, overcoming obstacles, and employing educational programs to harmonize consumer values with sustainability objectives. This integration provides a new perspective on sustainable behaviour, assisting businesses and policymakers in advancing sustainable tourism practices.

detail.title: Aid Transitions and Agricultural Productivity: Evidence from Zimbabwe and Zambia after 2000

detail.abstract: This paper describes the structural impacts of foreign aid delivery methods on agricultural sector performance, distinguishing between long-term development capital and short-term humanitarian relief. Leveraging a post-2000 policy divergence where donors redirected Zimbabwe's capital aid entirely into humanitarian relief for political reasons while maintaining Zambia's structural lines, I evaluate a macro-panel of caloric land productivities (1980-2024). Panel estimations (FGLS and autoregressive) show that shifting to humanitarian aid correlated with a severe structural contraction: an immediate 41.32% yield drop that deepens to a 47.78% long-run cumulative loss. These results formalize the "humanitarian trap," demonstrating that emergency relief cannot substitute for capital accumulation.

title: Analysis of Bangladesh’s Largest Budget (2026-27): Economic Impact, Opportunities, and Challenges
affiliations: American International University Bangladesh (AIUB)

detail.title: Analysis of Bangladesh’s Largest Budget (2026-27): Economic Impact, Opportunities, and Challenges
detail.abstract: The proposed national budget for Bangladesh for the fiscal year 2026-27, amounting to BDT 9.38 trillion, marks a significant milestone as the nation approaches its graduation from a Least Developed Country (LDC) status in 2026. This research evaluates the macroeconomic implications of this substantial budget, with a particular focus on its potential impact on inflation and private investment. Employing a Mixed-Methods approach, the study integrates qualitative data from Key Informant Interviews (KII) with 15 leading economists and quantitative analysis using an Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) Regression Model based on 15 years (2010-2025) of time-series data. The regression analysis reveals a significant positive correlation: a 1% increase in the budget deficit is associated with a 0.45% rise in inflation. Furthermore, the study highlights that increased domestic bank borrowing to finance the deficit leads to a substantial "crowding out" effect on private investment. The findings suggest that while the budget positions Bangladesh for mega-projects and LDC graduation, underlying structural weaknesses in deficit financing and revenue administration could destabilize the macroeconomic environment. The paper concludes with data-driven policy recommendations aimed at fostering a stable economic outlook.

title: Who Ate the Lunch? A Belief Propagation Algorithm for Identifying Refund Hunters
affiliations: , Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Bombay and Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Decision Risk and Operations

detail.title: Who Ate the Lunch? A Belief Propagation Algorithm for Identifying Refund Hunters
detail.abstract: For online platforms such as UberEats and DoorDash, a central challenge in customer service is the lack of ground truth: when a customer reports that an order was never received, it is difficult for support agents to determine if the driver kept the food, a passer-by took the delivery, or the customer is falsely claiming a missing order. This fundamental uncertainty often results in platforms shouldering refunds and appeasement costs without holding either side of the market accountable. In this work, we propose a belief propagation (BP) algorithm for identifying strategic customers and drivers, considering both their frequency of platform use and the trustworthiness of the participants they had interacted with. In large markets, we show that our proposed BP algorithm approximately recovers the correct types on the driver side, and achieves the highest statistical power on the customer side. Additionally, there is an exponentially large gap (with respect to the number of orders per participant) in the ratio of false positive rates between our algorithm and a naive benchmark that only relies only on the average past refund rate of each participant. Extensive experiments on both synthetic data and data from our industry collaborator—a major Southeast Asian platform—demonstrate that the BP algorithm provides substantial and robust accuracy improvements.

title: Connected to the Rising Side: Board Political Networks and the Repricing of Firms in South Korea's 2024-2025 Regime Transition

detail.title: Connected to the Rising Side: Board Political Networks and the Repricing of Firms in South Korea's 2024-2025 Regime Transition
detail.abstract: We ask whether the stock market reprices firms connected to the incoming side of a transfer of power, exploiting South Korea's December 2024 martial-law crisis and the impeachment, judicial removal, and election that moved the presidency from the conservative bloc to the progressive opposition. Because Korea bans corporate donations and firms obscure their partisan identities-business groups hedge by placing affiliates on both sides-we hand-collect the political alignment of 1,281 outside directors at the 360 largest listed firms, coding each by the administration that appointed them and validating the measure with an inter-coder reliability check (Cohen's = 0.74). Progressive-connected firms earn an abnormal return of +2.1% (t = 2.5) around the National Assembly vote that suspended the President; conservative-connected firms fall when the opposition first moves against him. The effect survives industry, financial-sector, and state-ownership controls and clustering by business group, is absent in a placebo battery of ordinary trading days, and is concentrated in tight event windows. It concentrates in firms whose rents depend on government allocation and is unrelated to foreign ownership or size, consistent with an expected-rent channel. A connection's direction is priced at the moment power actually transfers-variation available only because democratic power alternates, distinguishing the setting from the one-party connection literature.

title: The MBZ Empowered Athlete Paradox: A Conceptual Framework for Student-Athlete Development in the NIL, Revenue-Sharing, and Transfer Portal Era

detail.abstract:
The purpose of this conceptual paper is to introduce, define, and theoretically ground the MBZ Empowered Athlete Paradox, a student-athlete development framework addressing the structural tension at the center of modern college athletics. The paradox posits that studentathletes have gained unprecedented external power through name, image, and likeness (NIL) rights, revenue-sharing participation, and expanded transfer mobility, while institutional developmental systems have not kept pace with the velocity of decisions athletes must now make.
Drawing on an integrative conceptual review (Jabareen, 2009), this paper synthesizes legal, policy, and scholarly literature across five domains: athlete compensation law; selfdetermination theory; athletic identity and role engulfment; financial literacy; and capacitybuilding leadership. Five findings are advanced: (1) external empowerment has accelerated through legal and economic transformation; (2) autonomy without corresponding competence and support produces developmental instability, even as autonomous experience can itself be developmental under enabling conditions; (3) financial literacy remains an underaddressed gap; (4) NIL and brand expansion may intensify athletic identity in ways that complicate post-sport transition; and (5) athletic departments require a shift from compliance-centered management to capacity-building leadership.
The paper defines the paradox’s two core constructs—External Empowerment and Internal Formation Readiness—proposes a five-domain developmental model, engages the counterargument that empowerment may itself produce developmental readiness, and establishes the institutional developmental obligation specific to athletic departments. Theoretical contributions, implications, limitations, and a future research agenda are discussed. The central claim is that competitive advantage belongs to programs treating athlete development as a strategic operating system, not a supplemental service.
