detail.abstract: This paper introduces a Discretized Digital Twin framework for organizational stability, bridging Leontief's Input-Output analysis with Social Network Analysis (SNA) and Queuing Theory. We propose the spectral radius λ 1 of the corporate technical matrix as a tractable structural proxy for workflow stability. By applying perturbation theory, we provide a principled method for AI investment prioritization. The framework is validated through a case study in a professional dubbing studio.

title: Flexible Jobs in Macroeconomic Stabilization
affiliations: Tilburg University

detail.title: Flexible Jobs in Macroeconomic Stabilization
detail.abstract: Can flexible jobs stabilize aggregate demand? Using euro area data, I document that a larger flexible employment sector is associated with significantly lower consumption and inflation volatility. I explain this finding in a heterogeneous agent New Keynesian model with a dual labor market. After adverse shocks, firms substitute toward flexible vacancies because they are cheaper to create and their wages adjust faster. This shortens unemployment spells and weakens precautionary saving. A larger flexible sector reduces consumption and inflation volatility but increases employment volatility and reduces welfare. For a 5 percentage point increase in the flexible employment share, the welfare loss is approximately 0.8\% of consumption. Thus, flexible jobs stabilize aggregate demand by concentrating employment risk on the workers least able to self-insure.

title: The Safe Asset without the Risk-free Rate: Spanning, Heterogeneity, and the kappa-ladder

detail.title: The Safe Asset without the Risk-free Rate: Spanning, Heterogeneity, and the kappa-ladder
detail.abstract: An interest-free monetary economy has, by construction, no instrument that pays the same in every state: the riskless intertemporal trade is gone. For a representative agent this costs nothing ; the open question is heterogeneity — who loses the missing bond, how much, and whether anything native to the interest-free world replaces it. We answer in three steps. First, in a two-agent general equilibrium with heterogeneous risk aversion we compute the spanning gap directly: the consumption-equivalent value of adding a riskless bond to the equity-only economy is 0.4–24 basis points of lifetime consumption across a wide heterogeneity grid — real, borne mostly by the more risk-averse agent, and small, consistent with the classical incomplete-markets literature. Second, we construct the kappa-ladder — a diversified portfolio of event-intensity claims (sovereign credit, agricultural loss, mortality, project completion) whose risk floor is set by the cross-domain correlation rho_x — and show it recovers 80–98.5% of the spanning gap at residual floor volatilities of 0.5–1%. Third, we ask what rho_x is: the full-universe sukuk panel (273 bonds with daily histories, 42 issuers) gives a measured within-credit correlation of 0.50 — proof that a single-domain ladder barely diversifies and that domains, not names, are the unit of diversification — while forty-four years of cereal-yield shocks give within-agriculture correlation 0.31 even between monsoon-coupled neighbours. With these measured blocks, a four-sleeve ladder (credit, agriculture, mortality, projects) has floor volatility 1.0–1.5% and beats the real-terms volatility of a nominal government bond with as little as one claim per domain. The deepest reframing is the benchmark itself: the "riskless" bond was only nominally safe — its real return always carried the inflation variance of the very printing press the interest-free architecture removes. Diversification across real event domains, not an issuer's promise, is the interest-free world's safe asset — and at measured calibrations it takes one claim per domain to build.

title: Axiomatic Models of Constitutional Interpretation: Originalism, Living Constitutionalism, Textualism, Structuralism, and Pragmatism
affiliations: Delta Economics & Finance

detail.title: Axiomatic Models of Constitutional Interpretation: Originalism, Living Constitutionalism, Textualism, Structuralism, and Pragmatism
detail.abstract: I formalize five leading theories of constitutional interpretation-originalism, living constitutionalism, textualism, structuralism, and pragmatism-as axiomatic decision models sharing a common set of primitives. Each theory is characterized by a distinctive objective function and constraint set, reflecting its core commitments regarding the source of legal authority, the treatment of textual ambiguity, and the permissible role of subjective judicial values. By translating these interpretive frameworks into comparable mathematical structures, I clarify the extent to which each can limit judicial discretion. The models reveal that while originalism and textualism impose the tightest formal constraints, no theory eliminates discretion entirely; textual ambiguity and the inescapable need for normative judgment ensure that residual discretion persists in every constitutional decision. I prove an impossibility theorem showing that complete elimination of discretion is unattainable under any axiomatic interpretation model. I further demonstrate that values and ambiguity interact multiplicatively, with ambiguity amplifying the influence of values. I conclude that the choice among interpretive theories is itself an irreducibly normative act that cannot be resolved by formal constraint alone.

title: Why Growth Does Not Always Strengthen Financial Markets? The Role of Institutions in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations

detail.title: Why Growth Does Not Always Strengthen Financial Markets? The Role of Institutions in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations
detail.abstract: Economic growth is widely expected to deepen financial markets by expanding savings, investment opportunities and demand for credit. Yet this relationship remains surprisingly inconsistent across developing economies. Why does growth strengthen financial markets in some countries but not in others? This study argues that institutional quality is the missing link. Examining nine ASEAN economies over the period 1997-2021, this paper investigates whether institutions condition the effect of economic growth on financial market development. Using fixed-effects panel estimation with panel-corrected standard errors and an interaction between GDP per capita growth and a composite measure of governance quality, this paper finds strong evidence of a non-linear growth-finance nexus. Economic growth significantly expands credit availability in economies with weaker institutions, where unmet financing needs remain substantial. In contrast, the effect diminishes as institutional quality improves, reflecting financial systems that are already structurally developed and less reliant on cyclical growth dynamics. The results remain robust to alternative specifications, additional controls, subsample analyses and the use of individual governance indicators. By revealing how institutions fundamentally reshape the growth-finance relationship, this study contributes to debates on financial development and offers important insights for policymakers pursuing financial integration and inclusive growth in ASEAN.

title: The Variance-Skewness Frontier
affiliations: HEC Montreal - Department of Finance and HEC Montreal - Department of Finance

detail.title: The Variance-Skewness Frontier
detail.abstract: We examine the relationship between the volatility and skewness of returns for randomly constructed, equally-weighted portfolios, and how investors choose between them. Although the expected return of a portfolio is independent of the number of stocks it holds, its expected variance and skewness are not. We show that the variance-skewness frontier is a concave function of portfolio size, with an interior tangency portfolio of approximately 9 stocks. Investors who like positively skewed returns and dislike variable returns can therefore choose their portfolio based on size alone. Our results help explain why mean-variance-skewness optimizers hold underdiversified portfolios.

title: Central Bank Credibility Loss and Financial Market Responses: Event Study Evidence from Turkey's Unconventional Rate -Cutting Cycle
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Central Bank Credibility Loss and Financial Market Responses: Event Study Evidence from Turkey's Unconventional Rate -Cutting Cycle
detail.abstract: This paper examines the financial market consequences of the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey's unconventional rate-cutting cycle between September 2021 and June 2023, during which the policy rate was reduced by a cumulative 1,050 basis points while annual inflation exceeded 80% at its peak. Using an event study methodology, this paper measures the real-time responses of the USD / TRY exchange rate and the 10-year Turkish government bond yield around each of the 22 Monetary Policy Committee decisions in the sample. The findings provide highfrequency, decision-level evidence of a severe and sustained loss of central bank credibility. Rate cuts were systematically associated with exchange rate depreciation and rising long-term bond yields, the opposite of what a credible easing cycle would produce, consistent with the theoretical predictions of a New Keynesian model operating under indeterminacy following a violation of the Taylor principle. The June 2023 policy reversal, a 650 basis point hike under new central bank leadership, produced directionally opposite market reactions, suggesting partial credibility recovery. These results complement the aggregate time-series analysis of Gürkaynak, Kısacıkoğlu and Lee (2023) with granular, decision-level evidence of how markets processed each individual policy announcement in real time. The findings carry broader implications for central bank independence and monetary policy credibility in emerging market economies.

title: Sycophancy and Editorial Compliance in LLMs: Evidence from Climate Misinformation
affiliations: Institut Louis Bachelier,  and

detail.title: Sycophancy and Editorial Compliance in LLMs: Evidence from Climate Misinformation
detail.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as information providers and fact-checkers, playing a pivotal role in shaping public discourse, especially on contentious issues like climate change. We build an experimental framework to assess two alignment-induced behaviors: sycophancy (drift toward user beliefs in conversation), and editorial compliance (refusal when users author misleading drafts). We find that, on the climate topic, conversational correction does not predict editorial refusal and that dispersion concentrates on post-denial discourse, not canonical denial. We also introduce the Climate Sycophancy Resistance Index (CSRI) which allow LLMs ranking on the sycophancy aspects. Our measures reveal strong crossmodel differences with overall scores ranging from 29% to 93.5%, which indicates there is still room for improvement. Model alignment to user preferences is important, but it should not come at the expense of poor scientific grounding.

detail.abstract:
This paper examines whether externally generated housing purchasing-capacity shocks modify housing price–income responsiveness. Building on the equilibrium-responsiveness framework developed in Sintes (2026b), the analysis evaluates whether exogenous variation in purchasing capacity alters the relationship between local income and housing prices in a supply-constrained housing market exposed to heterogeneous external demand.

The empirical setting is the Balearic Islands, a region characterized by strong non-local housing demand and substantial variation in exposure across municipalities. To identify external purchasing-capacity pressure, the paper employs a shift-share (Bartik) design combining predetermined municipality-origin exposure shares with origin-country housing purchasing-capacity shocks constructed from house-price appreciation and exchange-rate-adjusted wealth dynamics.

The results provide limited evidence that external purchasing-capacity shocks exert a homogeneous effect on housing price responsiveness. Aggregate Bartik estimates do not consistently support the benchmark prediction that higher external purchasing-capacity pressure weakens responsiveness to local income. However, origin-specific estimates reveal substantial heterogeneity across external-demand channels. Swiss and Nordic purchasing-capacity shocks are associated with weaker responsiveness, whereas other origin groups display different or statistically insignificant patterns.

These findings suggest that responsiveness effects depend on demand composition and marginal-buyer selection rather than on external demand per se. More broadly, the paper provides the first shock-based empirical test of the equilibrium-responsiveness framework and indicates that origin-specific shocks do not operate through a single homogeneous mechanism.

title: Impact of capping emissions on macroeconomic volatility: The case of Saudi Arabia
affiliations: Universidade de Vigo, University of Milan - Department of Environmental Science and Policy (ESP) and King Abdullah Petroleum Studies and Research Center (KAPSARC)

detail.title: Impact of capping emissions on macroeconomic volatility: The case of Saudi Arabia
detail.abstract: Can the pursuit of net-zero further destabilize oil-exporting economies already vulnerable to oil price shocks? Using an enhanced Environmental DSGE, we examine how different climate policy instruments designed to achieve the same domestic emissions reduction – an absolute cap on CO2, emissions, a fixed CO2 price, and a cap on the carbon intensity of non-oil GDP – affect Saudi Arabia’s macroeconomic volatility. We find that, compared to the absence of emissions reduction policies, an absolute cap stabilizes macroeconomic variables, whereas the price and carbon intensity policies result in higher macroeconomic volatility. The latter two policies, however, yield less volatile CO2 and energy prices. The sign of the correlation between the CO2 price and GDP - and, therefore, of the risk premium to apply for the public valuation of investments in emissions reductions - depends on the policy implemented. Therefore, choosing a climate policy instrument requires considering the trade-offs relating to its impact on economic stability.

detail.abstract: Housing prices are commonly linked to local income, yet the strength of this relationship varies substantially across locations and over time. Existing research documents such variation, but provides limited theoretical guidance regarding why housing price–income responsiveness differs across housing systems. This paper develops a framework in which responsiveness emerges as an endogenous equilibrium outcome rather than a fixed structural characteristic of housing markets. The model considers a supply-constrained housing market with heterogeneous buyers—ordinary local residents, affluent local residents, and external buyers. Under persistent scarcity, equilibrium prices depend not only on aggregate demand conditions but also on the composition of buyers capable of clearing the market. As external exposure increases, equilibrium-clearing participation may progressively shift toward demand segments with different purchasing-capacity structures. This process may weaken the role of ordinary local purchasing capacity in price formation while simultaneously transforming resident composition. As a result, housing prices may become increasingly disconnected from ordinary local affordability while remaining associated with observed local income through endogenous resident-composition change. The framework introduces equilibrium admissibility as a mechanism linking scarcity, affordability, resident transformation, and housing-price formation. More broadly, it proposes that housing price–income responsiveness should be understood as an equilibrium property shaped by scarcity and equilibrium-clearing composition. This interpretation provides a theoretical foundation for understanding why responsiveness may vary across locations, over time, and across exposure regimes.

title: Mutual Intelligibility among Slavic Languages
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Mutual Intelligibility among Slavic Languages
detail.abstract: A large body of work establishes that linguistic distance correlates with the mutual intelligibility of closely related languages. Two questions, however, remain unsettled: how much of that relationship survives out of sample, and which dimension of distance carries the signal once the strong collinearity among dimensions is taken seriously. We address both for the Slavic family, re-analysing published, uniformly collected intelligibility scores for thirty directed language pairs among Bulgarian, Croatian, Czech, Polish, Slovak, and Slovene, together with published lexical, phonological, and syntactic distances and a transparently coded morphological distance. Using leave-one-language-out cross-validation, a model based on linguistic distance alone predicts the intelligibility of an entirely held-out language with R²_CV = 0.63 (permutation p = 0.0005), confirming out-of-sample generalisation. Yet three intuitively appealing refinements do not yield the gains one might expect. First, a Shapley (LMG) decomposition shows that lexical and phonological distance are statistically indistinguishable co-predictors and that roughly eighty per cent of explained variance is shared among dimensions, so the common practice of naming a single "most important" predictor by stepwise selection is not defensible. Second, weighting edit distances by corpus word frequency-a natural operationalisation of mental-lexicon activationdoes not improve and tends to degrade prediction across four weighting schemes. Third, the intelligibility asymmetries that distance models famously fail to capture are shown to be nonstructural: directed lexical-distance asymmetry is essentially uncorrelated with intelligibility asymmetry (r =-0.11), and the single large asymmetry in the sample (Slovene-Croatian) is attributable to exposure rather than structure. We conclude that linguistic distance is a robust but coarse predictor whose ceiling is set by non-structural factors, and we argue that out-of-sample evaluation and variance partitioning should replace in-sample stepwise regression as the default in intelligibility research.

title: Automation and Involuntary Unemployment
affiliations: Yildiz Technical University - Department of Economics and Bogazici University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Automation and Involuntary Unemployment
detail.abstract: Which policies best mitigate automation-induced involuntary unemployment? A common view favors universal basic income (UBI) financed by robot taxes. We examine this in an efficiency-wage model with heterogeneous skills and task-based automation. We show instead that the optimal policy sets both UBI and robot taxes equal to zero whenever wage taxes and subsidies are available. Robot taxes distort adoption decisions, while UBI leaves shirking incentives unchanged. Targeted wage subsidies redistribute income and at the same time decrease total unemployment. Simulations calibrated to U.S. data confirm that optimal wage taxes and subsidies reduce total unemployment and inequality, and, moreover, increase total output. When wage instruments are unavailable, however, robot-tax-financed UBI can still improve low-skilled workers' welfare even under risk-neutrality.

detail.title: The Asymmetric Impact of Oil Price Demand and Supply Shocks on Financial Constraints

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of International Financial Markets, Institutions & Money

detail.abstract: By separating aggregate oil price shocks into demand and supply components, we examine their effects on firm-level financial constraints using 60,925 firm-year observations from 2002-2021 across 65 countries globally. Controlling for year and firm fixed effects, we find that oil demand shocks are negatively related to firms' financial constraints. In contrast, oil supply shocks dampen firms' ability to obtain external financing. Additional analysis reveals that the impact of oil price shocks on financial constraints is more pronounced for firms belonging to the oil industry, oil users, oil-related and non-oil substitute subsectors, and for firms in non-oil-exporting and oil-consumer countries. We further observe that competitive industries and high market liquidity exacerbate the impact of oil price shocks on financial constraints. Our mechanism tests show that profitability and investment decrease (increase), while production costs, sales volatility and cash flow volatility increase (decrease) in response to oil price supply (demand) shocks, all of which are signs of firms experiencing binding (unbinding) financial constraints. Our main findings are robust to various modelling techniques and measures of financial constraints.

detail.abstract: The European Union (EU) has continued to be a worldwide leader in setting international norms, particularly in competition law policy, data protection and platform governance. In digital market regulation, after the EU Digital Markets Act (DMA), several countries have adopted or are considering the adoption of digital markets competition regulations (DMCR) similar to the DMA. While some have challenged the notion that the DMA and its goals of ensuring contestability and fairness in the market should not be the blueprint for adopting DMCRs in other countries, at this juncture, it is impossible to overstate the influence of the EU DMA on future DMCRs. We contribute towards this scholarly debate on the influence of the DMA beyond the EU by focusing on a region that, despite competition agencies' regulatory enforcement in digital markets, has not received adequate scholarly attention: Africa.

detail.abstract: Traditional "digital divide" frameworks, fixated on binary metrics of physical access, fail to reflect the complex, mutually constitutive relationship between technological system and social stratification. This paper reconceptualizes digital exclusion by shifting the analytical focus from mere connectivity to digital social inequality. Guided by Halford and Savage's (2010) paradigm, we synthesize three foundational sociological frameworks rarely discussed together: T.H. Marshall's theory of social citizenship, Amartya Sen's Capability Approach, and Pierre Bourdieu's theory of capital. By mapping these theories onto the tripartite dimensions of Access, Skills, and Outcome, we argue that digital inclusion is not a neutral leveling mechanism, but a deeply stratified process of accumulating and converting "technical capital." Empirically, this theoretical architecture is operationalized within the intersecting stratifications of gender, caste, and geography in Nepal, utilizing data from the Nepal Living Standards Survey (NLSS-IV). We demonstrate how structural barriers mediate the convertibility of digital skills, frequently resulting in a "digital reproduction of inequality" where marginalized groups are systematically prevented from translating digital engagement into tangible socioeconomic mobility. While grounded in the specific socio-cultural topography of Nepal, this synthesized framework transcends its local boundaries, offering a universally applicable analytical lens for global scholars and policymakers to investigate how socio-technical networks actively produce, stabilize, and reproduce social inequalities across diverse international settings.

title: Comparative Advertising and Trademark Disputes in the Digital Age: An Analysis of India's Legal Framework for Social Media Comparative Advertising

detail.title: Comparative Advertising and Trademark Disputes in the Digital Age: An Analysis of India's Legal Framework for Social Media Comparative Advertising
detail.abstract: Comparative advertising has historically occupied a controversial position within Indian trademark law. Whilst permissible in principle, such advertising has been fettered by the two fundamental principles that it must be done honestly and must not denigrate competitors. The recent migration of brand communications onto digital channels (Instagram, YouTube and Twitter/X, in particular) has spawned a whole new genre of comparative advertising dispute, a type of issue not originally contemplated under the scope of the Trade Marks Act, 1999. The purpose of this paper is to analyze the framework that the Indian trademark law affords comparative advertising on social media, focusing on the interaction between Sections 29 and 30 of the Act and the principles of honest use and denigration with respect to the modes of advertising practiced on the various digital platforms. Using Indian judicial decisions, Advertising Standards Council of India's Digital Guidelines and what may still be a sparselytrodden area of Indian law, being comparative advertising online, this paper argues that the existing Indian legal architecture is structurally unsuitable for the resolution of comparative advertising disputes on social media, and provides a platform-specific, multi-factor contextual test for use in Indian court proceedings. The paper culminates with proposals for amendment of the existing legislation and for the establishment of a higher judicial standard.

detail.abstract: Investing based on high book-to-price (B/P) has been dubbed a "value" strategy, and "value" factors have been constructed based on the measure. detail.title: Reconciling AI Innovation With Copyright Values – Why Reliance on Individual Licences is not Enough

publicationDetails.detailsText: IViR Research Paper 2026, Amsterdam: Institute for Information Law

detail.abstract:
To ensure appropriate remuneration for the use of human literary and artistic works in the development and exploitation of generative AI models, both individual licensing and collective remuneration solutions have been proposed. The analysis sheds light on the heated discussion about the best remuneration mechanism and contrasts the current trend towards individual licensing with potential advantages of collective approaches that take AI output as a reference point. In principle, the increasing number of licence deals between AI developers and rights holders in the creative industries is a positive development. However, individual licensing is unlikely to offer equal chances for large and small repertoire owners. In particular, individual authors and performers may have difficulty to receive a fair share of the revenue accruing from GenAI licences. Moreover, the licence approach reduces the cultural diversity of GenAI models.

Against this backdrop, it is important to develop a more inclusive regulatory approach that ensures access to diverse training resources and fair remuneration for all authors and rights holders. To achieve this goal, a collective remuneration scheme is needed that offers fair remuneration when literary and artistic output is generated using weights, vectors and parameters that have been derived from human works during the AI training process. The adoption of this output-based remuneration system appears as a necessity rather than a mere policy option to avoid an unreasonable prejudice to legitimate author and rights holder interests in the sense of the European and international three-step test.

detail.title: Readiness Assessment of Ethiopian Higher Education Institutions for Artificial Intelligence (AI) Adoption

detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming higher education by creating new opportunities for enhancing teaching, learning, research, and institutional management. However, the successful adoption of AI depends on institutional readiness, technological capacity, human competencies, and supportive governance frameworks. This study assesses the readiness of Ethiopian higher education institutions for AI adoption by examining AI awareness, institutional preparedness, current AI applications, perceived opportunities and challenges, and factors influencing AI adoption practices. A quantitative research approach was employed using data collected from 318 faculty and staff members from selected Ethiopian public universities. Descriptive statistics and Ordered Logit, Ordered Probit, and Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression models were used to analyze the data. The findings indicate that Ethiopian higher education institutions demonstrate moderate readiness for AI adoption. While respondents reported growing awareness of AI and recognized its potential benefits for teaching, research, and institutional transformation, institutional support mechanisms, including AI training, policies, technical support, and funding, remain insufficient. AI adoption was positively and significantly influenced by AI knowledge and awareness, institutional readiness, AI integration in teaching and learning, and AI integration in institutional management. Conversely, technical, organizational, and governance challenges significantly constrained AI adoption. The study highlights that institutional readiness is the strongest determinant of AI adoption practices. The study concludes that Ethiopian higher education institutions possess emerging foundations for AI adoption but require strategic interventions to strengthen digital infrastructure, develop AIrelated policies, enhance human capacity, and establish effective governance frameworks. The findings provide important implications for policymakers and university leaders seeking to promote responsible and sustainable AI integration in higher education.

detail.abstract: Rapid advances in artificial intelligence have renewed concerns that earlier automation forecasts may understate the range of occupations exposed to technological change. This paper provides an ex-post assessment of how U.S. occupational labor-market outcomes evolved during a period of rapid AI advancement. We combine Frey and Osborne's (2017) estimates of occupational computerization risk with Tomlinson et al.'s (2025) AI applicability scores based on Microsoft Copilot usage, matching both measures to O*NET occupational classifications and U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics employment and wage data for 2019 through 2024. We first assess how recent developments in robotics, large language models, and generative AI have narrowed the engineering bottlenecks that Frey and Osborne identified in perception and manipulation, creative intelligence, and social intelligence. We then compare employment and wage changes across occupations with high and low AI applicability scores and across occupations classified as having high, moderate, or low probabilities of computerization. The results complicate a simple displacement narrative. Occupations with high AI applicability scores experienced overall employment and wage growth between 2019 and 2024, while occupations with high and moderate automation-risk scores experienced weaker employment performance than low-risk occupations. Wages increased across all automation-risk groupings. These patterns suggest that exposure to AI and automation does not map mechanically onto job loss, at least in the short run, and that task-based measures of technological exposure are better understood as indicators of occupational restructuring than as direct forecasts of employment decline.

title: Inclusive (Intellectual) Properties
affiliations: SciencesPo

detail.title: Inclusive (Intellectual) Properties
detail.abstract:
Property and intellectual property are creatures of western legal modernity, fundamentally and historically shaped by the liberal ideology of possessive individualism. At the core of property, and intellectual property, is the right to exclude others from using the resource. Yet, property is a plastic instrument that can be strategically used to share a resource and include others. In intellectual property particularly, there are several cases where the right has been exercised to organize and imagine a more inclusive production process and use entitlements (eg, open collaborative creation, copyleft licensing, traditional knowledge and cultural expressions, public domain).

In the overall storytelling of (intellectual) property, such cases are seen as oddities or exceptions to the rule of exclusivity. I propose to add a story in that narrative around a new notion of inclusivity and inclusive properties to designate those situations where several people share the use of a resource without the possibility of totally excluding others. Rather than speaking of non-exclusive properties, the term ‘inclusive’ denotes a positive approach: communality of use and non-exclusion is not a lack, a defect, but a fullness. It is not the absence of exclusion that defines it, but the presence of inclusion, the flip side of exclusivity. Adding inclusive properties to the monolithic model of exclusive property enables some deconstruction of that paradigm and rhetoric, and its consequences (namely, its extractive and individualistic norms), as well as a transformation of intellectual property from a technique of commodification to an experiment of alternative exercise of rights, and collective practices of creation and innovation, of community-building and belonging.  Instead of looking at intellectual property as a market device, it could highlight its diversity as a mode of participation to a cultural sphere.

Banking crises are commonly associated with bank runs and banking panics, yet our empirical understanding of bank runs is constrained by a lack of bank-level data. In a new paper, we use large language models (LLMs) to extract information on bank runs from millions of digitized historical newspaper pages, creating the most comprehensive database of bank runs in U.S. history. Every bank run episode that we identify is documented on a companion website where users can browse and examine individual episodes, and read the original newspaper articles. In this post, we describe how we built this dataset and discuss what its basic features reveal.

detail.title: When Green Policies Backfire: Deforestation and Sri Lanka’s Fertilizer Ban
detail.abstract: Economic regulations often generate unintended consequences beyond their intended scope. We exploit Sri Lanka's abrupt 2021 nationwide ban on chemical fertilizer imports as a quasi-natural experiment to identify how hard input constraints reshape land-use decisions. Comparing areas differentially exposed based on agronomic suitability for fertilizer-intensive crops, we find a 135% increase in deforestation in high-dependency areas, alongside declining rice yields, consistent with farmers substituting land expansion for lost productivity. Protected areas substantially attenuated this response, nearly fully offsetting the ban's cumulative effect in fully covered cells, suggesting conservation policy provides effective protection when external shocks sharply raise deforestation incentives.

title: Carbon Taxes versus Cap-and-Trade under Uncertainty Shocks

detail.title: Carbon Taxes versus Cap-and-Trade under Uncertainty Shocks
detail.abstract: This paper compares dynamic outcomes under a carbon tax and an emissions cap when the economy is hit by productivity uncertainty shocks in a two-sector New Keynesian setting. It shows that price and quantity instruments cease to be close substitutes once abatement is costly to adjust, with consequences for both volatility and welfare. The main results are: (i) compared to a tax, the quantity instrument yields lower volatility and higher welfare under dirty-sector productivity uncertainty, but higher volatility and lower welfare under clean-sector uncertainty; (ii) the magnitude of the volatility and welfare gaps is governed by the ease of adjusting abatement; and (iii) the two policies are otherwise close substitutes when abatement is freely adjustable, with taxes and caps generating near-identical aggregate dynamics and differing substantially only on the emissions and abatement margins.

detail.abstract:
Runs on financial institutions are one of the salient markers of financial crises. But the role of runs in crises is a topic of longstanding debate. Runs can be seen as the key turning point, whereby even small shocks can generate severe crises with widespread bank failures. Another view is that runs are mainly a symptom of deeper rot in the financial system, exacerbating crises rather than being their primary cause. Understanding this debate has first order implications for how to think about financial crises and the appropriate policy responses. In this post, we use a new database of more than 3,000 bank runs (introduced in our companion post) to show that poor fundamentals are central to explaining both when runs occur and when they have severe economic effects. We argue that this evidence tempers the view that small shocks can have outsized real effects through self-fulfilling run dynamics.

detail.title: Heat Stress and Labor Share: Evidence from Indian Manufacturing
detail.abstract: Climate change poses significant challenges to labor markets in developing countries, where workers face high exposure to extreme heat and firms have limited adaptive capacity. This paper examines how heat stress affects the labor share—measured as labor compensation relative to firm sales—using a large panel of Indian manufacturing firms. Exploiting within-firm temperature variation over time, we find that heat stress significantly reduces the labor share, with results robust across alternative specifications. This decline is driven primarily by production adjustments, especially capital-labor substitution. We also present suggestive evidence that heat stress may strengthen firms’ market power and interact with labor regulations in shaping firm responses. Combining our estimates with climate projections, future warming is likely to intensify labor share declines across regions. Our findings identify climate change as an important and underexplored driver of distributional change in developing economies.

detail.abstract: Using a novel dataset on U.S. natural disasters and high-frequency measures of economic activity, we evaluate the effectiveness of federal disaster assistance. Exploiting quasi-random variation in whether aid from the Federal Emergency Management Agency is granted or denied, we compare otherwise similar events. States receiving aid recover within 20 weeks, whereas denied states face deeper and more persistent contractions. Recovery is stronger when aid is timely and generous, and includes direct transfers. Pre-disaster mitigation lowers future disaster frequency and costs, while stronger fiscal capacity enhances resilience by enabling governments to sustain post-disaster recovery.

title: LLM Generated Regression Results vs. Specialized Econometric Software (STATA)
affiliations: International Islamic University Malaysia

detail.title: LLM Generated Regression Results vs. Specialized Econometric Software (STATA)
detail.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer unprecedented assistance in economic research, yet researchers often mistakenly trust these tools to perform native statistical calculations on raw data. This paper exposes the mathematical limitations of LLMs and proposes a structured workflow for safely integrating artificial intelligence into econometric analysis. The proposed three-phase strategy enables researchers to use LLMs for conceptualization and code generation while ensuring that all final computations are executed in dedicated econometric software such as Stata. Through a detailed case study involving household income transfer data and quantile regression, this paper demonstrates that LLM-generated statistical outputs can produce fabricated coefficients that contradict empirical findings derived from authentic computation. The results confirm that while LLMs serve as effective cognitive assistants for structuring research designs and generating preliminary code, they cannot substitute for the deterministic mathematical operations required in rigorous econometric analysis. This paper contributes to the growing literature on responsible AI integration in the social sciences by offering a practical, replicable methodology that preserves scientific validity while improving the productivity gains when using AI tools.

title: Econstellar: An Open-source AI-augmented Research Engine for Computational Financial Econometrics

detail.title: Econstellar: An Open-source AI-augmented Research Engine for Computational Financial Econometrics
detail.abstract: A reader of an empirical paper is ordinarily asked to trust its numbers, because the means of checking them is not supplied. The first version of Econstellar, an open research engine for financial econometrics, addressed part of that difficulty by serving the computations behind our published work from a public web address, so that a result could be rerun rather than taken on trust. This second version makes the checking machinery itself the subject. Each of the twenty-three served methods, seventeen in the first version, six added since now, ships with a public, failable evaluation: an expected value with a stated source, a live re-run , and a verdict that renders red on the public page when it fails, because the suite is never edited to pass. Headline empirical claims carry robustness badges graded against pass rules registered before any grid of re-estimations was run, and claims we have not tested appear as explicit untested rows rather than as silences. The reproduce-the-paper facility distinguishes a genuine rerun that matches a published number exactly; a directed contagion figure to a difference of 0.0000, a channel-attribution table to 0.000 percentage points, a Hurst panel to within 4.882 × 10-9 from results that remain honestly pending. A daily systemic-connectivity index now appends itself each morning without an operator, recomputed in full from the stored panel; we state plainly that it is not the validated index of the accompanying study. One pre-registered analysis was re-anchored after its baseline failed to reproduce a published value, and the amendment is documented rather than concealed. The system is open-source and live at a public address. Our aim is unchanged from the first version, but stricter: that a research claim should arrive together with the apparatus for doubting it.

detail.abstract: Macroeconomic stylised facts (SF) are essential for understanding the inherent nature of an economy and for the calibration of theoretical models. However, the conventional approach to deriving these facts—typically involving log-transformation, mechanical detrending (growth cycle approach) and point estimation—is fraught with methodological limitations that distort the true statistical properties of time series. This paper proposes a novel approach that prioritises the preservation of the original data-generating process. By adopting a growth rate cycle approach without log-transformation and utilising the rolling estimation technique instead of static point estimates, the proposed methodology captures the temporal evolution of an economy and its response to structural shocks. Applying this novel approach to the Indian economy for the period 1996:Q2 to 2023:Q3, we demonstrate that traditional point estimates fail to reflect the dynamic nature of macroeconomic regularities, particularly in the post-pandemic era. Our findings highlight significant shifts in volatility, cyclicality and persistence across key variables, providing a more robust and durable framework for policy formulation.

title: Fiscal Narratives and Inflation
affiliations: Heidelberg University and

detail.title: Fiscal Narratives and Inflation
detail.abstract: This paper investigates how media narratives on fiscal policy shape household's inflation expectations. We collect a large corpus of newspaper articles reporting on fiscal policy from four major German newspapers spanning from 2006 to March 2025. Using a large language model (ChatGPT) we introduce a strategy to automatically identify different fiscal narratives in text and construct narrative indices out of this data. We then estimate the effect of these narrative indices on household inflation expectations and find that they all have a positive significant effect varying in size. Lastly, we measure how fiscal narratives affect the transmission of a government spending shock to the economy and find that some of the narratives have an amplifying effect while others dampen the impact.

title: Liveness under Macro Winters: Mechanism Design for Fee-Only Blockchains

detail.title: Liveness under Macro Winters: Mechanism Design for Fee-Only Blockchains
detail.abstract: Every blockchain whose consensus layer is financed purely by transaction fees — by design (zero-emission chains) or by destiny (Bitcoin as its block subsidy decays) — faces a liveness hazard that emission-funded chains conceal: in the aftermath of a persistent macroeconomic shock, transaction volume can remain below validator operating cost for months. We show the binding risk is the duration of such "winters," not their depth, and that the intuitive remedy — counter-cyclical fee multipliers — is both pro-cyclical for users and manipulable by the validators who produce the volatility measurements. We propose instead a pre-funded mutual support pool (a liveness sleeve) with three design commitments: a conjunction trigger (volume and a stress index, each sustained, so that the one signal validators control never suffices alone); a shortfall payout capped at a published reference operating cost; and a slow payout decay whose role, we show, is not to discourage idleness but to make a validator's receipts strictly increasing in its own honest fee income — without decay, censoring one's own fee base is payoff-neutral inside the subsidised state. Under the shortfall structure, censorship aimed at forcing the trigger is strictly dominated whenever the support floor lies below normal income (Proposition 1). Monte-Carlo experiments on six-year paths with heterogeneous validators locate the feasible design window — replacement ratio beta in [1.2, 1.6] of reference cost with decay at most 4% per week — and a reinforcement-learning adversary (a 35%-stake cartel free to censor up to 75% of transactions) converges to near-zero censorship, never beating honesty on matched evaluation episodes. Survival of a thirty-validator set through a black-swan winter (volume -85%, half-life twelve months) rises from 56% to 77% with the sleeve in place. The mechanism requires no emission, no fee increases on distressed users, and no discretionary bailout authority.

detail.abstract: Medicare home health and hospice services represent a documented federal program integrity priority. This paper develops and validates an unsupervised anomaly detection and risk stratification framework applied to 11,501 Medicare-certified providers (5,730 home health agencies, 5,771 hospices) with at least 11 beneficiaries in the 2023 Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Post-Acute Care Utilization Public Use File. The framework combines a weighted statistical risk layer using eight engineered features per provider type with an Isolation Forest machine learning layer using fixed hyperparameters (contamination 0.02, 100 estimators, random seed 42). The Composite Risk Score weights the two layers at 60 percent statistical and 40 percent machine learning, and stratifies providers into five percentile-based tiers. At the 95th percentile cutoff the framework flags 287 home health agencies and 289 hospices for investigative review. Directly observed sample excess against state median peer benchmarks is $156.0 million for home health and $133.3 million for hospice.

title: The κ-Chain: A Sovereign Islamic Financial Infrastructure Layer

detail.title: The κ-Chain: A Sovereign Islamic Financial Infrastructure Layer
detail.abstract:
We propose the κ-Chain: a sovereign Layer 1 blockchain whose native monetary primitive is the convergence intensity κ, derived from the random stopping time representation of perpetual futures contracts (Ackerer, Hugonnier & Jermann 2025), rather than the risk-free interest rate r that underlies every existing financial blockchain. The theoretical foundation rests on six working papers (Ahmed & Bhuyan 2026a–e; Ahmed 2026f) that establish: (i) the interest parameter ι is separable from and eliminable from no-arbitrage pricing (the Separation Theorem); (ii) κ is formally isomorphic to the hazard rate λ in the Duffie-Singleton credit framework, giving a complete riba-free pricing foundation for perpetual contracts, sukuk, takaful, and credit default swaps; (iii) the κ-yield curve can be estimated empirically from sovereign sukuk spread data across GCC and Southeast Asian markets; and (iv) these results are computationally validated against a live deployed protocol (Baraka Protocol, Arbitrum Sepolia). 
The κ-Chain is not a blockchain that adds Islamic financial products as applications. It is a blockchain where ι = 0 is the substrate — present in every transaction, every block reward, every pricing primitive — because the absence of interest is not imposed as a constraint but is the natural language of the pricing mathematics. We describe the full architecture, the validator economics, the monetary policy implications for central banks in OIC-member states, and a three-phase roadmap from the currently deployed Baraka Protocol v3 testnet to a sovereign Cosmos appchain. We document honestly what is built, what is proven, and what remains to be done.

detail.abstract: Medicare Part B injectable drug waste represents a documented federal program integrity priority. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services adopted the JW modifier in January 2017 and the JZ modifier in July 2023 specifically to enable systematic analysis of discarded amounts from single dose vials. The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 Section 11001 created a manufacturer refund obligation for discarded amounts above 10 percent. This paper presents the Medicare Waste Anomaly Risk Index (MWARI), an unsupervised composite risk scoring framework for detecting anomalous Medicare Part B injectable drug waste patterns. The framework integrates six engineered features (waste rate, waste dollars, waste to spending ratio, five year compound annual growth, low volume billing flag, and Inflation Reduction Act refund eligibility) through a weighted statistical layer combined 60/40 with an Isolation Forest machine learning layer. The system processes the complete 2023 analytical universe of 823 HCPCS codes and identifies 42 drugs in the top 5 percent risk tier with sample excess waste of approximately 550 million dollars (95 percent bootstrap confidence interval 338 to 809 million). Validation is performed through six procedures: 1,000 iteration bootstrap (flagged count coefficient of variation 0.0153), permutation feature importance, three year provider level temporal holdout (coverage 88.8 percent, mean lift 14.3 times), Office of Inspector General List of Excluded Individuals and Entities concordance, Department of Justice defendant cross reference, and threshold sensitivity. The framework is appropriate for unsupervised settings where no labeled fraud ground truth exists. All source data is publicly accessible from data.cms.gov and oig.hhs.gov. The complete analytical pipeline, results files, and reproducibility envelope are publicly available.

title: The Organizational Capability Management Theory of Procurement: Capability Access and Capability Availability as Procurement's Primary Outputs

detail.title: The Organizational Capability Management Theory of Procurement: Capability Access and Capability Availability as Procurement's Primary Outputs
detail.abstract: Procurement scholarship and practice define the function by its activities-spend management, sourcing, contracting, supplier management-leaving it without a distinctive theoretical object and exposed to the charge that what it buys, rivals can buy too. This paper proposes a theory in which procurement's object is neither spend nor suppliers but the organization's portfolio of external capabilities: capacities residing outside the legal boundary of the firm on which mission delivery depends. Under this Organizational Capability Management (OCM) view, suppliers are capability providers, contracts are capability-access mechanisms, and governance is the system that preserves capability availability over time. The function's primary outputs are therefore capability access-an exercisable means of obtaining a defined external capability when required-and capability availability-the persistence of that access under perturbation. The distinction is operationally consequential: access is documentary and observable, while availability is counterfactual until tested, so organizations systematically over-measure the first and under-measure the second. A signed contract is access; whether it holds under disruption is availability. Capability demand originates with stakeholders pursuing organizational deliverables, so the portfolio is derived from mission, not managed for its own sake; and access carries a present tense and a future tense-current access to capabilities in use, and frontier access to capabilities that may become mission-relevant-making innovation the forward form of the access output, co-equal with continuity as the stressed form of availability. The paper states the theory as eight propositions, positions it against the resource-based view, dynamic capabilities, the relational view, transaction cost economics, and the capability-sourcing literature-claiming the inversion of perspective, not the ingredients-derives business continuity and innovation as corollaries rather than adjacent functions, supplies an access/availability decomposition with measurable constructs for each component, and develops seven differential predictions on which the capability view and the prevailing spend view recommend different decisions. Scope conditions, limitations, and a research agenda are stated explicitly.

title: Holding Up the Market: Government Ownership, Corporate Signals, and the Limits of Intervention

detail.title: Holding Up the Market: Government Ownership, Corporate Signals, and the Limits of Intervention
detail.abstract: We study when and how government intervention transmits to equity prices, using Korea's 2024-2026 "KOSPI 7000" episode, in which the value-weighted market rose 191 percent with no identifiable net buyer. We argue that the market is inelastic not to demand in general but to the permanent and informational demand that arbitrage cannot offset, and we identify this distinction by contrast: anticipated, arbitrageable KOSPI 200 index reconstitutions are absorbed and leave no permanent price effect, whereas two government-created shocks are capitalized. First and most cleanly, a staggered difference-indifferences design-robust to self-selection under not-yet-treated controls-shows that Corporate Value-up disclosures raise a firm's price-to-book ratio by about 10 percent over eight months, an effect driven by concrete, verifiable commitments and mediated by selective foreign inflows. Second, the National Pension Service supports prices through the level of its holdings rather than the flow of its trades: it cut its domestic-equity weight from 21 to 11.5 percent over 2021-2024, and the rebound to 21 percent reflects price appreciation, not purchases. Third, the rally is largely a semiconductor revaluation (56 percent of the index gain) that the market accommodated with negligible net flow. Market inelasticity is conditional on the arbitrageability of demand.

title: Inflation Attention Thresholds Before and After the Inflation Peak
affiliations: National Bank of Slovakia and National Bank of Slovakia

detail.title: Inflation Attention Thresholds Before and After the Inflation Peak
detail.abstract: We study whether the inflation threshold that triggers household attention survives during disinflation. Using Google Trends data for 21 Eurozone countries plus the US, UK, and Switzerland during the 2021-2023 inflation surge, we estimate attention thresholds before and after peak inflation. In roughly half of the sample, no post-peak threshold emerges and attention declines linearly rather than through a regime switch. Structural-break tests reject symmetry in the inflation-attention relationship based on Google Trends in every tested country. For the United States, the data suggest a higher post-peak threshold, though this finding does not replicate under alternative attention proxies. We corroborate our main findings with GDELT news-coverage data.

title: The Right-Skew Puzzle in Chinese Equities
affiliations: Zhejiang University, Zhejiang University and New York University

detail.title: The Right-Skew Puzzle in Chinese Equities

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: The standardized innovations of daily Chinese A-share returns are predominantly right-skewed — a shape that risk models consume directly, yet one without an established explanation. On 538 CSI 800 constituents (2016–2026), the fitted Hansen skewness is positive for 99.3% of stocks (median +0.095), is robust to asymmetric-volatility filters, survives the exclusion of all price-limit days, and has a Bowley quantile measure of approximately zero: the asymmetry lives purely in the right tail. Two quasi-experiments dissect its causes. The 2020 ChiNext reform doubled daily price limits and sharply cut limit hits (first stage t = -4.4), yet innovation skewness did not move (minimum detectable effect 0.21, or 0.28 standard deviations): price limits are not the cause. Gaining shortability lowers tail skewness in the dominant 2019 margin-list expansion (-0.22, p = 0.02); the pooled estimate across batches is not significant, so we label this evidence suggestive. In the cross-section, right skew concentrates not in classic lottery stocks but in large, ordinarily quiet names with intermittent upside jumps. The bill is paid on the short side: a symmetric t understates 99% short-position Expected Shortfall in every skewness tercile, and the skew-t repair is monotone in the fitted skewness.

title: NBFI and Government Debt in Asia: Legal and Policy Implications

detail.title: NBFI and Government Debt in Asia: Legal and Policy Implications
detail.abstract:
This paper examines the evolving role of non-bank financial institution (NBFI) in Asian government debt markets and the associated regulatory and systemic challenges. It begins by defining and classifying NBFI, highlighting their growing importance in debt intermediation and providing an overview of government debt markets across key Asian economies, including China (Mainland), Japan, India, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (Hereinafter SAR), and Singapore. Asia provides an early-warning environment where sovereign–NBFI linkages are growing before crisis-scale amplification seen in advanced economies. The study then analyzes the legal and regulatory landscape, comparing international standards on market access, capital adequacy and prudential oversight with regional practices.

A central focus is on the policy challenges arising from NBFI activities. This thesis began by analyzing the debate to regulate NBFI which includes information asymmetry and the gap of access to central banks between banks and NBFI. Then it’s followed by the discussion on the market trend given the growing reliance on NBFI in the government debt market. Consequently, the paper identifies issues as a result of such a shift.

Based on these findings, the study offers policy recommendations from three perspectives: ex ante mechanisms, ex post mechanisms and continuing regulatory monitoring mechanism to strengthen oversight of NBFI and safeguard financial stability. By integrating lessons from international frameworks and regional experiences, the paper provides a comprehensive perspective on managing NBFI-related risks in government debt markets while maintaining efficient capital allocation.

title: Whether The Environmental Clearance in India is a Progressive Step towards the Protection of the Environment, or a Disguise in Reality?
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Whether The Environmental Clearance in India is a Progressive Step towards the Protection of the Environment, or a Disguise in Reality?
detail.abstract:
One of the most essential instruments of environmental governance in India is the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA), which is intended to make sure that a project's environmental effects are assessed prior to implementation. This preventive approach is reflected in the EIA Notification, 2006, which requires prior environmental clearance for certain projects. However, there are now major concerns about the performance of the environmental regulatory framework due to the increasing practice of ex post facto environmental clearances.

This paper examines the legal and constitutional validity of retrospective environmental clearances in India. It tracks the development of the EIA framework, examines how executive notifications gave rise to the ex post facto clearance regime, and analyses the judicial reactions in important rulings including Alembic Pharmaceuticals, Common Cause, Vanashakti, and CREDAI. The research argues that retroactive clearances violate the goals envisaged by the Environment (Protection) Act of 1986, diminish environmental accountability, and weaken the precautionary principle.

The paper further argues that ex post facto environmental clearances shift environmental assessment from a preventive precaution to a mechanism for regularizing infractions by analysing concepts of delegated legislation, natural justice, legitimate expectation, and the rule of law. It finds that earlier environmental clearance must be viewed as a substantive legal necessity rather than a procedural formality that may be validated retroactively in order for environmental governance to continue to be successful.

title: Fundamentals in Management Causal Discussions
affiliations: Australian National University, RSFAS and Australian National University (ANU) - Research School of Finance, Actuarial Studies and Applied Statistics

detail.title: Fundamentals in Management Causal Discussions
detail.abstract: We propose a novel framework of extracting fundamental characteristics from textual data based on causal sentence structures. Preserving the causal relationship by separately extracting topics from cause and effect parts of sentences result in improved information processing compared to simple topic analyses. Peer firms identified from this causality-based topic analysis show strong return comovement both at the monthly level and around earnings announcements. Returns of smaller firms, more central firms, firms with higher market beta and idiosyncratic volatility can be predicted by their peers' returns. Fundamental news seems to travel more from bigger firms to their smaller, less transparent peers with simpler operations, and from earlier announcers to their later announcing peers. Evidence supports the efficacy of considering causal sentence structures in extracting information.

title: NetZeroNomy: A Unified Net-Growth Formula Integrating Four-Component Capital, Governance Efficiency, and Mandatory Depletion Accounting
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: NetZeroNomy: A Unified Net-Growth Formula Integrating Four-Component Capital, Governance Efficiency, and Mandatory Depletion Accounting
detail.abstract:
Background: Gross Domestic Product (GDP), the dominant economic measure since Kuznets (1934), systematically excludes natural capital depletion, governance quality, and the multiplicative dynamics of sectoral integration. Despite decades of critique and alternatives including the Inclusive Wealth Index (UNEP, 2023), the Genuine Progress Indicator, and Doughnut Economics (Raworth, 2017), no prior framework has proposed a single mathematically unified formula capturing all four deficiencies simultaneously.
Methods: We derive NetZeroNomy v3.1, a formula for Net Economic Energy (Enet) that integrates: (i) a four-component capital base Capt = Captn + Capth + Captm + Capts, calibrated against SEEA (UN et al., 2021) and IWI (UNEP, 2023); (ii) a governance confidence gate G(p) ∈ [0,1] as a structural multiplicative operator; (iii) a four-vector sectoral synthesis term Vⁿ with integration depth n = Σᵢωᵢ; and (iv) a mandatory depletion penalty ΔCapt(−) = Σᵢ max(0, Captᵢ(t−1) − Captᵢ(t)). A formal sustainability constraint S(t) ⊇ S(t−1) is derived from the Brundtland definition (WCED, 1987).
Results: The formula satisfies three scientific consistency conditions: precision (each symbol has exactly one referent), consistency (no double-counting across terms), and completeness (no hidden assumptions). Applied to the Ho Chi Minh City – Binh Duong – Vung Tau mega-region, the framework predicts that raising G(p) from 0.32 to 0.68 and increasing integration depth n from 1.1 to 2.8 would produce Enet growth exceeding 11–13% per annum without additional capital investment.
Conclusions: NetZeroNomy offers the first growth theory in which sustainability and economic expansion are structurally inseparable rather than traded off. The framework is empirically tractable, policy-actionable, and positions ΔCapt (−) as the critical unmeasured variable in current national accounts.

title:
From Pay-per-Call to Flat Rate:
Two-part Tariffs, Deadweight Loss, and Surplus Distribution in Indian Telecom
affiliations: Indian institute of technology delhi

detail.title:
From Pay-per-Call to Flat Rate:
Two-part Tariffs, Deadweight Loss, and Surplus Distribution in Indian Telecom
detail.abstract: India's telecom sector underwent a structural transformation after Reliance Jio's entry in September 2016, shifting the industry from per-minute and per-megabyte pricing to bundled flat-rate plans. This paper uses the theory of two-part tariffs to examine whether Indian telecom pricing, before and after Jio's disruption, can be read through the lens of surplus extraction, deadweight loss, and market power. The central argument is that the pre-Jio pricing regime, characterized by high per-unit charges and negligible fixed fees, was consistent with a monopolist operating well above marginal cost and generating substantial deadweight loss. Jio's entry forced prices toward marginal cost and restructured the industry's tariff design into something much closer to the two-part ideal: a fixed monthly subscription paired with effectively zero per-unit charges on voice and data. This shift reduced deadweight loss and reallocated surplus from incumbent firms to consumers, though at the cost of severe revenue compression across the industry. The postconsolidation period after 2021, as a reduced set of three private operators has steadily raised fixed fees, represents a partial reversal of these gains.
