title: Is a Land Restoration Boom Required in India?
affiliations: IIM Jammu and University of Delhi

detail.title: Is a Land Restoration Boom Required in India?

publicationDetails.detailsText: HRC Journal of Economics and Finance, Volume 2, Issue 1 (Jan-March, 2024) ISSN: 2583-8814 (Online)

detail.abstract: India's forest policy aims to achieve a 33% tree cover nationwide, yet the current tree cover stands at 24.56% as reported in the ISFR 2021 report. As per official sources, a major focus for achieving this target has been put on the Trees outside forest (TOF) regions. Despite witnessing extensive tree planting within short durations, concerns about their sustainability persist. Research has highlighted the dismal failure of such initiatives due to factors such as inadequate maintenance, low survival rates, insufficient study on suitable saplings, and the absence of post-evaluation reports. This paper thereby proposes land restoration companies as a potential solution to assist India in realizing its ambitious targets. Their maintenance ethic is what differentiates them and gives them a comparatively higher success rate. Further, by breaking down the economics behind these companies, the paper tries to prove how they are more cost-effective than initiatives taken up by the government in the long run. Lastly, the research delves into the challenges encountered by such companies, specifically examining funding and land-related issues. The study culminates by proposing measures necessary to bolster a restoration boom in India.

title: Personnel Professionalization and Judge Performance: Evidence from China's Judge Quota Reform
affiliations: , School of Economics, Jinan University and

detail.title: Personnel Professionalization and Judge Performance: Evidence from China's Judge Quota Reform
detail.abstract: Do personnel professionalization reforms that remove lower-ability bureaucrats enhance or reduce performance? In a tournament-theoretic model, these reforms seek to improve performance through selection of higher-ability agents. However, they also alter incentives for remaining incumbents: peer pressure increases effort, while reduced competition decreases it, leading to an ambiguous net effect. We investigate this question by exploiting China's 2014 Judge Quota Reform, a largescale professionalization that eliminated approximately 40% of judges. Using a novel dataset of over sixteen million first-instance judgements from about 2,700 courts, we find that a one-percentage-point increase in the judge elimination rate improves performance (proxied by lower textual similarity between judgements) by 0.05 percentage points. A magnitude accounting reveals that the positive selection effect dominates the net negative influence from altered effort incentives. Our results manifest a critical trade-off in state capacity building: the lasting benefit of a higher-ability workforce incurs a persistent cost by weakening effort incentives, underscoring the necessity of complementary incentive structures in reform designs.

title: Common Vendors and Systemic Cyber Risk in Banking
affiliations: Aalto University School of Business and

detail.title: Common Vendors and Systemic Cyber Risk in Banking
detail.abstract: Banks increasingly rely on common technology vendors, trading scale economies for shared exposure. Because a widely used vendor is a more valuable target for a strategic attacker, outsourcing raises systemic risk through a single point of failure. Two distortions follow. Banks and vendors internalize their own losses but ignore those borne by depositors and customers, so the market over-concentrates. Deposit insurance prevents runs but weakens the private discipline that vendor pricing would otherwise provide. Correcting both requires pricing concentration at its marginal external cost-through capital, vendor charges, or vendor liability-a prescription that extends to other shared financial infrastructure.

title: Spatiotemporal Simulation of Multi-Operator Regional Transit Using GTFS Data: An R Pipeline for Public Participation in Transportation Policy
affiliations: Nanzan University

detail.title: Spatiotemporal Simulation of Multi-Operator Regional Transit Using GTFS Data: An R Pipeline for Public Participation in Transportation Policy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: The accurate visualization of regional public transit is essential for sustainable urban planning and evidence-based policymaking. Many municipalities still face "data deserts" where official General Transit Feed Specification (GTFS) data is unestablished or its publication has been discontinued, while existing dynamic simulation tools often rely on complex, server-side infrastructure that presents high barriers to entry. This study presents a lightweight, infrastructure-free R-based pipeline that automatically converts static GTFS data into dynamic GeoJSON formats, enabling flicker-free spatiotemporal transit visualization. The pipeline's efficacy is demonstrated by constructing an integrated, multi-operator regional transit simulator for Chita City, Higashiura Town, Obu City, and commercial Chita Bus lines. Additionally, an ongoing, experimental pilot model for Agui Town—where official GTFS distribution has been discontinued—is briefly presented to illustrate the technical boundaries and challenges of third-party data reconstruction from public documents. The pipeline affords a reproducible baseline platform for the evaluation of cross-boundary transit connectivity and collaborative consensus-building.

title: Commonwealth and War: Body, Bond, and the Default of Plural Sovereignty

detail.title: Commonwealth and War: Body, Bond, and the Default of Plural Sovereignty
detail.abstract: The idea of the commonwealth has named two different things. It has named a body: a multitude united under a common power for a common good, from Cicero's res publica to Hobbes's civitas. And it has named a bond: an association of sovereigns who share a good without sharing a power, from the Achaean koinon to the Commonwealth of Nations and the Commonwealth of Independent States. This paper tests both forms against the problem each was meant to solve, the problem of war. Drawing on bargaining theory, I show that a definable class of goods whose value derives from being taken without consent cannot enter any bargain; that coercion consumes the room for agreement to a finite point of no return; and that war is therefore the default output of any plurality of armed sovereignties, however thickly bonded. The two modern commonwealths of states supply the natural experiment, and war between members recurred in both. The body fares no better at the global scale, since a single world commonwealth would maximise the organisational capture that manufactures war from within. The concept's own history then does what neither form can do alone: the commonwealths of Cicero, of Hobbes, and of Kant's warning name three distinct types of the world body, and the type, not the bare existence, determines what its violence becomes. The commonwealth, I conclude, is best understood not as an answer but as the standing question of how to hold plurality to a common good.

title: One Person Companies in India: A Decadal Assessment 2014-2024
affiliations: and Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad

detail.title: One Person Companies in India: A Decadal Assessment 2014-2024
detail.abstract: One Person Company (OPC) was introduced in India under the Companies Act, 2013, and registrations began in 2014 with the first official data release in 2015. An OPC is defined as a company that has a single shareholder. By design, OPCs are meant to offer sole proprietors the benefits of a corporate structure, including a separate legal identity, limited liability, the ability to convert into other types of companies, along with minimal administrative burdens and compliance requirements. OPCs, have been in existence for over a decade, and amendments to the law are now being contemplated. This study outlines the legal framework governing OPCs and undertakes an empirical analysis of key performance parameters over the ten-year period from 2014 to 2024.

title: The Consumer Value of Ad Personalization: Evidence from Meta
affiliations: Meta Platforms Inc, Northwestern University and Northwestern University

detail.title: The Consumer Value of Ad Personalization: Evidence from Meta

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Deisenroth and Manjeer are employees of Meta and own stock in that company. Wernerfelt is a part-time contractor for data access; his salary is donated to charity.

detail.abstract: An apparent tension that has emerged in regulating digital advertising centers on the use of detailed consumer data. If advertisers can use more data in their ad delivery, there is evidence ad effectiveness will increase; in contrast, some believe the use of such data may pose potential privacy risks or other harms to consumers. These privacy concerns have motivated a large share of regulation around the world, yet there is little evidence on how consumers actually value being served ads based on more versus less data. In this paper, we conduct a large-scale field experiment with 12 million Facebook users where some were randomly assigned to receive less personalized ads. Our treatment condition leverages the 'less personalized ads' experience that Meta created in response to demands from the European Commission. Combining both log data and custom surveys, we estimate effects on more than 40 outcome variables to paint a holistic picture of the consumer experience. We have two main findings. First, under decreased ad personalization, not only do the average levels of ad engagement fall substantially, but users report both less satisfaction with their ads experience and a decreased user valuation for the platform overall. Second, leveraging detailed user demographics from Meta, we conduct a heterogeneity analysis to study if any sizable subgroups exist that appear to increase their engagement meaningfully under decreased ad personalization. We find no evidence of such groups. Net, our results are consistent with ad personalization in this context conveying benefits, not costs, to consumers.

title: When is a Composite Response a Structural Primitive?

detail.title: When is a Composite Response a Structural Primitive?
detail.abstract: A local response is often used as if it were a structural primitive: observe how behavior moves under one incentive, then ask what would happen under another. This paper asks when that step is valid. The di!culty is that an observed response is a composite of productivity, cost, measurement, and capacity primitives. It remains a faithful object only on domains where those primitives move together. At a frontier-a capacity limit, an eligibility threshold, or a notch-the response can fan out into distinct components and stop supporting the counterfactual. I characterize the response's validity domain, the counterfactuals that survive after fan-out, and the minimal regime information that restores a point answer. The framework is a triage step between the general Lucas warning and bespoke structural modeling: a pre-structural diagnostic for fan-out, a specification-free identified set for what survives, and the least extra object that repairs the counterfactual. A public-data diagnostic at the conforming-loan limit, where a documented response is known to be composite, illustrates how the object is visible in administrative data.

title:
Evaluating the Adoption Rate of Climate-resilient Farming Practices in Rural Maharashtra: 
A Case Study of RRI Skill and Knowledge foundation Interventions

detail.title:
Evaluating the Adoption Rate of Climate-resilient Farming Practices in Rural Maharashtra: 
A Case Study of RRI Skill and Knowledge foundation Interventions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they are affiliated with the RRI Skill and Knowledge Foundation, the institution responsible for the agricultural training interventions evaluated in this study. This research was conducted to evaluate program efficacy, and the authors declare no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have inappropriately influenced this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: For this case study, verbal and written informed consent was obtained from all participating farmers prior to data collection. Field metrics and household performance parameters have been strictly anonymized to protect participant privacy.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported and funded through the internal institutional resources and program budgets of the RRI Skill and Knowledge Foundation.

detail.abstract:
Smallholder farmers in the semi-arid West Maharashtra region face severe and accelerating climate vulnerabilities, compounded by extreme structural dependencies on volatile chemical-input cash crop systems. This paper presents an empirical impact evaluation of a targeted, multi-tiered behavioral and technical training intervention deployed by the RRI Skill and Knowledge Foundation across a sample of N = 240 agrarian households (consisting of 120 treatment and 120 control farmers). Utilizing a robust Difference-inDifferences (DiD) estimation framework, we analyze multiseason variations in agronomic productivity, total operational expenditures (OpEx), and net household profitability across three regional anchor crops: Cotton (Kapas), Soybean, and Pigeon Pea (Tur). 

Our behavioral framework evaluates the efficacy of community-embedded Vikas Mitras (peer agricultural leads) and seasonally aligned micro-learning modules engineered to systematically reduce the acute risk premiums and loss aversion that typically stymie organic transition processes. The empirical results reveal an elegant economic paradox: while initial transition phases experience a planned stabilization or marginal compression in absolute crop yields (ranging from 4.17% to 9.33%), the complete eradication of commercial synthetic inputs yields a profound, systemic reduction in out-of-pocket operational expenditures (ranging from 45.24% to 53.16%). Consequently, net farm profitability increases immediately and significantly across all three crop portfolios. Furthermore, the localized decentralization of bio-input formulation effectively insulates smallholders from exploitative informal credit channels, providing a highly scalable, financially autonomous operational blueprint for regional climate adaptation policies across semi-arid developing economies.

title: Price Dispersion and Inflation: New Cross-sectoral and International Evidence

detail.title: Price Dispersion and Inflation: New Cross-sectoral and International Evidence
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between price dispersion and inflation, shedding light on one major source of the cost of high inflation. By analyzing novel product-level web-scraped data from over 60,000 restaurants and supermarkets across 18 countries facing high and low inflation periods, I uncover new evidence of a significant positive correlation between inflation and price dispersion. My findings reveal that the average annualized inflation, ranging between zero and 20 percentage points across countries within a condensed time frame, is significantly associated with higher price dispersion in both the restaurant and supermarket sectors. The estimates indicate that the marginal effect of suboptimal inflation on product-level distortions is positive, economically significant in all inflation environments and heterogeneous across sectors. Cross-sectionally, I find that an increase of annualized inflation from zero to 10 percent increases inefficient price dispersion for supermarkets by 46% and for restaurants by 73%. Finally, the relationship between inflation and price dispersion does not flatten much at higher inflation, so that the marginal cost of additional inflation does not vanish as inflation rises -- a pattern standard menu-cost models do not generate. This indicates a sustained impact of inflation on price dispersion, implying that accommodating higher inflation levels incurs substantial welfare costs.

title: Ostrovskii's Arithmetic of Probability Laws
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Ostrovskii's Arithmetic of Probability Laws
detail.abstract: The arithmetic of probability laws studies factorization of measures under convolution. The analogy with integer arithmetic is real but breaks in three ways: factorization is not unique, indecomposable laws are abundant, and the whole theory is analytic, because factoring a law means factoring its characteristic function. We give a proof-oriented account from Cramér (1936) through Khinchin, Linnik and Marcinkiewicz, then survey I.V. Ostrovskii's program (1960s-1990s): the class I 0 of laws without indecomposable components, ridgefunction generalizations of Marcinkiewicz's theorem, the resolution of Linnik's conjectures on the class L, the multidimensional theory, the class I α 0 , the zero sets of entire characteristic functions, and Kingman's semigroup. Throughout we supply the analytic background-Hadamard factorization, the strip of analyticity, Phragmén-Lindelöf indicators, Nevanlinna deficiency-needed to read the statements. We close with the links to the Laguerre-Pólya class and the Riemann Ξ-function, to Pólya frequency functions and total positivity, to generalized gamma convolutions and Thorin measures, and to arithmetic on abelian groups.

title: Stablecoin Depegging, Financial Intermediary Balance Sheet Constraints, and Liquidity in the U.S. Traditional Money Market
affiliations: East China Normal University (ECNU), East China Normal University (ECNU) and East China University of Science and Technology - School of Business

detail.title: Stablecoin Depegging, Financial Intermediary Balance Sheet Constraints, and Liquidity in the U.S. Traditional Money Market
detail.abstract: As the stablecoin market has expanded rapidly, the linkages between stablecoins and the U.S. traditional money market have grown increasingly close. This paper examines the dynamic effects of stablecoin depegging on liquidity in the U.S. money market. We develop an analytical framework for money market liquidity that incorporates stablecoins, and demonstrate how depegging events transmit liquidity stress to the traditional money market by tightening the balance sheet constraints of financial intermediaries. Empirical analysis based on local projections reveals significant market heterogeneity: liquidity in the Treasury bill market follows a non-monotonic path, improving initially before subsequently reversing; liquidity in the commercial paper market deteriorates significantly on the day of the shock; and liquidity deterioration in the repo market exhibits a delayed peak. Further analysis indicates that the impact of depegging on intermediary balance sheets is primarily reflected in a rise in the marginal cost of expanding balance sheet capacity, rather than a substantial drawdown of capital. When intermediary capital is under stress, liquidity deterioration across all three markets is significantly amplified. These findings provide empirical evidence of risk coupling between crypto-asset markets and traditional money markets, with policy implications for the design of macroprudential regulatory frameworks for stablecoins.

title: Design and Simulation-Based Feasibility Study of a Resilient Offline-First Campus Mesh Network for Federal Polytechnic Monguno
affiliations: Federal Polytechnic Monguno, Federal Polytechnic Monguno and Federal Polytechnic Monguno

detail.title: Design and Simulation-Based Feasibility Study of a Resilient Offline-First Campus Mesh Network for Federal Polytechnic Monguno

declarations.ethicsApproval: FPM/REC/IBR/2026
declarations.funderStatement: IBR/2026/FPM

detail.abstract: Federal Polytechnic Monguno operates in one of Nigeria's most digitally isolated environments. Situated in Borno State a region still recovering from the devastating impact of insurgency the institution contends daily with near-total absence of stable internet connectivity, leaving both staff and students cut off from the digital tools that modern polytechnic education demands. Students cannot reach research databases, e-learning platforms, or digital libraries. Staff struggle to share files, conduct meetings, or submit institutional reports through digital channels. Administrative processes that should take minutes stretch into hours, and the broader academic mission of the institution suffers as a consequence. This paper presents a simulation-based feasibility study investigating whether a resilient, solar-powered, offline-first wireless mesh network can provide a practical solution to this digital exclusion challenge. Rather than assuming ideal conditions, the study is grounded in Monguno's actual operational realities unreliable grid power, weak telecom coverage, limited technical capacity, and a post-conflict infrastructure environment. Using wireless mesh networking parameters drawn from comparable low-infrastructure campus scenarios, the study models network topologies, evaluates node placement strategies, estimates bandwidth performance under local usage patterns, and develops a cybersecurity threat assessment appropriate to community-scale academic networks. Findings confirm that an offline-first mesh architecture is technically feasible for Federal Polytechnic Monguno, provided deployment follows a phased approach with strategic node placement, renewable energy integration, and foundational cybersecurity controls. The study recommends that TETFund and institutional management priorities localized campus networking infrastructure rather than awaiting broader national broadband expansion an approach that enables meaningful digital participation independent of external connectivity. The proposed architecture offers a replicable model for similarly underserved tertiary institutions across Nigeria's NorthEast .

title: When Does the Pie Rule Fail? Equilibrium and Instability in Derivative Contracts with Mutual Swap Rights on an Additive Lattice

detail.title: When Does the Pie Rule Fail? Equilibrium and Instability in Derivative Contracts with Mutual Swap Rights on an Additive Lattice
detail.abstract: We propose a stylized derivative contract inspired by the "pie rule" in combinatorial games: both counterparties hold mutual swap rights allowing either to reverse positions at any time, subject to a fixed exercise cost 𝑐. We formalize this Reciprocal Swap Right Option (RSRO) as a discrete-time sequential stopping game on an additive binomial lattice and characterize its equilibrium properties. Three results emerge. First, under symmetric information and distributional symmetry, the unique subgame perfect equilibrium is fair-neither party is systematically advantaged (Theorem 1). Second, when one party holds private information about the underlying's drift, adverse selection breaks fairness: under a restricted prior-rule equilibrium, the informed party exercises selectively, exploiting the uninformed counterparty (Proposition 10). Third, in a multi-party extension with perpetual-futures-style funding, under a simplified aggregate exercise rule with ordered-queue timing, initial imbalance triggers cascading exercise-a "swap rush" exhibiting strategic substitutability (Theorem 3). The critical threshold 𝑐 * = 2(𝑇-1)𝜎 delineates the region where swap rights discipline fairness without deadweight loss.

title: Money, Inflation and Monetary Policy Regimes in India: Evidence from VAR and Time-Varying Models

detail.title: Money, Inflation and Monetary Policy Regimes in India: Evidence from VAR and Time-Varying Models
detail.abstract: Can money growth still provide useful information about inflation in an era of inflation targeting? This paper revisits this question for India using monthly data from 1992 to 2025 and examines how the money-inflation relationship has evolved across successive monetary policy regimes. Combining cointegration analysis, VAR and VECM models with rolling and Time-Varying Parameter VAR techniques, the study evaluates both long-run monetary linkages and short-run predictive dynamics under changing policy frameworks. The results reveal a persistent long-run relationship between money growth and inflation but little stable short-run predictive power. Monetary transmission is found to be highly regime dependent, with stronger effects during the multiple-indicators framework and substantially weaker effects under the interest-rate corridor and inflation-targeting regimes. Forecasting exercises further show that models allowing for structural change outperform conventional specifications. The findings suggest that money aggregates retain diagnostic value but are of limited use as short-run operational policy instruments.

title: Do Perpetual Futures Dampen or Amplify Speculative Bubbles?

detail.title: Do Perpetual Futures Dampen or Amplify Speculative Bubbles?
detail.abstract: Perpetual futures are symmetric instruments: longs and shorts post identical margin, and zero net supply pairs every levered position with its opposite. We graft one onto a resale-option bubble market whose single asymmetry is that buying requires storage while shorting requires borrowing. Symmetry delivers a neutrality benchmark; its failure makes the funding rate the published shadow price of the short-side constraint. Leverage and borrow capacity trace a dampening-amplification boundary with an absorbing region. Endogenizing arbitrage capacity yields multiple equilibria, a supply fold, a capacity trap, and an equilibrium-dependent leverage threshold. Under belief neutrality, welfare rises; funding-rule standards dominate leverage caps.

detail.abstract: We study the indirect economic consequences of natural disasters for households using high-quality household-level data from Norway. Universal natural disaster insurance in this setting fully compensates direct physical damages, allowing us to isolate indirect effects. Linking a municipality-level measure of disaster severity to detailed transaction data measuring household expenditures, and using a matched difference-in-differences design, we find large and persistent effects on consumption: the cumulative spending fall up to four years after an event amounts to as much as 45 percent of the direct damages. Population-wide administrative records on income, wealth, housing transactions, and labor-market outcomes allow us to uncover the underlying mechanisms. First, labor income falls while unemployment increases after disasters, particularly when damages are concentrated among firms, consistent with disruptions to local labor markets. Second, housing wealth declines persistently, and homeowners cut spending more than renters despite similar income losses. Our results show that the household costs of natural disasters extend beyond the insured value of destroyed property, as households remain exposed to losses transmitted through local labor and housing markets.

title: Which Stock Screens Actually Work? A Survivorship-free Audit of 16 Fundamental Metrics — ROIC, Value, Momentum, and Quality — on the S&P 500 (2010–2024)

detail.title: Which Stock Screens Actually Work? A Survivorship-free Audit of 16 Fundamental Metrics — ROIC, Value, Momentum, and Quality — on the S&P 500 (2010–2024)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of Zyberno.com, a venture that applies fundamental-analysis research of the kind audited here, and therefore has a professional and prospective financial interest in this research area — though he presently draws no income from the venture and funds its operation himself. This is disclosed in the interest of full transparency. The study is designed to be resistant to author bias: the universe is mechanically defined and survivorship-free, every screen is evaluated with the same pre-stated, benchmark-invariant statistics, null results are reported in full, and the complete dataset and replication pipeline are published (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20650537) so that any reader can independently reproduce — or refute — every result.

detail.abstract:
Which stock screens actually work? We audit sixteen fundamental screens on the complete, survivorship-free S&P 500 (2010–2024) and find that return on invested capital (ROIC) is the most predictive of them all. ROIC's rank correlation with five-year forward excess returns is +0.11, its top-minus-bottom quintile spread is +3.0 percentage points per year, and its edge holds in both halves of the period (Fama-MacBeth t = +5.9). The textbook sustainable-growth screen — ROIC × reinvestment rate — does not work: it multiplies a positive factor (profitability) by a negative one (reinvestment), and the two cancel; we call this the sustainable-growth paradox. Value was the weakest family of the era: book-to-market was the single worst screen tested (−0.13) — a faithful portrait of the quality-led 2010–2024 regime, not a verdict on value investing. The celebrated academic quality screens fade on large caps: ROE, gross profitability (Novy-Marx), accruals (Sloan), the Piotroski F-score, and asset growth all sit near zero, and ROIC beats ROE — the most popular quality metric — seventeen-to-one on identical firms. After risk adjustment, no screen earns significant alpha: every long-short portfolio's intercept against the Fama-French five factors plus momentum has |t| < 1, so on the large-cap S&P 500 these screens deliver factor tilts, not a free lunch.

The audit is built to be trusted. The universe is the complete point-in-time S&P 500 — every constituent-year, including firms later acquired or delisted — with dividend-reinvested total returns, filing-date entry, and CRSP-style delisting handling. We also show why common backtests flatter themselves: roughly 72% of S&P 500 stocks underperformed the cap-weighted index, so a one-sided screen scores ~72% "accuracy" with no skill at all; honest evaluation requires benchmark-invariant statistics, which we use throughout. The full dataset and code are published so every result can be reproduced, extended to other regimes, or refuted.

Companion paper: "The Brina Gap: A Framework for Identifying Growth Mispricing in Equity Markets" (Working Paper v3.0), DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20651608.

title: Financing Higher Education Through Equity, Not Debt: The Case for a Graduate Tax
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Financing Higher Education Through Equity, Not Debt: The Case for a Graduate Tax
detail.abstract: How should higher education be financed when neither full public funding nor conventional student loans deliver on the promises of equity and efficiency made on their behalf? This article evaluates the three principal financing models-full public provision, income-contingent loans (ICLs), and a graduate tax (GT)-against a common normative benchmark: education free at the point of use, with costs allocated according to the beneficiary-pays principle. I argue, first, that full public funding is structurally regressive, subsidising the predominantly affluent population that captures the graduate premium out of general taxation. Second, while ICLs correct the capital market failure that justifies state intervention, they do so through a debt instrument that allocates the entire risk of variable graduate earnings to the individual borrower. A graduate tax, by contrast, is an equity instrument: repayment is a function of realised income rather than a predetermined debt, providing superior insurance against poor labour-market outcomes and a closer approximation of the theoretically optimal tax on the graduate premium. Third, drawing on behavioural economics, I argue that the GT mitigates debt aversion among low-income students, weakens the commodification dynamic that pushes students towards narrowly remunerative degree choices, and aligns universities' financial interests with the long-run professional success of their graduates. The article concludes by addressing standard objections to the graduate tax-hypothecation, emigration, and transition costs-and drawing implications for the design of higher education funding reform.

title: Exact Robustness Radius of Positional Scoring Rules via Greedy Allocation

detail.abstract: How many voters must change their rankings to overturn an election outcome? This paper provides an exact characterization of positional scoring rules, including plurality, Borda, and $k$-approval. We study the minimum number of ranking modifications required for the runner-up to catch up to the winner; the same analysis applies to any challenger, so the full margin of victory can be obtained by minimizing over all challengers. To analyze this problem, we introduce the \emph{reduction potential} of a voter, defined as the maximum possible reduction in the winner--runner-up score gap achievable by modifying that voter's ranking alone. The robustness problem then reduces to an additive covering problem. Our main theorem gives an exact greedy characterization: the robustness radius equals the smallest integer $k$ such that the cumulative sum of the $k$ largest reduction potentials is at least the initial score gap. This yields an $O(n(m+\log n))$ algorithm, and an $O(n)$ algorithm when the number of candidates $m$ is fixed. We further show that the linear programming relaxation satisfies the exact ceiling relation $\lceil R_{\mathrm{LP}}\rceil = R$. Moreover, using majorization theory, we prove that robustness decreases as voter influence becomes more concentrated. Experiments on synthetic impartial-culture elections and five real-world preference profiles from the PrefLib library (Netflix Prize~ID~00004, AGH Course Selection~ID~00009, T-Shirt Design~ID~00012, Clean Web Search~ID~00015, and Mechanical Turk Dots~ID~00024) illustrate the theoretical findings and demonstrate practical efficiency.

title:
Digital Leakage or Financial Inclusion?
The Unintended Effects of M-pesa on Household Savings in Rural Kenya

detail.title:
Digital Leakage or Financial Inclusion?
The Unintended Effects of M-pesa on Household Savings in Rural Kenya

contentType.other: A paper I have written and I would like it published

detail.abstract: Mobile money technology, typified by Kenya's M-Pesa, has been widely celebrated as a vehicle for financial inclusion and poverty alleviation in Sub-Saharan Africa. Launched in 2007 by Safaricom, the platform now serves over 40 million active users and processes transactions exceeding Kenya's annual GDP, making it one of the most consequential financial innovations in the developing world. Yet the relationship between M-Pesa adoption and household savings behaviour-particularly in rural Kenya-remains empirically contested. While a dominant body of literature documents consumption smoothing, poverty reduction, and increased savings rates among M-Pesa users, emerging evidence suggests that the frictionless liquidity enabled by mobile money may also induce what this paper terms "digital leakage": the unintended erosion of household savings through increased impulsive spending, intensified social transfer pressures, and substitution of disciplined informal savings institutions with more accessible but less commitment-binding digital wallets. Drawing on an integrative review of empirical literature published between 2011 and 2024, FinAccess household survey data (2019, 2021, 2024), and secondary data from the Central Bank of Kenya and Safaricom, this paper undertakes a critical and theoretically grounded analysis of M-Pesa's dual effects on rural household savings. The paper constructs a conceptual framework that reconciles competing theoretical predictions from standard lifecycle savings theory, behavioural economics, and social capital theory. Our findings reveal that M-Pesa's effects on savings are heterogeneous and condition-dependent: while it demonstrably expands access to formal and semi-formal savings instruments and buffers rural households against idiosyncratic shocks, it simultaneously facilitates transfer network obligations and lowers behavioural commitment thresholds that previously anchored informal saving. Policy implications for digital financial product design, regulatory frameworks, and rural financial literacy programmes are discussed.

title: Can Free Zone Entities Import Petroleum Products Into Free Zones and Transfer Them Into Nigeria’s Customs Territory Without NMDPRA Licences Under the PIA?

detail.title: Can Free Zone Entities Import Petroleum Products Into Free Zones and Transfer Them Into Nigeria’s Customs Territory Without NMDPRA Licences Under the PIA?

keywords: Petroleum Industry Act NEPZA; OGFZA; Free Zones; Export Processing Zones; Oil and Gas Free Zones; Petroleum Importation; Petroleum Regulation; Customs Territory; Dangote Refinery; Petroleum Licensing;; Concurrent Jurisdiction; Customs Law; Energy Law; Oil and Gas Law; Transfer Pricing; Tax Incentives; Regulatory Compliance; Administrative Law; Nigerian Petroleum Sector; Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Operations; Free Zone Regulation; Import Licences; Regulatory Risk; Nigerian Energy Regulation.

detail.abstract:
This article examines the unresolved interaction between Nigeria’s free zone regime and the petroleum regulatory framework established under the Petroleum Industry Act 2021 (“PIA”), particularly in relation to the importation of petroleum products into Nigerian free zones and the subsequent transfer of such products into Nigeria’s customs territory for domestic supply. The issue has assumed increasing commercial significance in light of recent policy developments aimed at reducing petroleum importation and promoting domestic refining capacity following the operational commencement of the Dangote Refinery.

The article considers whether Free Zone Enterprises (“FZEs”) established under the Nigeria Export Processing Zones Act (“NEPZA Act”) or the Oil and Gas Export Free Zone Act (“OGFZA”) may lawfully import petroleum products into free zones without obtaining licences, permits, and approvals from the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (“NMDPRA”), and thereafter evacuate those products into Nigeria’s customs territory outside the licensing and supervisory framework established under the PIA.

Drawing from the PIA, the NEPZA Act, the OGFZA, subsidiary legislation, and principles of statutory interpretation, the article argues that the customs and fiscal incentives granted under Nigeria’s free zone framework do not displace the sector-specific licensing and regulatory regime established under the PIA. The article further contends that neither the NEPZA Act nor the OGFZA expressly excludes petroleum operations within free zones from the NMDPRA’s jurisdiction and that the preservation provisions contained in the free zone legislation support the continued applicability of the PIA to petroleum importation activities conducted within free zones.

The article also examines the customs, tax, transfer pricing, and regulatory risks associated with attempts to utilise free zone structures as a mechanism for circumventing petroleum importation controls and downstream licensing requirements. In addition, it highlights unresolved issues concerning concurrent regulatory jurisdiction, the sequencing of approvals, and the absence of a coherent operational framework governing interactions between free zone authorities and petroleum regulators in Nigeria.

The article concludes that although petroleum products may lawfully be imported into Nigerian free zones, subject to applicable approvals, there is presently no sufficiently clear statutory basis to conclude that free zone entities may import petroleum products outside the NMDPRA licensing framework solely by reason of their free zone status. The article therefore underscores the urgent need for clearer regulatory coordination among the NMDPRA, NEPZA, OGFZA authorities, and the Nigeria Customs Service in order to promote legal certainty, regulatory coherence, and commercial predictability within Nigeria’s petroleum sector.

detail.abstract: Federal Medicare improper payments totaled 31.70 billion dollars in fiscal year 2024, with Part D accounting for 3.58 billion dollars. Existing supervised approaches to Part D prescriber risk detection commonly suffer from label leakage when the OIG List of Excluded Individuals and Entities (LEIE) is merged without time-stamped filtering, inflating accuracy metrics that collapse under honest temporal validation. This paper presents a national-scale anomaly detection framework that analyzes the full universe of 1,380,665 Medicare Part D prescribers using six engineered features, a statistical z-score risk layer, and an Isolation Forest unsupervised machine learning layer. The framework applies explicit EXCLDATE filtering of LEIE labels, computes permutation feature importance, bootstrap confidence intervals, and reports temporal holdout validation through coverage and persistence rather than supervised classification. Of 69,034 providers flagged at the 95th percentile of combined risk score, 65,023 (97.61 percent) reappear in the 2023 universe with mean cost per beneficiary of $8,414 versus population mean $979, yielding 8.59x mean lift. The AUC of the combined risk score against the 2023 newly-excluded LEIE target is 0.417, below random, demonstrating that LEIE concordance is a surveillance signal rather than a fraud probability validation. The methodology, code, and persisted result files are publicly available for verification.

title: Direct Electrical Energy Extraction from Fusion Plasma [PDEE 1.0] Part Two: The Mechanisms

detail.title: Direct Electrical Energy Extraction from Fusion Plasma [PDEE 1.0] Part Two: The Mechanisms

detail.abstract: This paper, the second in a two-part study, examines the other two proposed mechanisms for the direct electrical extraction of energy from magnetically confined fusion plasmas—MHD rotational separation (MHDRS) and high-Z radiative photo-conversion (HZRPC)—and contextualises them within the broader landscape of direct energy conversion through a comparative survey of existing DEC concepts. Building on the unified Hamiltonian framework established in Part One, each mechanism is analysed as a trajectory within a control-vector space whose coordinates (the X-factors) quantify the geometric, spectral, and kinetic coupling between the plasma and an external extraction structure. The classification of extraction channels into distinct H-subspaces—bulk kinetic, wave-particle, and radiative—provides a common coordinate system in which otherwise disparate concepts can be compared on equal physical footing. For MHDRS, a limitation theorem is derived showing that the geometric coupling penalty in closed-field-line toroidal geometry renders inductive rotational extraction sub-threshold at reactor scale, though rotation-velocity scaling leaves a narrow accessible window. For HZRPC, a multiplicative efficiency structure with three independent ceilings is shown to constrain net conversion below practical thresholds under tokamak conditions. The DEC survey establishes that existing electrostatic, travelling-wave, and inductive schemes occupy the geometrically favourable open-field-line limit, clarifying why they succeed where toroidal inductive extraction does not. A near-term experimental hierarchy is proposed to test each mechanism's dominant uncertainty. The analysis positions direct extraction not as a single feasible route but as a structured landscape in which feasibility depends sharply on geometric access.

title: Detecting Accounting Fraud through Email Data: Evidence from the Enron Corpus
affiliations: Neu-Ulm University of Applied Sciences and University of Giessen

detail.title: Detecting Accounting Fraud through Email Data: Evidence from the Enron Corpus
detail.abstract: This study examines the potential of data-driven methods for detecting accounting fraud using large-scale email data. Using the Enron corpus, a publicly available dataset of corporate email communication during the major accounting scandal, we analyze whether systematic patterns in email behavior can be used to identify senior management individuals involved in fraudulent activities. We construct a set of variables capturing textual sentiment, network characteristics, and communication timing. These features are incorporated into a first-stage logit model that estimates the probability that an individual email originates from a fraud-related actor. Building on these estimates, we implement a second-stage logit model that aggregates email-level signals to classify employees as fraudsters or non-fraudsters. The empirical results reveal strong predictive performance. In particular, network-based measures emerge as the most informative predictors, suggesting that individuals involved in fraud occupy distinct structural positions within the organization's communication network. The findings provide insights into how communication behavior differs between fraud-related and non-fraud-related individuals and highlight the potential of email-based monitoring as an early-warning tool in fraud detection.

title: A County Level Composite Equity Index for Medicare Access Disparity Stratification

detail.abstract:
Background. Medicare program integrity faces a persistent county level analytical gap. The Government Accountability Office High Risk Series (GAO 23 106203, April 2023) identifies Medicare program integrity as a high risk area requiring enhanced oversight capabilities. The November 2024 CMS Rural Urban Disparities in Health Care in Medicare Report (produced with the RAND Corporation) documents that Medicare Advantage enrollees in rural areas score below the national average on more than a third of clinical care measures. No prior published framework integrates the access, quality, and equity dimensions at the county level with documented federal database concordance testing.

Methods. This paper introduces the Healthcare Equity Index (HEI), a composite county level scoring methodology integrating three dimensions (access at 30 percent, quality at 30 percent, equity at 40 percent). The analysis covers 29,538,265 Medicare fee for service beneficiaries across all 3,198 U.S. counties for the 2019 to 2022 data window, producing 12,785 county year observations. Six federal data sources are integrated: CMS Medicare Geographic Variation Public Use File, HRSA HPSA Primary Care and Mental Health designation databases, Area Health Resources Files, USDA Rural Urban Continuum Codes 2023, and U.S. Census American Community Survey 5 year estimates.

Results. The methodology identifies 255 high risk counties (8.0 percent of the universe) affecting 2,484,783 underserved beneficiaries with directly observed annual excess Medicare spending of 2.75 billion dollars under a peer benchmark method and 6.63 billion dollars under a state median peer baseline method. Counterfactual scenario decomposition under documented equalization assumptions ranges from 20.8 to 36.7 billion dollars annually. Validation: HRSA HPSA Primary Care concordance 98.4 percent (251 of 255), Mental Health concordance 96.9 percent (247 of 255). Bootstrap resampling (1,000 iterations) yields 95 percent confidence intervals of [233, 277] for flagged count and [1.42, 4.42] billion dollars for sample excess. Spatial Spearman rank correlation rho equals 0.94 for adjacent years and 0.88 across the full 2019 to 2022 span.

Contribution. The paper makes the methodology, the code, the persisted result files, and the reproducibility envelope (SHA 256 hashes for all source files) publicly available for independent verification. The framework is generalizable to other federal program integrity domains.

title: Regime-Preserving Bootstrap for FX Fair-Value Models

detail.title: Regime-Preserving Bootstrap for FX Fair-Value Models
detail.abstract:
This paper documents a regime-preserving bootstrap procedure for validating the out-ofsample robustness of FX fair-value strategies (BEER, FEER, PPP). The central idea is that standard bootstrap methods (IID, Moving Block, Stationary Block) destroy the economic regime structure of macro-FX data and thereby systematically bias Sharpe ratio inference. We propose two regime-aware resamplers-Regime-Uniform (block resampling within macroregimes) and Regime-Markov (block resampling with calibrated Markov transition matrix)and validate them using five structure metrics, a Sharpe loss metric, an arrangement distance, a stationarity gate per Section 11.7, and Wilcoxon paired tests with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR. 
Applied to a BEER pricer for three currency pairs (EURUSD, GBPUSD, USDJPY) with B = 1999 bootstrap replicates, the key finding is: Regime-Markov reduces the bootstrap Sharpe loss by a factor of 1.3× compared to Regime-Uniform (the simpler block resampler without transition structure) and by a factor of 4.6× compared to the naive IID benchmark. The Markov transition structure provides the additional gain over pure block resampling. The calibrated transition matrix passes the Section 11.7 stationarity gate (TV drift = 0.10), validating forward projections over short horizons of ∼3-5 Markov steps. We document the complete metric definitions, the implementation, and the honest limits of cross-pair generalization.

title: Warping the Glass: Measurement Integrity in Measurement-based Monetary Systems

detail.title: Warping the Glass: Measurement Integrity in Measurement-based Monetary Systems
detail.abstract: A measurement-based monetary system replaces chosen policy rates (committees) with measured ones (sensors): credit intensities read from markets, money valued by measured backing, triggers fired by observed stress. This removes the committee as a capture target and creates a new one — when the policy variable is a measurement, corruption migrates to the measuring layer. The attacker no longer debases the coin or lobbies the committee; it warps the glass. We analyse the full measurement stack of such a system layer by layer and derive the calibration each layer needs to make warping unprofitable. Three results organise the paper. First, for stake-weighted-median oracles we derive the manipulation frontier in closed form and show implementable slashing requires a depth rule: the value the oracle may reprice per detection window must be capped relative to bonded stake (at our calibration, roughly 7%) — a leverage limit on the measurement itself. Second, for the social layer (registrars attesting real-asset backing) the same structure reappears: honesty requires collateral >= attested value / audit probability, which makes single-registrar attestation unscalable and yields a quorum rule under which safe attested value grows approximately quadratically in the attestation quorum. Third, local no-profit calibrations do not compose: we exhibit a mixed attack — an in-band oracle bias inflating the value of fraudulently attested collateral — whose cross-term is priced by neither layer's defense. Composition is restored by an end-to-end audit: a sequential (CUSUM) monitor of the divergence between system prices and an independent instrument bounds total distortion regardless of source. Calibrated on a real 14-year, 7-country panel of credit intensities against sovereign CDS (per-country correlations 0.989–0.998), the monitor detects a 25-basis- point warp at the first observation and caps the optimal slow attack at roughly 10 bp-years of repriceable notional. The residual trust assumption is identified exactly: at least one audit instrument must remain beyond the attacker's reach.

title: Thorin Positivity, GGC Factorization and the Riemann Xi Function
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Thorin Positivity, GGC Factorization and the Riemann Xi Function
detail.abstract: We assemble a single probabilistic framework for the Riemann Hypothesis (RH) organised around one principle: RH is the positivity of a Thorin measure. We show that the reciprocal completed zeta ratio ξ(σ)/ξ(σ + s) is, for σ > 1, the Laplace transform of an infinitely divisible (ID) law; that the associated Thorin density ν σ is unconditionally nonnegative for σ > 1; and that RH is equivalent to the chain U σ ≥ 0 ⇐⇒ ν σ completely monotone ⇐⇒ F σ Stieltjes/Pick ⇐⇒ λ n ≥ 0 (Li), with pointwise positivity ν σ ≥ 0 a necessary condition whose exact strength we determine via Landau's oscillation theorem. We give an explicit-formula representation of the Thorin density and the trigonometric-moment identity λ n = 2 τ >0 (1-cos nθ(τ)). We analyse Kristiansen's signed mixing measure, prove that elementary regroupings cannot repair its sign, and promote the resulting unconditional quasi-infinitely-divisible (QID) quotient factorisation to a central theorem. We then design, in full implementable detail, a numerical protocol to test hyperbolic complete monotonicity (HCM) of the mixing densities, and prove that the slice densities, being truncation-type and discontinuous, can never be HCM, relocating the GGC-upgrade question from the mixing densities (settled negatively) to the component laws. We make concrete progress on the open problems: a Landau-type detection theorem showing pointwise positivity forces every extremal zero onto the line, with the explicit first-negativity bound ν 1/2 (π/2aγ 1) < 0 for an off-line first zero; the equivalence of Gaussian-family Weil positivity with pointwise Thorin positivity; the existence and uniqueness, under RH, of a Krein string with closed-form Weyl function m(s) = (ξ ′ /ξ)(1 2 + √ s)/(2 √ s) and Weyl-matched potential q(x) = 16π 2 e 4x ; a determinantal-pushforward conjecture for the Thorin point process; and, for the GGC questions, two theorems that settle the ends of the truncated-Gamma problem: the centred truncated Gamma is itself a GGC for every truncation level, with explicit Laplace transform, while its logarithm fails infinite divisibility below a positive phase boundary, by a uniformlimit argument; a one-line absolute-monotonicity criterion governs the regime in between. We close with the wider equivalence network (Hermite-Biehler/de Branges, Nyman-Beurling-Báez-Duarte, Weil positivity, the Pólya-Jensen/PF ladder) and a Minimal Positivity Lemma in both original and quotient form.

detail.abstract: Social media has become an essential element of today's youth's everyday life due to the quick growth of information and communication technology. Platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, YouTube, Twitter, and TikTok are dramatically influencing the younger generation's mental processes, identity development, social interactions, and consumer behaviour. Four important communication and psychology theories Uses and Gratification Theory, Social Comparison Theory, Media Dependency Theory, and Social Cognitive Theory are used in this study to analyse how social media affects young people. The study employs a descriptive-analytical research methodology based on secondary data, involving a review of national and international academic journal articles, books, and standard reports. The results indicate that social media plays a positive role in knowledge acquisition, creative expression, digital literacy, and the expansion of socioeconomic opportunities; at the same time, excessive and uncontrolled use is associated with mental stress, sleep problems, feelings of inferiority arising from social comparison, lack of focus, and reduced academic productivity. The study also clarifies that the direction and intensity of the impact depend on the purpose of usage, the duration, and individual psychological factors. Finally, suggestions at the policy, educational, and institutional levels for responsible and balanced social media use are presented, providing a foundation for future empirical research.

title: The Price of Productivity: Deriving Urban Agglomeration Economies through Land Valuations
affiliations: The University of Sydney and The University of Sydney

detail.title: The Price of Productivity: Deriving Urban Agglomeration Economies through Land Valuations
detail.abstract: Agglomeration economies exert a centripetal pull on the urban economy, offering firms productivity gains through spatial proximity. Transport investments are expected to enhance these gains, conventionally captured in Cost-Benefit Analysis (CBA) as Wider Economic Benefits (WEBs). This paper structurally derives agglomeration elasticities for Greater Sydney using a novel panel of statutory land valuations and wage data. We find that economy-wide elasticities are relatively low; auto accessibility (0.026) yields higher aggregate productivity returns than transit (0.004). Stratifying by land-use reveals substantial spatial heterogeneity. Regional and strategic centres exhibit the strongest capacity to absorb agglomeration benefits, whereas gains within the central business district appear exhausted. Increased auto access yields negative elasticities in industrial zones, as passenger traffic induces costly operational frictions. These findings suggest current CBA elasticities may be overstated. Productivity-focused investment should target regional hubs, protect industrial areas, and avoid default central business district expansion.

title: Cryptocurrencies: The Network vs. The Chain

detail.title: Cryptocurrencies: The Network vs. The Chain
detail.abstract: This paper studies whether fast-settlement payment layers can replace secure baselayer blockchains in a search-theoretic monetary model. The Chain provides secure but costly and probabilistic settlement, while the Network provides instant, cost-free payments but exposes users to cyberattacks and requires sellers to incur adoption costs. In the Chain-only benchmark, buyers choose settlement intensity after bargaining. Because they do not internalize the full trade surplus, settlement intensity is inefficiently low, reducing trade efficiency and weakening the monetary value of tokens. Introducing the Network generates multiple payment equilibria. Under exogenous cyberattack risk, Chain and Network payments may coexist: the Network provides fast settlement and fallback liquidity when Chain settlement fails, while the Chain remains valuable for its security and universal acceptance. If cyberattack risk is sufficiently low, pure Network payments can arise, although pure Chain payments may also persist because Network acceptance is costly for sellers. When cyberattack risk is endogenous, broader Network adoption increases exposed balances and strengthens hackers' incentives. This security externality weakens the Network's value as fallback liquidity and eliminates the pure Network-payment equilibrium. The Chain, therefore, survives as a secure settlement anchor. The welfare analysis shows that Network adoption is not always welfare-improving: its paymentefficiency gains must outweigh seller adoption costs and, under endogenous attacks, the resource costs of hacking. Fast-settlement layers can improve payment efficiency, but they do not generically replace secure base-layer settlement.

detail.abstract: European inflation governance assigns price stability to a single institution, a single instrument, and a single analytical framework in which inflation reflects excess demand and unanchored expectations, and in which supply disruptions are treated as transitory disturbances. This paper examines the post-pandemic inflation episode in 28 European countries through an alternative framework, the conflict theory of inflation, which treats rising prices as the outcome of political conflict between capital and labor over the distribution of value added. The paper introduces the Non-Accelerating Inflation Rate of Profit (NAIRP), defined as the highest level of unit profit that can be sustained without accelerating inflation, and derives the windfall profit tax rate required to hold realized profit at that level. The NAIRP is the profit-side counterpart of the non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment, with the windfall tax serving as a policy instrument rather than as the object of analysis. To examine these dynamics empirically, the paper decomposes the GDP deflator into profits, wages, and taxes, and traces the contribution of each component to inflationary pressure over the period 2001-2024. Results show that firm profits were the dominant driver of inflation in 12 of 28 countries during 2021-2024, accounting for about 44 percent of cumulative deflator inflation across the 27 countries excluding Türkiye, well above their structural share of roughly 35 to 38 percent of output value, while wage costs predominate in Central and Eastern European economies. This elevated profit share is a structural break from the pre-pandemic period rather than a cyclical fluctuation. Under the NAIRP framework, a windfall profit tax averaging about 46 percent of excess profits, and below 50 percent in most countries, would have held profit at the NAIRP and neutralized the profit-driven component of inflation without monetary tightening. The composition of European inflation and the set of available policy responses both change when the analytical framework changes, which supports the case for pluralism in the knowledge base of EU economic governance.

detail.title: A Nutrient Recommendation System for Soil Fertilization based on Evolutionary Computation
detail.abstract: This paper presents a machine learning-based Nutrient Recommendation System for soil fertilization aimed at improving crop yield and maintaining soil fertility. The system analyzes soil parameters such as Nitrogen (N), Phosphorus (P), Potassium (K), pH, temperature, and humidity to recommend the most suitable fertilizer type for specific crops. Multiple supervised learning algorithms-K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Random Forest (RF), Artificial Neural Network (ANN), and Support Vector Machine (SVM)-were implemented and compared to identify the most accurate model. Among these, the KNN algorithm achieved the highest accuracy of approximately 90%, demonstrating superior performance for small to medium-sized agricultural datasets. The proposed model offers a cost-effective and easily deployable solution for precision agriculture, enabling farmers to make data-driven decisions, minimize fertilizer wastage, and enhance soil health and crop productivity.

detail.abstract:
Biosecurity is often framed as an individual responsibility, but collective approaches to managing shared disease risk across a territory provide an alternative paradigm. This study engaged 16 farmers and six other actors from the French poultry sector in a longitudinal case study to investigate the potential for communities sharing disease risks to take a collective approach to improving biosecurity. 

Semi-structured individual interviews identified shared epidemiological links between participants, used as the basis for two communities in the Southwest and Greater West regions of France. Facilitated workshops allowed us to investigate the extent to which epidemiologically defined communities could constitute a community of practice, and their potential for taking collective action.

We developed three themes through a reflexive thematic analysis of farmer perspectives – shared links and mutual dependencies within communities, community narratives around farmers’ lived experiences of disease epidemics, and framing of responsibility for collective biosecurity. 

The workshops facilitated a recognition of hidden disease risks between farmers from different production sectors, broadening farmers’ sense of engagement within the community. Analysis of community narratives and framings showed that farmers felt they had a limited degree of agency to control infectious diseases or to enact collective action, framing this as the responsibility of centralised actors such as government and producer organisations. The findings suggest the importance of facilitated dialogue to foster a sense of community related to disease management and highlight the need for innovative mechanisms to provide support for local solutions identified by farmers within existing institutional frameworks.

title: How to Detect and Measure the AI Dangers to Democracy
affiliations: Université Libre de Bruxelles and Yale University - Digital Ethics Center

detail.title: How to Detect and Measure the AI Dangers to Democracy
detail.abstract: Research on artificial intelligence and democracy has grown quickly over the last decade. A shared conclusion in this literature is that AI does not create new democratic problems so much as it makes old ones worse. We now see this across information ecosystems, in elections, and in public administration. However, despite growing evidence, we lack a clear way to prioritize risks in this area, compare them across domains, and identify where democratic control is most likely to break down. So, our problem is: How can we systematize the problems that AI systems pose to democratic processes? This paper argues that principal-agent theory may fit the task. In many phases of democratic systems, principals delegate key functions to AI systems and their providers without really being able to monitor how these systems operate or the outputs they produce. Treating AI as a delegation problem helps identify accountability gaps and other governance failures. Most importantly, as we shall illustrate, it provides metrics for empirical assessments of AI impact on democracy. As a second analytical element, we draw on the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (NIST 2023) and its seven characteristics of trustworthy AI, which supply substantive criteria for evaluating delegated tasks: the principal-agent perspective identifies where democratic delegation is most exposed, while the trustworthiness criteria specify what principals should assess when agents act on their behalf. Operationalized across the three domains through measurable indicators and domain-specific trustworthiness criteria, we propose an analytical framework that centers on institutional assessability as the central condition for democratic control over AI. However, we stress that how severe a harm is, and how much risk is acceptable, are evaluative judgments that current methodologies neither acknowledge nor operationalize. This becomes acute when such evaluative judgments are (silently) delegated to private vendors. We identify this as a strong limitation left for future work.

title: Does Environmental Performance Reduce Corporate Borrowing Costs? Evidence from Japan

detail.title: Does Environmental Performance Reduce Corporate Borrowing Costs? Evidence from Japan
detail.abstract: As environmental sustainability becomes increasingly important in financial markets, understanding its influence on corporate financing costs has attracted growing attention. This study examines the relationship between environmental performance and corporate bond pricing in Japan over the period 2010-2023. Using panel-data estimation techniques, the findings reveal a significant negative association between environmental performance and corporate bond yields, indicating that firms with stronger environmental practices benefit from lower borrowing costs. The results suggest that bond investors incorporate environmental considerations into credit risk assessments and reward firms with effective environmental risk management. In addition, larger and more profitable firms tend to face lower financing costs, whereas highly leveraged firms incur higher borrowing costs. This study contributes to the sustainable finance literature by providing evidence from Japan and highlighting the role of environmental performance as an important determinant of debt financing costs.

Across 16 independent walk-forward retraining windows (2010-2025), the training optimizer selects varied configurations (median w_pyth=0.57, range 0.50-1.00)-evidence that the objective surface is so flat that training noise determines which configuration minimizes each window's MAE. Despite this variation, the fixed champion configuration outperforms window-specific optimization out-of-sample in 12 of 16 trials, by an average of 0.012 wins, consistent with the interpretation that fine-tuning on a flat surface adds noise rather than signal. Using publicly available play-by-play data from 26 seasons (2000-2025), we find that a weighted blend of Pythagorean win expectation (~75%) and raw point differential (~25%), combined with regression toward the league mean, outperforms both naive baselines and more complex multi-factor composites and does so consistently. WARPS beats the Pythagorean baseline in 25 of 26 seasons (96%), including 4 of 4 held-out validation seasons (2022-2025). The improvement is statistically significant (Diebold-Mariano p < 0.0001). A 2D parameter heatmap shows 100% of tested configurations fall within 0.05 wins of the optimum-a completely flat basin. The fixed champion outperforming window-specific optimization by 0.012 wins confirms that identifying any reasonable parameter region substantially dominates coefficient fine-tuning. 
Equally important is what did not improve forecasts: EPA per play, success rate, explosive play rate, and turnover differential-the standard toolkit of modern NFL analytics-each received zero weight in the representative champion configuration once Pythagorean expectation and point differential were included. Strength-of-schedule adjustment, era-aware regime shift, and garbage-time filtering each produced null results. The central finding is not that WARPS found a better set of weights. It is that a simple points-based relationship is persistent, stable, and resistant to improvement from the enhancements tested here. 
Against Vegas preseason lines, WARPS has a higher MAE (2.216 Vegas vs 2.364 WARPS over the 2015-2025 overlap), confirming the market incorporates information not present in statistical models. All data and code are open source and reproducible.

detail.title: Inflation Surprise Pricing of Tail Risk: Era-Conditionality Across Monetary Policy Regimes
detail.abstract: We examine whether the price of inflation surprise risk in equity tail risk premia is stable across monetary policy regimes. Using the 25 Fama-French size-value portfolios, we construct Cornish-Fisher CVaR (CF-CVaR) as a portfolio-level tail risk characteristic and interact it with AR(1)-based CPI surprises in a Fama-MacBeth cross-sectional framework. Pooled across the full sample, the interaction carries no statistically significant price of risk, consistent with opposing-sign effects across monetary eras that cancel in aggregation. Conditioning on Bear-regime months partitioned at the zero lower bound boundary, we document a sharp sign reversal: the interaction coefficient is positive and significant in Bear-regime months before 2013 (λ3 = +0.0623, t = 3.24, p = 0.009) and negative in Bear-regime months after 2013 (λ3 =-0.0464, t =-1.84, p = 0.076). A Chow test confirms a structural break at the era boundary (F (1, 40) = 10.12, p = 0.003). The sign reversal is consistent across four subsample splits and robust to Newey-West HAC standard errors. A two-stage least squares specification confirms that FM-OLS is correctly specified (Hausman p = 0.674; first-stage F = 25.88). We interpret these findings as evidence that the channel through which inflation surprises interact with tail risk pricing depends on the monetary policy transmission environment.

detail.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is transforming the way people work by increasing productivity and changing workflows. Yet, little is known about the optimal way to use it in order to balance both productivity and the psychological experience of work (i.e., control, responsibility, and creativity). We examined different strategies, which we call GenAI collaboration strategies, and their associated productivity benefits and psychological costs. In two pre-registered experiments, we examined two common uses of GenAI, using it to draft versus edit. First, using GenAI, relative to not using it, improved productivity but degraded control, responsibility, and creativity. Second, we identified the optimal GenAI collaboration strategy: using GenAI to edit. Productivity was similar between collaboration strategies, but using GenAI to draft further hurt people's psychological experience of work. Yet, the majority of people chose the suboptimal strategy, including a sample of teachers creating lesson plans for a class. GenAI is a powerful tool to increase productivity, but it is not without costs. Thus, it is not enough for organizations to provide employees with GenAI; how people use GenAI has implications for their psychology.

However, criticism and calls for continued work into its foundations and defining conditions continue to emerge. The paper offers an integrated approach to conceptualise and theorise about innovation ecosystems, while offering resolutions to issues of stability and change, process and history, multileveled and multidimensional phenomena and an understanding of time and space.

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence as a Driver of Digital Transformation in Global Business
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a fundamental driver of digital transformation in global business, reshaping how organizations operate, compete, and create value in increasingly dynamic markets. The rapid growth of digital technologies, big data, cloud computing, and advanced analytics has accelerated the adoption of AI-powered solutions across various business functions. Through technologies such as machine learning, natural language processing, computer vision, and intelligent automation, AI enables organizations to enhance operational efficiency, improve decision-making processes, optimize resource allocation, and deliver personalized customer experiences. Businesses across industries are leveraging AI to automate routine tasks, predict market trends, manage risks, strengthen supply chain resilience, and support innovation initiatives. Despite these benefits, the integration of AI into business operations presents significant challenges, including data privacy concerns, cybersecurity risks, algorithmic bias, workforce displacement, and regulatory compliance issues. This study examines the role of artificial intelligence as a catalyst for digital transformation in global business, exploring its applications, benefits, challenges, and strategic implications. The analysis highlights how AI-driven technologies are transforming organizational structures, business models, and competitive strategies while creating new opportunities for growth and innovation. The study concludes that AI is no longer merely a technological tool but a strategic asset that is redefining business performance and long-term competitiveness. Effective governance, ethical implementation, and continuous workforce development are essential for maximizing the benefits of AI-driven digital transformation in the evolving global business environment.

title: When Structure Decides: A Force-diagnostic Reading of Organisational Failure under Pressure

detail.title: When Structure Decides: A Force-diagnostic Reading of Organisational Failure under Pressure
detail.abstract: Behavioral interventions in organizations consistently fail to produce durable change under conditions of sustained pressure. This paper argues that the underlying cause is not motivational or cultural but structural: organizations are governed, under load, by four force laws — the Structural Load Vector™, Energetic Tension™, Archetypal Momentum™, and the Environmental Field™ — that shape behavior independently of intention, communication, or leadership style. Drawing on Kampf Alignment Physics® (KAP), a structural framework for diagnosing and redirecting human systems under pressure, the paper applies force-diagnostic analysis to four documented cases from 2023–2025: the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank (2023), the Boeing 737 MAX 9 door plug blowout (2024), the NHS England structural reorganization (2023–2025), and post-merger integration failure as documented in cross-sector empirical evidence from the same period. Each case is read through the lens of one or more dominant laws, with all characterizations of organizational conduct grounded in the findings of primary regulatory and investigation reports. Cross-case analysis identifies four convergent force patterns and practical intervention points. Implications are drawn for executive education, governance design, and leadership development curricula.
