detail.abstract: The Riemann Hypothesis asserts that all non-trivial zeroes of the zeta function ζ(s) lie on the critical line Re(s) = 1 2. While traditional approaches rely heavily on arithmetic and algebraic number theory, this paper introduces a complementary topological and geometric framework. We model the distribution of numbers as an unclosed, open-ended three-dimensional helical spiral wrapping around a static, unbending control axis governed by a primary residue node (3 mod 9). By evaluating the binary doubling orbit under the map T : Z 9 → Z 9 , T (x) = 2x (mod 9), we isolate a deterministic, selfcancelling material manifold M = {1, 2, 4, 8, 7, 5} whose unit-vector sum vanishes identically on the complex unit circle: k∈M e i2πk/9 = 0 (the Net-Zero Theorem). We propose that the critical line Re(s) = 1 2 represents the absolute geometric mirror axis of a self-inverting toroidal vortex, and that non-trivial zeroes manifest as nodes of destructive wave interference while prime numbers emerge as discrete nonresonant vertices sustaining infinite helical expansion without structural drift. We state this formally as a conjecture and delineate the open operatortheoretic steps required to elevate the framework to a complete proof.

title: Multi-Product Pricing under Rational Inattention: Evidence, Estimation, and Field Deployment from Airline Ancillaries
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS) - Institute of Operations Research and Analytics, , Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) - Antai College of Economics and Management, Xi'an Jiaotong University (XJTU) and NUS Business School - Department of Decision Sciences

detail.title: Multi-Product Pricing under Rational Inattention: Evidence, Estimation, and Field Deployment from Airline Ancillaries
detail.abstract: We study the joint pricing of close substitutes when customer attention is unevenly distributed across products and data on any single (product, context) cell are too thin for fully separate demand estimation. Airline ancillaries, product-line variants, subscription tiers, and hotel room categories all share this structure. The standard multinomial-logit benchmark imposes homogeneous substitution and therefore cannot represent the product-level asymmetries observed in such markets. We develop a generalized rational-inattention demand model with product-specific attention weights. The seller's revenue problem is convex in the induced purchase probabilities and admits a semi-closed-form solution: each product's optimal price decomposes into its effective cost, a product-specific attention markup, and a common demand term that depends on the segment only through a single scalar, the aggregate purchase probability. Pricing therefore reduces to a one-dimensional root search regardless of assortment size. Calibration reduces to a linear program over the KKT residuals of the consumer's problem, with a finite-sample error bound governed by the ℓ 1minimum gain of the design matrix. When per-segment data are sparse, we pool neighboring segments and replace segment-specific intercepts with a linear function of observable features. The total parameter error decomposes into statistical error, merging bias, and approximation bias; the corresponding bias-variance trade-off is operationalized in deployment by a split-sample cross-validation procedure for configuration selection. A revenue-loss bound quadratic in the ℓ 1 parameter error links sample size to revenue and motivates three pricing rules of increasing data appetite: a segment-based rule, a feature-based rule, and a propensity-based rule (deployed as the PCP arm). We evaluate the framework in collaboration with a low-cost airline. Across five checked-baggage tiers, the cheapest weight tier (20 kg) is nearly two orders of magnitude (≈ 80×) more price-sensitive than the highest (40 kg), and cross-tier substitution is small relative to own-price response; both patterns are inconsistent with homogeneous substitution. In a randomized field deployment over 48 origin-destination pairs, the segment-based and feature-based rules each raise baggage revenue by 7-8% (𝑝 < 0.01) relative to uniform pricing, and their posted-price distribution first-order stochastically dominates that of the carrier's incumbent rule: average posted prices fall while revenue rises.

title: E-Waste Reverse Supply Chain with Retail-Based Collection Service
affiliations: University of Kentucky - Gatton College of Business and Economics and Gatton College of Business & Economics

detail.title: E-Waste Reverse Supply Chain with Retail-Based Collection Service
detail.abstract: We study a reverse supply chain in which a retailer serves as a collector for old electronics and offers both a trade-in program for functional used products and a recycling program for end-of-life e-waste. Old electronics owners face heterogeneous disposal hassle costs and choose whether to use the collector's programs, sell functional used products through alternative venues, or retain their used products or e-waste. We characterize the collector's optimal payment strategy, considering owners' choices. The collector induces one of two distinct payment regimes depending on the value from e-waste. When the value from e-waste is high, the collector adopts an efficient payment strategy under which all participating owners recycle e-waste through the collector. When the value from e-waste is low, the collector adopts an inefficient payment strategy under which some owners sell functional used products but retain e-waste. The two regimes differ in the collector's strategic priorities and in the roles played by trade-in and recycling payments. We further identify a substitution effect between channel convenience and monetary incentives: while both are important for owner participation, the profit-maximizing collector may strategically reduce payments when the collector channel becomes more convenient. As a result, improving channel convenience can counterintuitively lower the e-waste collection rate, whereas increasing e-waste value consistently improves collection outcomes. These insights remain robust when introducing an e-waste processor with pricing power and when owners are heterogeneous in their awareness of the recycling program. These findings provide managerial and policy insights for retail-based collection systems for small electronics.

title: A Study on Public Safety and Policing in Europe

detail.title: A Study on Public Safety and Policing in Europe
detail.abstract: Western European states combine high incomes and substantial policing budgets with conspicuously high levels of recorded property and street crime, while several less affluent Central and Eastern European and small states record markedly less. This study asks whether the cross-national and within-national structure of European property crime is better explained by criminal-justice certainty-the probability that an offence results in an identified offender and a sanction-than by police capacity (officers per capita) or economic development. Building on the economic model of crime and on the criminological evidence that the certainty of punishment deters more reliably than its severity, we specify an expected-cost model of offending in which the apprehension probability is produced by guardianship and detection capacity subject to institutional constraints. We test the model on a panel of thirty European jurisdictions observed annually between 2008 and 2024, using harmonised Eurostat data on police-recorded theft, robbery and burglary, police personnel, and suspected and convicted persons. Three results are robust. First, across countries, recorded theft rises with income (an estimated elasticity of about +0.9), contradicting the premise that affluence or policing budgets purchase safety. Second, within countries, police strength carries a positive, not a protective, coefficient, consistent with reverse causation, whereas measures of apprehension and sanction certainty are negatively and significantly associated with theft and robbery and survive lagging, sample restriction and firstdifferencing. Third, the certainty effect is concentrated in exactly the high-frequency street offences-theft and robbery-that dominate visitors' and residents' victimisation risk. We interpret these findings through the guardianship channel, locate the surveillance-privacy tradeoff within the apprehension-production function, and argue that marginal investment in certainty dominates marginal investment in headcount or in sentence severity.

title: The Economics of ESG: Norms, Disclosure, and the Political Economy of Climate Risk Regulation

detail.title: The Economics of ESG: Norms, Disclosure, and the Political Economy of Climate Risk Regulation
detail.abstract: I examine the economics of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) criteria through four interconnected lenses: the emergence of ESG as a normative framework and its intellectual genealogy from corporate governance to GRC (governance, risk management, and compliance) to IFRS accounting standards; the economic functions and limits of disclosure regulation; the empirical relationship between ESG performance and financial performance; and the comparative political economy of ESG regulation across five jurisdictions, with particular attention to the recent reversal of U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) climate disclosure rules. Drawing on stakeholder theory, signaling theory, and the economics of information, I argue that ESG occupies an ambiguous space between value-relevant information and value-driven preference. A formal model demonstrates that mandatory disclosure reduces information asymmetry and lowers the weighted average cost of capital, but only when disclosure is credible and comparable. A game-theoretic extension shows that the credibility coefficient λ depends critically on regulator ideology β R , with anti-disclosure regimes driving enforcement to zero. The SEC's March 2024 climate rules-requiring Scope 1 and 2 emissions reporting for large accelerated filers-represented a compromise between financial materiality and stakeholder demands. However, the subsequent stay and rescission under Acting Chair Uyeda and Chair Atkins illustrate the fragility of ESG regulation in the face of political contestation over the purpose of disclosure. Comparative analysis reveals that the United States is an outlier among major economies (European Union, Canada, Japan, Brazil) in its reversal of mandatory climate disclosure. Meta-analytic evidence confirms a positive but modest average effect of ESG performance on financial performance, though causality remains contested and reverse causality is substantial. I conclude that ESG's economic significance depends on whether it evolves from organized hypocrisy toward genuinely normative practice-a transition that hinges on the resolution of fundamental disagreements about materiality, regulatory authority, and the legitimate purposes of the corporation.

title: The Sincerity Test: Executive behavior across the Political Cycles of ESG (1953-2026)

detail.title: The Sincerity Test: Executive behavior across the Political Cycles of ESG (1953-2026)
detail.abstract: Executive engagement with environmental, social, and governance (ESG) issues is frequently treated as a stable strategic orientation. This paper argues instead that it is better understood as conditioned behavior-a response that tracks the intensity of external pressure more closely than any underlying conviction. Combining upper-echelons theory with institutional and legitimacy perspectives, it offers a periodization of the phenomenon across four phases, from the postwar ethics of corporate responsibility to the 2026 regulatory retrenchment in the European Union, and develops the notion of a sincerity test: when institutional pressure recedes, the resulting divergence between firms that persist and firms that retreat or fall silent reveals the motivational frame that drove adoption in the first place. The argument integrates the mainstream business-case literature with critical work on decoupling and symbolic compliance, and outlines implications for longitudinal research and board oversight.

detail.abstract:
The latest method is called Waiting Thread Hijacking (WTH), which hijacks threads in a waiting state and modifies return addresses on the stack to execute code. Unlike the conventional TEH technique, WTH does not require thread suspension or direct context modification, making it less dependent on APIs that are usually monitored by Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) products.

This technical report analyzes WTH in detail, including its underlying mechanics, operational requirements, execution workflow, advantages, limitations, and practical considerations. The technique is placed in the broader context of process injection and thread manipulation and compared to related techniques such as Thread Execution Hijacking, APC Injection, Early Bird APC, PoolParty, and Module Stomping.

The report also touches on defense by pointing out detection opportunities from behavioural telemetry, stack integrity analysis, memory forensics, and threat hunting methods. Mitigation strategies and Purple Team recommendations are also provided to guide detection engineering and adversary emulation activities. The findings reveal WTH is an advancement in process injection tradecraft that uses legitimate OS behaviour to decrease traditional detection indicators. For offensive security practitioners and defenders alike hoping to improve modern endpoint detection and response capabilities, knowing what it can and can’t do is important.

title: Trustworthy AI in Central Banking: International Practices and Financial Stability Risks
affiliations: School of Finance, Renmin University of China

detail.title: Trustworthy AI in Central Banking: International Practices and Financial Stability Risks
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), and especially recent advances in large language models and foundation models, is becoming relevant to central banking in two distinct ways. It is a tool that can improve macroeconomic analysis, supervisory technology, payment oversight, anti-moneylaundering monitoring, cyber resilience, and financial stability surveillance. It is also a new source of risk that central banks must understand as stewards of monetary and financial stability. This paper reviews emerging international practices in the use of AI by central banks and financial authorities, and connects those practices to the computer science literature on trustworthy AI and AI safety. The central argument is that, for central banks, trustworthiness is not merely a model-level property. It is also a financial stability condition. Model failures, biased decision systems, privacy leakage, prompt injection, data poisoning, third-party concentration, algorithmic herding, and autonomous market responses can become systemic when many financial institutions rely on similar data, similar infrastructures, or similar foundation models. The paper proposes a framework that links trustworthy AI dimensions-robustness, safety, fairness, privacy, explainability, accountability, and human oversight-to core central bank functions. It concludes with a research agenda for central banks focused on model governance, AI-enabled supervision, privacy-preserving data cooperation, stress testing of AI-related shocks, and international coordination.

title: Society 5.0 as an Enabler for Circular City Declarations: A Policy Integration Framework for Japan

detail.title: Society 5.0 as an Enabler for Circular City Declarations: A Policy Integration Framework for Japan
detail.abstract: Japan has emerged as an early and ambitious actor in urban circularity, yet its recent circular city commitments risk remaining declaratory rather than operational. The Universal Circular Cities Declaration proposed to globalize this agenda (Herrador, 2024), and the dedicated declaration designed for Japan on the basis of the European Union's experience (Herrador et al., 2024), both articulate compelling principles while leaving open the central question of implementation: through what institutional and technological infrastructure are such declarations to be enacted at the city scale? This paper argues that Society 5.0-Japan's national vision of a human-centred, data-driven "super-smart" society-supplies precisely the missing operational backbone. Adopting a conceptual, theory-building approach grounded in document analysis of Japanese and European policy texts and structured comparison, the paper develops a four-pillar integration framework linking Society 5.0 to circular city goals: (i) Digital Infrastructure, mobilizing IoT, AI, big data, and digital twins for material-flow monitoring; (ii) Governance Innovation, aligning Society 5.0's cyber-physical coordination with multi-level circular governance; (iii) Stakeholder Engagement, operationalizing the declaration's participatory commitments through human-centric design; and (iv) Metrics and Evaluation, embedding circular-city indicators within data-driven monitoring. The framework is assessed against EU practice and probed for limitations including political will, funding, data privacy, and the digital divide. The analysis offers Japanese national and local governments a concrete pathway from symbolic commitment to measurable circular transition, with transferable relevance for circular-city governance across Asia and beyond.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the effect of New York City's (NYC's) congestion pricing program on emergency medical service (EMS) response times. The program imposes a 24-hour toll on vehicles entering southern Manhattan's congestion relief zone (CRZ) and is intended to reduce traffic congestion while generating revenue. Reduced traffic within the CRZ may enable EMS responders to reach medical incidents more quickly. Using a difference-indifferences identification strategy, I find that EMS response times for incidents occurring within the CRZ decreased by approximately 15 seconds following the introduction of congestion pricing. Heterogeneity analyses show that incidents occurring during the non-peak toll period-primarily nighttime hours-are, on average, 19 seconds faster. These results suggest that overall improvements in response times are driven largely by nighttime conditions, which occur when fewer drivers travel into or through the CRZ for daily activities and necessities.

detail.abstract: Enhancing sustainable development performance requires an assessment of the relative roles of economic sectors in this process. However, comparative empirical evidence regarding the sectoral structure of sustainable development is limited, particularly for Türkiye. Therefore, this study examines the long-run relationship between sectoral structure and sustainable development in Türkiye by focusing on agriculture, industry, construction, and services. The empirical analysis uses annual data for the period 2000-2022 and proceeds in three steps. First, the stationarity properties of the variables are examined using ADF, PP, and Zivot-Andrews unit root tests. The Johansen cointegration test is then applied to determine whether a long-run equilibrium relationship exists among the variables. Finally, long-run coefficients are estimated using the DOLS estimator, while the FMOLS estimator is used as a robustness check. The findings show that all sectoral shares are positively associated with the sustainable development index in the long run. Based on the DOLS results, the services sector has the highest coefficient at 0.882, followed by the agriculture, industry, and construction sectors with coefficients of 0.302, 0.265, and 0.193, respectively. The FMOLS robustness check supports the DOLS long-run estimates. The study contributes to the literature by providing comparative sector-level evidence for Türkiye. It also highlights that sustainable development strategies should not rely on a single sector, but should be designed through balanced and sectorspecific policies that account for sectoral differences.

detail.abstract: How do public training systems respond when a new technology changes expected skill demand? I link 2017-2024 administrative records from local boards under the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act to AI exposure, prior AI-training experience, provider listings, and state funding. After Chat-GPT's launch in 2022, boards serving more AI-exposed workers and with greater prior experience show a 3-percentage-point larger rise in training participation, about 30 additional trainees per 1,000 participants. Training content shifts much less toward AI-related fields. Eligible-provider listings expand, but listed programs do not automatically translate into funded AI training. The access response is larger in state-years with greater formula allotments, and training activity becomes more concentrated in boards with established routines. The findings show that public workforce systems can expand access when resources and delivery experience are in place. Targeted AI retraining, however, depends on whether those systems convert provider availability and fiscal support into funded participation.

title: Does Deep Arbitrage Stabilize or Destabilize Perpetual Futures Markets?

detail.title: Does Deep Arbitrage Stabilize or Destabilize Perpetual Futures Markets?
detail.abstract: A perpetual futures market can be priced efficiently and still run. This paper integrates two findings that pull in opposite directions: (1) deeper arbitrage capacity stabilizes the funding rate and the underlying bubble, and (2) larger positions raise the hazard of auto-deleveraging, the rule confiscating winning positions to close uncollateralized losses. Embedding a global-games run stage in an entry model of arbitrage capacity yields a solvency ceiling: the market limits its own depth. Equilibrium run risk is hump-shaped in lendable supply, and a single elasticity ratio locates where restraining entry raises welfare. A mutualized buffer levy reconciles depth with safety.

title: Household Financial Fragility in India: A Composite Index and a Bayesian Early-Warning LSTM

detail.title: Household Financial Fragility in India: A Composite Index and a Bayesian Early-Warning LSTM
detail.abstract: Household financial fragility-the inability to absorb modest income or expense shocks-is a central determinant of welfare in low-and middle-income economies, yet survey-based measures of it are scarce for Indian households. Using the second wave of the India Human Development Survey (IHDS-II, 2011-12, 𝑁 = 42,152 households), we construct a six-component Financial Fragility Index (FFI) combining debt burden, consumption stress, asset deficit, employment concentration, dependency pressure, and a distress-borrowing flag; components are z-standardised, equally weighted, and quartile-binned into four fragility states. Three classifiers (logistic regression, random forest, isotonic-calibrated LightGBM) predict the binary Fragile/Distressed label from a disjoint non-financial covariate set, with a held-out ROC-AUC of 0.751 / 0.754 / 0.760 respectively and a leave-states-out generalisation AUC of 0.736±0.015. We then extend the cross-sectional baseline into a Bayesian temporal early-warning system (Sect. 4): a macro-anchored monthly trajectory simulator with Poisson-distributed medical, disaster, and crop-failure shocks builds 24-month per-household panels; a two-layer LSTM with Monte-Carlo Dropout forecasts whether the household will cross the high-fragility threshold in the next three months; and a credible-interval decision rule converts the posterior into a Low / Medium / High triage tier. The LSTM attains a 3-month-ahead ROC-AUC of 0.982-beating naive carry-forward, a per-household Kalman filter, and an NGBoost benchmark-and the resulting High tier captures 89% of all stress events at a 97% per-tier purity.

title: What Predicts World Cup Success?

detail.title: What Predicts World Cup Success?
detail.abstract: A popular view in sports economics, associated with Kuper and Szymanski's Soccernomics, holds that a country's wealth and population are key drivers of its success in international football: larger populations provide bigger talent pools, and richer countries can better fund youth development. This paper tests that claim using 63 countries that played at least three FIFA World Cup matches across the eight tournaments from 1994 to 2022. A regression of points-per-game on log population and log GDP per capita (2023) explains only 13.5% of the crosscountry variation. Adding a single variable, a country's total number of FIFA World Cup matches played all-time (a proxy for accumulated footballing infrastructure), raises the explained variation to 52.9%, and in a combined model this variable is the only statistically significant predictor (p < 0.001), while population and GDP per capita become indistinguishable from zero. The results suggest that current economic resources matter far less for World Cup performance than a country's accumulated history at this level.

detail.abstract: Classic theories of commitment financing establish a synergy between making credit lines and taking deposits. We empirically document that private credit lenders are increasingly providing commitment financing to their portfolio companies despite not using deposit financing. The utilization rates and maturities of their credit commitments are comparable to those of banks, and borrowers draw upon them in stressful times. We show that private credit lenders provide this liquidity using a combination of credit lines from banks, uncalled capital commitments, fund advisor support, and fund equity inflows. Although credit lines from banks are ultimately deposit-backed, our findings indicate that private credit lenders are able to substitute, at least in part, alternative funding sources for bank deposit-backed financing.

title: A Non-Hegelian Dialectic of Progressive Adequation: Toward a Methodology of Scholarly Framework Development

detail.title: A Non-Hegelian Dialectic of Progressive Adequation: Toward a Methodology of Scholarly Framework Development
detail.abstract: This paper articulates a dialectical method operative in the development of metatheoretical frameworks, distinguishing it from the Hegelian tradition that has dominated philosophical accounts of dialectic in scholarly discourse. The method is characterized by five move-types (clarification, correction, reduction, addition, integration), a dual-track initiation structure (revelatory and confirmatory), a rhythm of alternating accretion and sculpting phases, and a succession of individually open-ended movements that nonetheless converge onto something. The engine of the dialectic is not negation — as in Hegel — but insufficiency and generative inner pressure; tension is one mechanism among several, not the sole driver of movement. The method is multidimensional, iterative, constructive-developmental in orientation, and keeps first-order commitments outside its structure — making it an uncommitted instrument capable of serving many different intellectual projects. Its emancipatory dimension is structural rather than teleological: multidimensionality itself enacts freedom by opening genuine possibility space that uni-dimensional methods foreclose. A genuinely novel feature is the role of AI as an always-on dialectical partner — a structural condition that makes a qualitatively different mode of dialectical practice possible. The method’s relationship to prior traditions is characterized as transcend-and-include: preserving what is genuinely valid in each tradition while going beyond its limitations. Partial resonances are drawn from Socratic maieutics, Peircean inquiry, Gadamerian hermeneutics, Lakatosian methodology, and Basseches’ dialectical thinking — the closest partial predecessor in structural conception. Thirteen structural departures from Hegel are identified. The paper did not emerge through philosophical reasoning but through reflexive examination of actual practice, and the method has no established lineage — a recurring structural feature of work that originates outside established traditions. The paper is itself an instance of the method it describes.

detail.abstract: Impact evaluation relies on credible counterfactual construction, and propensity score matching has long served as the default tool for this task. Recent criticism, most notably the "propensity score paradox" identified by King and Nielsen (2019), has questioned whether propensity score matching reliably improves covariate balance relative to simpler alternatives. This paper develops and applies a tolerance-based exact matching approach that departs from coarsened exact matching at one specific point: categorical variables are matched exactly, while numerical variables are matched within fixed tolerance bands (typically five to ten percent) rather than fixed-width bins. The approach is combined with the Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) differencein-differences estimator to allow for staggered treatment timing. Using a hypothetical, synthetic dataset constructed to reflect the structure of administrative firm-level data, three matching specifications are compared against propensity score matching. The tolerance-based approach achieves substantially tighter covariate balance (standardized mean differences between 0.00 and 0.08) but retains a smaller matched sample (n=71), while propensity score matching achieves looser balance (0.22-0.28) with a larger sample (n=386). The paper does not claim that one method dominates the other; rather, it argues that the trade-off between balance and sample size should be made explicit and auditable, and that the tolerance-based approach offers a transparent alternative for settings where the propensity score's statistical opacity is a practical concern.

title: Alternating Swap Rights: How Repeated Exercise Can Reduce Deadweight Loss

detail.title: Alternating Swap Rights: How Repeated Exercise Can Reduce Deadweight Loss
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Alternating Swap Right Option (ASRO), a repeated-exercise extension of the Reciprocal Swap Right Option (RSRO). In the ASRO, exercise does not terminate the contract. Instead, exercise reverses the parties’ positions, transfers the exclusive exercise right to the counterparty, and allows the game to continue until maturity. Although repeated exercise is mechanically feasible, backward-induction verification for horizons up to (T \leq 5) shows that equilibrium exercise is concentrated at the penultimate period and occurs at most once. The mechanism works through a credible deterrence effect: early exercise gives the counterparty the next exercise right, making retaliation possible and rendering early exercise unattractive. Under symmetric binomial dynamics, randomized initial allocation of the exercise right preserves ex ante fairness, while the no-exercise threshold remains identical to that of the RSRO, (c^* = 2(T-1)\sigma). Within the verified horizons, the ASRO strictly reduces exercise probability and deadweight loss relative to the RSRO for all (c < c^*). The results suggest that expanding the exercise opportunity set can tighten equilibrium behavior by making exercise self-deterring. A full proof of exercise concentration for arbitrary finite horizons, together with continuous-time and multi-party extensions, remains open.

title: The Shadow Value of Attention: Recommendation Ranking with Inventory Dynamics
affiliations: University of California, Davis - Graduate School of Management and University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill

detail.title: The Shadow Value of Attention: Recommendation Ranking with Inventory Dynamics
detail.abstract: Recommendation engines and inventory systems are typically optimized separately: the former allocate scarce consumer attention to stimulate demand, while the latter manage the operating costs created by that demand. We study recommendation order as a dynamic exposure-allocation problem for an online retailer selling N substitutable products. Demand depends on product demand potential and recommendation position; the firm earns margins, incurs holding and backlog costs, and replenishes inventory at fixed-plus-linear cost. We formulate the problem as a discounted continuous-time Markov decision process whose state space grows exponentially in N. To obtain a tractable policy, we relax the coupled ranking problem into a multi-mode restless-bandit problem with one-copy-per-position constraints. We show that replenishment has a threshold structure, the relaxed single-product problem admits a partition over inventory states, and the relaxation yields a closed-form index for each product-position-inventory state. The index measures the shadow value of assigning recommendation attention by internalizing demand potential, margin, inventory state, backlog cost, replenishment cost, and the incremental attention created by a higher position. The resulting policy converts an exponentially large dynamic program into a scalable assignment rule. In a four-product benchmark solvable by exact dynamic programming, a bootstrapped index closely tracks the optimum, with an average optimality gap of 3%, while reducing weighted-average cost by 92% relative to demand-only ranking and by 94% relative to myopic control. In large-catalog simulations, the index improves on static demand- and margin-based rankings, reducing discounted cost per item by up to 65.6% under stressed demand.

detail.abstract: This article interrogates whether strategic nuclear superiority-defined beyond assured second-strike capability-translates into geopolitical and crisis-bargaining advantages in the India-Pakistan dyad. Engaging with Matthew Kroenig's Superiority-Brinkmanship Synthesis Theory (SBST), this study argues that the South Asian nuclear context presents a structural anomaly that fundamentally challenges SBST's predictive utility outside the great-power framework in which it was developed. Drawing on five crisis episodes from 1998 to 2025-including the landmark Pahalgam-Operation Sindoor crisis of May 2025and employing comparative case analysis, nuclear posture modeling, and a novel Asymmetric Deterrence Index (ADI), this paper advances three original theses. Third, that the 2025 crisis revealed a nuclear silence pattern not captured by existing theory. The article proposes Contextual Deterrence Theory (CDT) as a revised framework calibrated for asymmetric nuclear dyads.

detail.abstract: As generative AI transitions into large-scale commercialization and hyperscale data center construction, the binding constraint on compute expansion has shifted materially from chip supply to power availability. Using daily return data from January 2023 to June 2026 (N=874), this paper employs a DCC-GARCH(1,1) framework to examine the time-varying co-movement between semiconductor assets (SOXX) and energy infrastructure assets (URA-global uranium/nuclear, and XLU-utilities). A two-sample t-test confirms this shift is statistically significant (t=3.395, p<0.001). Individual GARCH(1,1)-t estimates document strong volatility persistence across all three assets (α+β≈0.95-1.00), and sub-period analysis shows that the SOXX-XLU correlation also widened from near-zero (0.006) to 0.139 over the same horizon. These findings document an emerging physical-financial nexus: AI mania is crossing the boundary of the virtual economy to generate measurable volatility co-movement in the physical infrastructure of energy supply. The results carry direct implications for cross-asset allocation, factor model construction, and systemic risk monitoring.

detail.abstract: This study examines the convergence dynamics of provincial-level labor productivity in Turkey over the period 2006-2024. detail.abstract: This paper examines the critical role of cross-cultural leadership and cultural intelligence (CQ) in mitigating friction and fostering inclusive collaboration within global project environments. Utilizing Geert Hofstede’s six-dimensional framework of national culture, this study analyzes how distinct variations in key dimensions—specifically Power Distance, Uncertainty Avoidance, and Individualism versus Collectivism—manifest as communication and operational friction among diverse team members, such as those from the United States, India, Japan, and Brazil. By integrating theoretical frameworks from cross-cultural communication with the actionable leadership principles outlined in Kouzes and Posner’s Exemplary Leadership model, this paper explores practical strategies for global managers. The findings highlight the necessity of cultivating cultural intelligence to navigate misalignments in authority, risk tolerance, and team dynamics. Ultimately, this research provides a strategic roadmap for international project managers seeking to transform cultural diversity from a point of friction into a driver of cohesive, high-performing global team collaboration.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether carbon price uncertainty transmits to stock market volatility in China's high-emission sectors following the launch of the national Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS) in July 2021. Using 1,072 daily observations on China Carbon Allowance (CEA) prices and Shenwan sector indices for electricity, steel, and cement over the period July 2021-December 2025, we document three findings. Second, event-window analysis around annual compliance deadlines reveals time-varying transmission: carbon uncertainty significantly amplifies electricity volatility in the 60-day window preceding the 2023 deadline (delta = 0.0448, p = 0.033) and the 60-day window following the 2024 deadline (delta = 0.0981, p = 0.008). Our results distinguish between a dormant average variance channel and an active tail-risk channel, with implications for climate stress testing and carbon-aware portfolio risk management.

title: Reverse Fiduciary Risk in Nonprofit Governance: A Position Paper

detail.title: Reverse Fiduciary Risk in Nonprofit Governance: A Position Paper
detail.abstract:
Nonprofit governance theory traditionally assumes a one-directional model of fiduciary vulnerability in which organizations must be protected from the potential misconduct or negligence of their directors. This article challenges that assumption by introducing Reverse Fiduciary Risk, a new concept describing the structural vulnerability of fiduciaries in volunteer-dependent nonprofits. In many small organizations, directors and officers perform essential operational, administrative, and managerial work without compensation, reimbursement, or formal recognition. Their unpaid labour becomes the organization’s de facto workforce, creating a form of structural dependence that inverts the conventional fiduciary relationship.

Drawing on governance theory, volunteerism scholarship, and the doctrine of unjust enrichment, the article demonstrates how this dependence exposes fiduciaries to economic, emotional, and reputational harm. It argues that the presumption of gratuitous intent—long used to dismiss claims arising from volunteer labour—fails to account for situations in which fiduciary contributions are essential rather than discretionary. Through an illustrative case study and doctrinal analysis, the article shows how reverse fiduciary risk shapes board dynamics, fuels internal disputes, and may give rise to restitutionary claims when organizations are enriched at the expense of their fiduciaries.

By naming and theorizing reverse fiduciary risk, the article fills a critical gap in nonprofit governance scholarship and offers a framework for more equitable, transparent, and sustainable organizational practices. It calls for governance reforms that acknowledge the economic value of volunteer labour, protect fiduciaries from structural exploitation, and strengthen the long-term health of the nonprofit sector.

detail.title: Can Explainable Artificial Intelligence Restore Applicant Trust? A Research Proposal Examining the Effects of Explainability on Procedural Justice, Organizational Attraction, and Intention to Apply
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being adopted in recruitment and selection processes. Although organizations use AI-enabled hiring systems to improve efficiency and consistency, recent research indicates that applicants often react less favorably to AI-based hiring than to human-based hiring. Prior studies have identified trust and procedural justice as key psychological mechanisms underlying these reactions. However, little research has investigated whether explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) can mitigate applicants' concerns regarding AIenabled hiring decisions. Drawing upon Signaling Theory and Organizational Justice Theory, the present research proposes that explainability enhances trust in AI and procedural justice perceptions, which subsequently improve organizational attraction and intentions to apply. A randomized experimental design comparing human recruiters, AI recruiters without explanations, and explainable AI recruiters is proposed. The study contributes to the growing literature on AI-enabled recruitment by moving beyond documenting negative applicant reactions and examining a theoretically grounded intervention capable of improving applicant perceptions.

title: The Ossification Frontier for Operational Processes

detail.title: The Ossification Frontier for Operational Processes
detail.abstract: This paper studies the ossification decision in recurring operational processes: once flexible execution is available, which parts should be hardened into standardized process capital, which should remain adaptive, and when should that boundary move? Generative AI makes this problem especially salient with the prevalent use of model-mediated execution, but the framework applies more broadly to dynamic standardization problems beyond AI. We formulate a hidden-state dynamic process-design model in which a manager chooses the width of a standardized backbone, preserves scarce specialist capacity for uncovered and failed cases, and can audit to learn whether expansion to standardization is safe. The model features a latent reliability frontier, stochastic failures, failure-induced rework, convex congestion, redesign frictions, and targeted frontier audits. Several results emerge. First, the relevant expansion criterion is queue-adjusted reliability, not raw predictive accuracy. Second, when failures generate su!ciently costly recovery work, higher workload can induce a retreat to the core: the optimal backbone narrows rather than widens to protect specialist capacity. Third, exception-process design is a first-order complement to standardization: reducing recovery burden can expand the safe scope of standardization without improving predictive performance. Fourth, learning is localized at the boundary and depends on environmental durability: routine operation reveals only what is already standardized, so targeted frontier audits are most valuable when codified gains are su!ciently persistent. Under economically interpretable monotonicity conditions, these forces imply a cuto" width within the ranked design space. A numerical study and an empirical design show how the framework can be implemented with enterprise workflow data.

title: The Unified AI Adoption Model: Bridging Individual and Organizational AI Readiness

detail.title: The Unified AI Adoption Model: Bridging Individual and Organizational AI Readiness
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) implementation is often treated as a tool-selection problem, yet research on technology uptake, human-AI interaction, organizational change, and AI risk management suggests that outcomes depend on the relationship among people, workflows, governance, and institutional purpose. This article develops the Unified AI Adoption Model, a dual-level approach that integrates the Personal AI Adoption Framework (PAAF) and the Scalable AI Adoption Framework (SAAF). PAAF guides individuals through seven stages-Familiarize, Learn, Evaluate, Experiment, Protect, Ingrain, and Grow-while SAAF guides organizations through Discover, Fund, Plan, Experiment, Guardrail, Scale, and Govern. The article positions AI uptake as a coordinated learning and governance process rather than a onetime deployment. The analysis draws from technology acceptance theory, diffusion of innovations, AI literacy, cognitive offloading, human-AI collaboration, change management, and current U.S. federal AI guidance. A government-sector scenario involving a state human services agency illustrates how the model can support case-processing assistance while preserving human review, privacy, accessibility, transparency, and public trust. The article concludes with implications for practice and a research agenda for empirically testing AI maturity across individual and organizational levels.

detail.abstract:
Conventional accounts of military technology suggest that advances in precision weapons, real-time intelligence, and modern logistics should compress the duration of armed conflicts by enabling rapid and decisive outcomes. Yet a number of contemporary conflicts have proven remarkably persistent. This paper proposes a theoretical framework, the Bohra Asymmetric Utility Model (BAUM) v1.5, as one possible explanation for this puzzle.

The central proposition is that a conflict may become increasingly costly, and even irrational, for those directly engaged in fighting it while remaining beneficial for actors that supply the inputs sustaining it. BAUM formalizes this possibility through a distinction between Receivers—direct conflict participants who bear the costs of continued warfare—and Providers—actors whose welfare may be positively associated with the continuation of supply relationships linked to the conflict. The framework introduces the concepts of the Poison–Meat Divergence and the No Coordination Assumption, under which conflict persistence may emerge from the aggregation of individually rational incentive structures without requiring coordination, collusion, or conspiracy among Providers.

The paper situates the Receiver–Provider distinction in relation to existing ripeness and spoiler theories and develops a formal conceptual model describing divergent utility trajectories between Receivers and Providers over time. The framework is presented as a theoretical contribution intended to generate testable hypotheses for future research rather than as an empirical explanation of any particular conflict. The paper argues that the Receiver–Provider distinction may offer a useful analytical lens for examining why some conflicts appear to persist beyond points at which they have become increasingly costly for the parties directly engaged in fighting them.

detail.title: Intent-Aligned Evaluation of Clinical Predictive Models: A Phase-Based Methodological Framework
detail.abstract: ObjectivePredictive models in healthcare fail to transition from development into clinical practice impact iwhen their development and evaluation misalign with the model’s intended clinical purpose. A screening model, for example, may be inappropriately evaluated using criteria suited to a treatment recommendation system, given that precision requirements differ. We provide a solution to this misalignment with a methodological framework that aligns evaluation criteria with a predictive model’s declared clinical intent, defined as the clinical purpose and use context of the model, specified at study inception.MethodsWe developed the framework in a phased approach of (1) targeted literature review of reporting guidelines, staged-evaluation frameworks, and implementation science models for predictive models in healthcare; (2) iterative refinement through co-author input from clinical, methodological, and implementation perspectives; and (3) retrospective simulated application of the framework to four predictive models drawn from prior clinical research, comparing standard practice with framework-informed steps.ResultsThe framework specifies five lifecycle phases of a predictive model for clinical application (proof of concept, design and preliminary testing, performance and safety testing, large-scale evaluation, and post-deployment monitoring) and four types of intent (real-time decision support, screening, clinical research, and translation). It includes explicit re-entry rules for retrained or repurposed models, and integrated assessment of prediction heterogeneity, human-AI interaction effects, and system entanglement at specific phases. A four-step operational procedure (intent declaration, phase assignment, selection of phase- and intent-appropriate criteria, and documentation of advancement decisions) supports application during model development. Retrospective application to different predictive models illustrates that the framework produces different implications for action across intent categories and lifecycle stages than a standard non-specific approach would yield.ConclusionThe framework offers a structured methodology for aligning predictive-model evaluation with declared clinical intent, complementing existing frameworks and consensus principles for trustworthy healthcare AI. Prospective application of the framework by independent teams can assess its usability, inter-rater consistency in intent and phase assignment, and effects on downstream evaluation decisions so that the framework can be employed broadly.

detail.abstract: In Europe, how and when a given security and the relevant rights incorporated into it come into existence is mostly left to national law. The creation of debt securities generally implies a contractual relationship between the issuer and the securities holder. As such, all the contractual elements required under the relevant legal system (in particular the necessary presence of a counterparty and the payment of a subscription price) must be in place for the debt securities to exist.  In some instances, issuers may want to retain their own debt securities from the outset  in their treasury, for example to use these securities as collateral to obtain central bank liquidity. Legally, unless there are explicit exemptions or specific regimes, retaining debt securities at issuance generally requires going through an issuance and repurchase process, and results in an issuance settled with a counterparty to bring to existence the debt securities, followed by an immediate repurchase by the issuer from that counterparty. Recent legislative developments in Luxembourg provide an alternative issuance path for the European Stability Mechanism and the European Commission.

detail.abstract:
This Essay examines how late-twentieth-century fiduciary practice at institutional-investor scale did not alter the governing doctrine of prudence but changed what became visible as proof of prudence. Prudence remains a doctrine of fiduciary judgment exercised with loyalty, for the exclusive benefit of beneficiaries, under circumstances then prevailing. Yet institutional fiduciary practice increasingly demonstrates compliance through operational proxies — including diversification, benchmarking, consultant review, delegation, and portfolio theory — that may be relevant evidence of prudence without being substitutes for fiduciary judgment itself.

Using trust-law prudence as a baseline and the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA) as a contemporary application, the Essay examines whether operational demonstrations of compliance continue to make beneficiary-oriented fiduciary judgment visible or instead function as practical substitutes for it. The Essay argues that fiduciary doctrine remains formally intact, but that institutional demonstrations of prudence increasingly rely upon administrable proxies whose relationship to fiduciary judgment is indirect, assumed, or difficult to observe.

The resulting concern is not doctrinal change but doctrinal visibility. If prudence remains a conduct standard, the conduct required by prudence must remain capable of being observed, evaluated, and enforced.

title: Service-Induced Congestion in Memory-Constrained LLM Serving

detail.title: Service-Induced Congestion in Memory-Constrained LLM Serving

publicationDetails.detailsText: Sauder School of Business Working Paper Forthcoming

detail.abstract: In large language model (LLM) serving, each request accumulates persistent graphics processing unit (GPU) memory during service as its key-value cache grows with every generated token. Under high concurrency, aggregate memory usage therefore increases endogenously over time: the service process itself creates future capacity pressure. When memory capacity is exceeded, systems evict active requests, discarding cached state and restarting them later, which wastes computation and reduces throughput. We develop a discrete-time dynamical model of memory-constrained LLM inference that captures admission, memory growth, and eviction under continuous batching. In the saturated-input regime, the system admits both eviction-free fixed points and limit cycles with evictions. For homogeneous workloads, we show that the eviction-free equilibrium is unstable and that, except for a Lebesgue-measure-zero exact-capture set, the system converges to a unique worst-case limit cycle that is asymptotically stable outside this exceptional set, with throughput losses as large as 50%. For heterogeneous workloads, we prove a stability criterion in the two-class common-input setting and explain how the survival-polynomial mechanism generalizes to multiple classes and heterogeneous-input lengths. Under an input-dominated scaling regime, coprime decoding lengths stabilize the eviction-free equilibrium, while non-coprime lengths create synchronized modes that drive instability. These results characterize when workload heterogeneity desynchronizes completions and helps stabilize memory-constrained serving. More broadly, we identify service-induced congestion as a structural instability mechanism and derive scheduling design principles for sustaining high throughput.

detail.abstract: People of all ages and backgrounds regularly use AI companions-virtual friends, lovers, and confidantes powered by artificial intelligence. As a new form of relationship, this development poses novel doctrinal and policy questions for family law. As a doctrinal matter, what does child neglect look like when a parent d elegates caretaking to an AI companion? How should standards for elder neglect adapt to the widespread use of robotic caregivers? Should lawmakers impose mandatory reporting requirements on therapy bots if children share experiences of abuse or neglect? And can people designate an AI companion as a health care proxy? As a policy matter, should the government promote or discourage AI companionship? And how should policymakers approach the technology's potential to further entrench inequality, with well-off families continuing to access human teachers and therapists, and lower-income children, who are disproportionately children of color, having only the AI version of these critical supports? This Essay identifies these questions with the goal of initiating a debate among lawmakers and family law scholars.

title: The Meritocracy Mirage: Aporophobia and the Ideological Justification of Inequality

detail.title: The Meritocracy Mirage: Aporophobia and the Ideological Justification of Inequality
detail.abstract: This paper is a conceptual and historical analysis that synthesises existing literature on meritocracy and aporophobia to explore their ideological interrelation. As introduced and argued here, an important mechanism in the idea of meritocracy is aporophobia, that rejects and blames the poor for their own poverty. Correspondingly, the concept of meritocracy is used to justify structural aporophobia, which systematically constrains equality of opportunities in a way that perpetuates inequalities. Meritocracy justifies aporophobia through the concept of deservingness, effectively working as two sides of the same coin: both poor and wealthy people deserve their situation, as they are responsible for their fate. That is, the meritocratic-aporophobic mindset assumes that the wealthy are wealthy because they worked hard, and that the poor are poor because they didn't. This not only reinforces social stigma but also has structural repercussions for policymaking and the systemic entrenchment of inequalities. Understanding the relationship between aporophobia and meritocracy is essential to comprehend how they operate together to justify inequalities.

detail.abstract: Innovation booms are often fueled by easy financing, allowing new technology firms to pay high wages that attract skilled labor. Studying the information and communication technology (ICT) boom in the late 1990s, we show that high-skill workers who joined the ICT sector during the boom experienced sizeable long-term earnings losses. These earnings patterns stem from accelerated skill obsolescence rather than worker selection or the subsequent bust in the ICT sector. Moreover, during the boom, financing disproportionately flowed to firms whose workers would later experience the largest productivity declines, amplifying the negative effect of labor reallocation on aggregate human capital accumulation.

title: Post-Adoption Incentives for Permanency: A Systematic Review

detail.title: Post-Adoption Incentives for Permanency: A Systematic Review
detail.abstract: Background: As of FY 2024, over 300,000 children are in the United States foster care system. Many of these children have spent years in care, and others reach adulthood without reconnecting with their caregivers or being adopted. To help incentivize new caregivers to adopt children in care and reduce the negative impact of long-term foster care, the federal government will subsidize Post-Adoption Incentives for Permanency (i.e., adoption assistance and adoption tax credits) for prospective adoptive parents.Aims: To assess, and provide a consensus on, all available literature that measures how post-adoption incentive programs affect adoption placement rates, adoption timing, and adoptee’s quality of lives, from an interdisciplinary perspective.Methods: A systematic review of six databases (Academic Search Premier, APA, EBSCO Criminal Justice, ERIC, Scopus, and WOS) was conducted using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Articles were assessed for scientific rigorousness and risk of bias using the Crowe Critical Appraisal Tool (CCAT).Results: A total of 1,078 articles were assessed for relevance to the research questions, and ultimately, 14 published, peer-review articles from 1992-2021 were included in the full text review. Overall, adoption assistance and tax credit programs have seen moderate success in 1) reducing time spent in care, 2) incentivizing new adoptions, and 3) increasing the quality of life for adoptees. However, the benefits of these programs have not been distributed evenly for all children and parents in care. Particularly, children belonging to a marginalized race and children who are older have had greater difficulties in reaching permanency despite additional financial assistance.Conclusions: While adoption assistance and tax credit programs have demonstrated reliable trends in boosting adoption rates, the timing until adoption, and adoptees quality of life, there is a need to address limitations for specific demographic groups. As such, there ought to be, in addition to post-adoption incentives for permanency, additional programs or permanency planning options for youth who face specific and demonstrable barriers to adoption.

detail.title: A REDCap-based methodological framework for audit-ready Good Clinical Practice training in a clinical research institution
detail.abstract: Background: Ensuring audit-ready GCP training that is integrated with institutional workflows remains challenging, particularly with costly and inflexible commercial e-learning platforms.Objective: To develop, implement, and evaluate a REDCap-based GCP training programme, assessing participation, completion, and learning performance across versions aligned with ICH GCP E6(R2) and E6(R3).Methods: A structured, self-directed programme was deployed in REDCap at a large clinical institution. Two consecutive versions (R2 and R3) were evaluated over fixed 65-day periods. Descriptive analyses covered enrolment, completion, certification, and quiz performance. Item-level responses identified knowledge gaps. A voluntary post-course survey was included in R3.Results: Enrolment increased from 75 (R2) to 143 (R3). Certification improved from 64% to 77%. Mean performance in R3 was high (96.1% correct), with one failure. Errors clustered in domains related to trial roles and principal investigator responsibilities. Survey responses (62%) indicated demand for practical, scenario-based content and downloadable materials.Conclusions: REDCap can be effectively repurposed to deliver scalable, audit-ready GCP training with integrated tracking and certification. Local-language delivery enhances accessibility, while item-level analytics support targeted content optimisation.
